item.title: Back To the Electoral College, And Why Getting Rid of It Is a Big Mistake
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: As the dust settled on the 2026 midterm elections, a number of stories were published noting that states now fully under Democratic control include enough electoral votes to make the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact a reality. To review, this is the plan, devised in the aftermath of 2000 presidential election, that would allow an end run around the electoral college. A sufficient number of states agree to award their electoral votes to the winner of the popular vote regardless of how their own voters voted in that particular state. Once a sufficient number of states agree, it’s done. The effect of the electoral college disappears even as its architecture remains.

item.title: This Week in Stupid: November 14 edition
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: As another stupid week comes to a close here in America, let’s look back at the dumbest fucking shit that happened.“A smart man washes his hands after he urinates. A wise man doesn’t urinate on his hands.”Um, Senator Kennedy? I have a question.I really wish more of his colleagues had gone to Oxford with him, because I’m pretty sure the entire MAGAverse has been pissing on its own hands for years.Tuesday: a septum is a terrible thing to waste“…was sentenced at Southwork Crown Court to ten years and six months in prison. One rape conviction. Three sexual assault convictions. He was convicted by the way, with no forensic evidence. No DNA. No police report from the time. Now, decades old, from allegations back from 1999.”Now there’s a good look. Defending the convicted rapist Russell Brand while seemingly having half the gross national product of Bolivia up one’s nostrils.Holy shit, can Don Jr. even feel his face right now? It doesn’t look like it.Do you know why Hunter Biden was able to clean himself up? Because he wanted to, and because he had a loving family willing to get him the help he needed.Cokey’s family is apparently too busy pissing on their own hands to help him deal with his shit.Wednesday: a sense of decency is a terrible thing to waste We can’t see Rick Santorum’s hands in the clip below, but I’ll wager good money that he was pissing all over them while recording it.“Face it, these are temporal issues. Yes, they matter. Of course they matter. You’re upset because prices are high. And I don’t think the president has done a particularly good job of explain why the war in Iran was so essential to fight radical Islam. But the reality is, you know, everybody has to look at what the bigger issues are in the country. And I understand paying a dollar more our two or three dollars more for diesel fuel has an impact on your family. But you have a responsibility to look beyond just comply what affects your pocketbook. And there may be a reason that you have to suffer financially for a higher good.” Can these idiots get any more tone-deaf? This is why your party got slaughtered at the polls, Rick. Voters won’t want to be lectured on how it’s their patriotic duty to shut the fuck up about gas prices.You know what? I hope the GOP keeps right on repeating this noxious nonsense, all the way to the 2028 elections. I hope they continue to be as repellent as possible. Maybe we can end up with zero elected Republicans. You may say I’m a dreamer, but I’m not the only one.Hey, did Rick Santorum and that dog he was seeing ever get married? I hope they’re very happy together.No, seriously, did he? For some reason, Senator Mushmouth really wants to know.Thursday: a mind is a terrible thing to have never had in the first place“Unfortunately, we were all wrong, races can be baught.”Oh my god, can I just say that I AM GOING TO MISS THIS WOMAN. She has been a boon to This Week In Stupid. She’s a one-woman perpetual motion dumbfuck-factory. By voting her out of office and removing her from the public eye, the people of Colorado’s fourth district have really made my job that much harder. And, I hope that wherever Lauren Boebert ends up next, she keeps washing her hands. For many reasons.Friday: the further adventures of Some Fucking Idiot™On Friday, some fucking idiot was missing in action. He had no public appearances, and —shockingly! — only posted three times to his crappy app. But not to worry, his ace team of cabinet-level hand-pissers were way too happy to step into the breach.You’ll never fucking guess what happened on Friday. Oh, and Marky Two-Names, the former failed plumber’s assistant now ostensibly in charge of homeland security was on the case, too. His main concern was that everybody called the plagiarism robot by its proper name.So, what was the fucking idiot doing while all this was going on? Did he go on TV to reassure a nervous nation? Did he say anything at all?All this, while every plane in the nation was stuck on the ground, leaving ONE AND A HALF MILLION air travelers stranded. And because the fucking idiot was missing in action, holed up god knows where in the White House with his beloved Diaper Nurse, not one reporter had the opportunity to stand up and ask, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’How fucking idiotic is that?And now, let’s put a close to This Week in Stupid and reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia.This photo has ‘June 15, 1996’ written on the back of it. I have no idea where it was taken.Here we are at some family event in the 1990s. that’s my uncle Alan and aunt Ellen, and there’s Katie in the background, seated at a table. Ms Spouse sure had style, didn’t she?Have a non-stupid Saturday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future:practice self-care. do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: I’m watching Alaska closely
item.author: 1axbu1qhql2swxa1lge2scp6h8nkgbk7gswfr3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Whoever said everything is bigger in Texas hasn’t been to Alaska. The Last Frontier is bigger than Texas, California and Montana combined.The largest national park in the country is in Alaska. Its name is one of my favorites: Wrangell–St. Elias.But Alaska’s size is more than a point of pride. It also makes voting there remarkably hard. The state’s beautiful but isolated landscape creates complications for voters, and dozens of polling places are in towns without road access.Voting by mail isn’t simple either, as extreme weather can cause days-long delays. In some remote villages, polling places without election workers fail to open at all.Though the networks still haven’t called Alaska’s Senate race, it is clear that Mary Peltola is poised to win and become the 56th member of the Senate Democratic caucus come January.Peltola’s likely victory and its close margin prove two truths. First, every vote matters, and the fight to ensure every vote is counted is essential to democracy. Second, Democrats can win anywhere they have the candidates and resources to compete.Sadly, Alaska’s elections have also been the target of one of Donald Trump’s fiercest attacks, and he is showing no signs of letting up.Less than two weeks before Election Day, Trump’s Department of Justice sued to block Alaska from certifying Peltola as the winner if she defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. My firm, Elias Law Group, intervened on behalf of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to fight back.We won: two days before the election, a federal judge dismissed the case. The DOJ has appealed but seems in a hurry to further litigate their defeat.Then the Trump DOJ launched criminal investigations without being able to confirm that any crime had been committed. In the days before the election, the DOJ leaked that I was among its targets.Trump has targeted me before. He hates me because I fight and win.After the 2020 election, I helped lead the legal effort that defeated him and his allies more than 60 times. My firm just helped Scott Colom unseat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and win Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race. Now we are fighting in Alaska.I have no doubt that Trump’s hatred of me is only growing. I wear his scorn as a badge of honor.But even the best legal work won’t protect democracy from Trump’s lies and smears. That requires pro-democracy platforms and outlets that tell the truth without fear or compromise.Democracy Docket covered the count in Mississippi from start to finish, and now its team is on the ground in Alaska. The team is watching and reporting closely, bringing readers daily updates and insights as the race unfolds.I created Democracy Docket for exactly this kind of moment. While other outlets offer horse-race coverage and both-sides analysis, Democracy Docket covers free and fair elections every day of the year through an uncompromisingly pro-democracy lens.We shine a light on the voting rights fights the national spotlight misses. It breaks down court cases months before Election Day and follows stories years before they reach the front pages of legacy media.After much discussion, Democracy Docket has decided to keep its paywall down, as it has been since Election Day, until the Alaska race is called. This was not an easy decision.But as Trump and the GOP continue to spread lies about this election, the stakes are too high to keep anything behind a paywall.Members keep Democracy Docket’s website and podcasts free for everyone and make it possible to keep the paywall down as the fight for Alaska continues. They also get my written analysis: what’s happening in the courts, what each ruling means for the next election, and where the fight is headed before anyone else is talking about it.If you’ve been reading my analysis since the paywall came down on Election Day, you already know what you’d be missing.If you can’t upgrade right now, I understand. As always, thank you for being a subscriber and reader. But if you do, I would deeply appreciate it.All eyes are on Alaska today, but at Democracy Docket, we will keep our eyes trained on the Last Frontier every day.The battle for free and fair elections does not end when the networks make their call. It lives on as long as we are willing to fight.

item.title: Why Your Shoes Come Untied
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Why do your shoes laces keep untying themselves? It could be because you're out there running all the time, which vibrates your shoes until the knot loosens. Yeah, that's not the case for most of us. It could be because you're tying them wrong. We are supposed to use a reef knot, a term I'd never heard, essentially a square knot with loops for easy untying. Yet some people tie a granny knot, which doesn't hold well at all. There are other knots that people swear by, but you have to have the motivation to learn them. Kids' shoes come untied all the time because they are so active and inattentive, so I used to double tie my kids' shoes or use those plastic clips to keep the knot in place. My feet are small, so I buy shoes from the kids' section because they cost less. My current tennis shoes are tied, then have a velcro strap that closes right over the knot, so no worries. If you need some help keeping your shoes tied, astrophysicist Josie Peters has the science of shoelaces to help you out. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: Hegseth’s ideal soldier? Straight, white, and male.
item.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708979-d186966748@mail180.sea101.rsgsv.net
item.content:encoded: I wish I could say that the Trump administration's lack of professionalism has ceased to amaze me, yet this week’s Veterans Day debacle left me speechless…again. In case you missed it, following a Veterans Day ceremony, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided impeachment by the skin of his teeth the day prior, was reprimanded after his entourage laughed and chatted loudly while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington, Virginia. It’s a sacred monument to honor unidentified soldiers who died in the line of duty. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel yelled. Seeing the Department of Defense’s group looking like rambunctious middle schoolers on a field trip on such hallowed ground is sad, to say the least. But Hegseth’s entire tenure leading the US military has been riddled with controversy. Since taking office, he’s tried to purge women, transgender people, and people of color from the military’s ranks with blatantly discriminatory policies. He used an unprecedented meeting of generals and admirals to “fat-shame” them. His end goal seems to be returning the military to a time when anyone who wasn’t a straight white man was deemed unfit to serve. “Black service members and Black veterans understand that we are either not welcome or we will exist within a permanent hierarchy in which white men are at the top,” Kyle Bibby, co-founder of the nonprofit Black Veterans Project, told host Al Letson. “Particularly straight white men.”, Bibby sits down with Letson to explain what life is like for today’s Black troops and how Hegseth has widened the gap of racial inequities in the military. Listen to it today.

item.title: Scientists Made Monkeys Watch Minions to Study Their Brains
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch . Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.Humans watching monkeys watching MinionsSettling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including , , , , Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, , , , , and “Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film , and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques. Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrificeWhen climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites. The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?Before Play-Doh, there was clay-dohThe fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.The ants are Benjamin-ButtoningWe humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study. “We will show that colonies of not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum. Thanks for reading! See you next week.

item.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header. Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, passing the host but not the full path to the page.

item.title: A Literary Map of the United States
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: There are many ways to read this map: as a peculiar road map of the United States, a potted history of the same, a metatext of American literature, a guide to American literary genres and their centers of gravity, and more. I will get to at least some of them later, but for now, I want to examine the effect that scholars call broadly “imaginative geography,” more precisely “toponymic capture,” and more elegantly “authorial inscription.” It is the process by which a writer’s vision of a place becomes so dominant that it effectively overwrites that place’s prior identity in the public imagination.We could say other parts of America have been “colonized” by other texts the same way King’s horror stories have influenced our perception of Maine. A gentler metaphor, from Rebecca Solnit’s Infinite City, is of cultural and literary memory as an “overlay.” It resides above physical geography like a transparency on an overhead projector, a slightly shifting but persistent presence. In Landmarks, the English nature writer Robert Macfarlane develops the idea that a sufficiently powerful text doesn’t just describe a landscape, but alters the mind that subsequently encounters it. He uses the verb phrase “to see through” to define it: you see the Suffolk coast through W.G. Sebald, the Mississippi through Mark Twain, the South (as a particularly “Gothic” place) through Faulkner.

item.title: Van Hollen Says the Filibuster Should Go
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: As I’ve noted, these leadership challenges don’t mean a lot if they don’t include abolishing the filibuster. This afternoon Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), who just announced what remains a fairly longshot challenge to Chuck Schumer, says he supports getting rid of it.“My personal opinion is that we need democracy in the United States Senate and that means allowing ultimately a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people, so that means 51 votes … My personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic — small “d” — provision. It’s not in our Constitution. It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people.”As you can see he’s framing this as his personal view. But that goes without saying. As I explained, a parliamentary leader isn’t a “decider,” as George W. Bush famously put it. He or she steers where their caucus wants to go. So it’s not a matter of him saying I will do this when I’m leader. But him pretty unequivocally supporting it is a big, big deal.

item.title: Trump’s new QAnon press secretary exposes his desperation
item.content:encoded: Even by first-day-on-the-job standards, Donald Trump‘s new press secretary is shockingly incompetent. Katie At her first White House briefing on Tuesday, Zacharia kicked things off by haltingly reading a lengthy statement about how she hopes to “only build on, only amplify, and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins” of Trump’s second term.The situation only grew worse. Zacharia took questions from just three reporters. Even though they were from friendly media outlets — Fox News, Breitbart and the Daily Mail — she still seemed overwhelmed. Her response to a softball question about her family was painful to watch; she said “my president” before correcting herself and saying “my husband.” After about seven minutes of questions, Zacharia threw in the towel, directing reporters to the tarmac where Trump would be boarding Marine One. “You can ask him all of the questions there!” she announced.Reviews of her performance were brutal.“Nikki McCann Ramirez, a political reporter for Rolling Stone, dubbed it a “Chat-GPT-ass first speech from the new press secretary.”But Zacharia found a defender in the only audience that ultimately matters. “I thought she was very good,” Trump shouted minutes later over the roar of Marine One’s engines while Zacharia, taking a spot usually held by presidential aide Natalie Harp, stood smiling over his shoulder. Of course the president thinks she’s great. Zacharia has the only traits that matter to Trump: She’s blonde, skinny and she appears to worship him passionately. Harp had better watch out; she’s got real competition for the role of most fervent Trump devotee. The president confirmed this by praising Zacharia not for any special skills but for being a “devoted fan” with “an unblemished record of support” for himself. But taking a step back, Zacharia’s hiring is revealing — and encouraging. It’s yet another sign that the president is putting his own cravings for adulation over political considerations.But taking a step back, Zacharia’s hiring is revealing — and encouraging. It’s yet another sign that the president is putting his own cravings for adulation over political considerations like winning the upcoming midterms for his party. “When stressed, Donald Trump retreats to his comfort zone,” investigative journalist Lindsay Beyerstein told me. Beyerstein, who is working on a book about conspiracy theorists called “Angry Minds,” noted that “Zacharia has a long history of pushing QAnon.”The term “QAnon” may seem like a blast from the past, and for good reason. According to a February 2022 report from PRRI, tens of millions of Americans — including 25% of Republican voters — affirmed the QAnon conspiracy theory that Democrats sexually abuse and kill children to drink their blood. In the haze of the Covid-19 pandemic and the disaster of Jan. 6, millions of Trump supporters turned to the myth that Trump was God’s emissary sent to earth to destroy this Satanic cabal of child-killers. After Trump blocked the release of Justice Department files on his long-time friend, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the fantasy that the former reality TV host is a holy warrior against pedophilia lost a lot of public appeal. But as far as Trump is concerned, QAnon is forever. Even as many of his voters quietly pretend the whole QAnon thing never happened, the White House was trying to revive the conspiracy cult over the summer. As The Bulwark’s Will Sommer reported in June, “The Trump administration launched a bizarre QAnon-themed social media campaign,” with various departments tweeting QAnon slogans. Sommer followed up his report by telling CNN that even “as the president faces persistently low approval rating,” the White House is trying to tell his voters something else: “[R]emember when you thought Trump was going to save the world?”As a political move, it’s a bad idea. Trump’s apparent narcissism and corruption were easier for voters to laugh off when the economy was doing well. But now that he’s goosed inflation with tariffs and the war on Iran, his methods are not so funny anymore. For his part, Trump seems increasingly less concerned with political realities and more worried about saving face and fluffing his own ego, even if that means pulling deeper into a bubble where he’s only surrounded by people who flatter him all day with pleasing lies about his greatness. “He’s reliving QAnon because it represents the bygone days when his supporters worshipped him like a god,” Beyerstein said. “Trump may not realized how played out QAnon has become because he doesn’t live in the real world.”Zacharia’s QAnon history is deep and troubling. As Popular Information’s Judd Legum reported, “Zacharia repeatedly used Truth Social to promote Pizzagate and other fringe conspiracy theories.” (Pizzagate is the original QAnon conspiracy theory — that Democrats sexually abuse and cannibalize children.) She repeatedly accused John Podesta, who headed Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign, of being a “pedophile,” posting in 2022, “The radical left Hollywood elitists are sick pedo cannibals.” Zacharia also reposted the false claims of another Trump sycophant, Ali Alexander, who wrote, “Democrats want to mask and rape your children. That’s their satanic platform.”Popular Information also looked into Zacharia’s claims that she was a lawyer and found “there is no evidence that [she] ever passed a bar exam.” The press secretary is not a member of the bar association in any state where she’s worked. In fact, according to Legum and his team, there is no whiff of documentation that she’s licensed to practice law anywhere.When she was standing next to Trump after her disastrous briefing, a reporter asked, “Where did she pass the bar exam?”The president looked quizzically at Zacharia, who replied, “When I moved to China.” Sharp readers will notice that China has no authority to grant law licenses anywhere in the United States. Such a clumsy diversion would never have happened under Karoline Leavitt, Zacharia’s predecessor who was, if nothing else, good at her job. A smooth character and fast talker, Leavitt deployed cartoonish Christian piety and a non-stop act of aggrieved victimhood to keep reporters too discombobulated to hold her feet to the fire about the administration’s various failures. There was little sense that she legitimately worshipped Trump; instead, she appeared to see him as a stepping stone for her own ambitions. This theory got another shot in the arm when Leavitt left the White House, implying she was going to be a housewife, only to walk right into a cushy job as a Fox News commentator. Trump reportedly floated Harp as Leavitt’s replacement, a move that was spun as a “joke” — even though “jokes” are not about humor for the president but instead a way to test boundaries. While press secretaries have long been spin doctors, under Trump the job morphed into one where blatant lies and gaslighting are readily employed to create over-the-top praise for the president. But clearly, this outward-facing propaganda was not enough for the president. Being Trump’s press secretary isn’t as much about distorting press coverage or bamboozling the public anymore. The position has been refocused on the task of giving the president more of the hardcore Natalie Harp treatment. Even as the midterms grow closer, Trump is abandoning the task of winning the public over, choosing instead to retreat deeper into a fantasy world.There, everyone loves him most of all.

item.title: The Surma Boys of Afghanistan
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I met a group of boys in a remote village who had developed their own distinct sense of style. They wore colorful eyeliner called surma, painted their fingernails with henna, and dressed in embroidered clothing and handmade hats decorated with flowers and butterfly clips.This wasn’t something they dressed up for. It was how they dressed every day, each with their own unique interpretation of style and self-expression.With no access to the internet and limited resources, they had created something entirely their own.

item.content:encoded: The attempt to pin the NVIDIA-Huang spy scandal on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is galloping forward. Earlier today Treasury Scott Bessent went on CNBC and squarely laid the blame on Lutnick for slow-rolling and loosely enforcing export controls on NVIDIA chips. item.title: Behind the Blog: Priorities, Priorities
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss getting inspired and how things get prioritized. We’re very short staffed this week (all is well; Joe is taking some much-deserved time off and Emanuel has been on paternity leave, which he’ll address in length soon) so please forgive the slightly slow week, but I still think we got some great stories out. Due to the aforementioned short staffedness, this is going to be a quick one from me.I was in beautiful Boulder earlier this week to hang out with the indie media journalists involved in the Start.Coop accelerator program. I don’t want to butcher their stated goals so you should just read about it on their site: “The Start.coop Accelerator for Worker-Friendly Media exists to address a critical gap in the media ecosystem: the lack of accessible support, capital pathways, and proven infrastructure for building worker-owned media companies. By focusing on cooperative ownership, the program advances a more equitable and resilient media economy—one where information, ownership, decision-making, and wealth are shared more broadly.” The 404 connection to is that we’ve been working with them and Defector’s brilliant Jasper Wang on the Shared Media Services program. If you’ve by Spumoni Cooperative on the site lately, for example, that’s fractional work done through them. with details about the SMS program, if you’re interested; Hell Gate also wrote about their involvement in the program in . In addition to illustration and design work, we’ve been very grateful for Pearl Leung’s help with triaging the support inbox while Emanuel’s on leave. It was really energizing to be in-person with so many people whose work I’ve admired and who are thinking way outside the box about what labor and business ownership looks like in media today. Something that’s stuck with me from the week is how everyone’s areas of coverage, backgrounds, and current operation models were so different, but most had a similar origin story: they built careers they loved, had those careers threatened or pulled out from under them, and said “fuck it, we’ll do it ourselves.” Many were laid off, saw their colleagues being laid off, or were forced to do the laying off themselves, but instead of decided that journalism as an industry was doomed, they (correctly) saw that the existing model of overpaid, out of touch execs churning through passionate, skilled workers like numbers in a spreadsheet was at the core of the problem — not that people don’t want to read the news, but that the news as a business is broken. It’s a story we can certainly relate to here. Unrelated to any of this, if you are in Boulder and can go to It's A Bodega and tell me how much this jacket cost (they were closed when I was there), I'd appreciate it: I have been working on some longer and more complicated stories that ended up not being ready for this week, and was also editing some articles from freelancers that will come out in the coming days/weeks. So I did write a few things this week but they were a bit more take-y rather than investigative or deeply reported. One of the joys of having our own site is that we can do a mix of takes and straightforward news stories and investigations. This was also the case at our old job, and I think it’s the right way to do things, as we’ve explained many times before. I think “view from nowhere, both-sides” journalism is bad and is inherently a choice. Pretending that we are reporter robots without opinions doesn’t pass the smell test, and I think that there are very few places that will be able to do a straightforward accounting of facts and have success doing it in an age of AI. I’m preaching to the choir here and feel like most of you get this, but I bring this up because every now and then we get an unsubscribe message or an email saying that we’re biased, or that they miss the “old” 404. This was a thing we got CONSTANTLY at VICE; people missing the “old VICE.” It is very funny to me that anyone thinks we are old enough to have an “old 404.” The overwhelming feedback on my recent blogs/essays has been positive, as there are very few oligarch defenders out there, and I think my election coverage in general was a bit preaching to the overwhelming majority of Americans who are fed up with Silicon Valley. Also, the comment sections of the last few articles I’ve done have been wild. Thank you all for mixing it up in there (respectfully). But I did get a few emails saying that I should “go back” to doing reported pieces or writing about things other than the election or AI or whatever. To which I say: I am! We all are doing a mix of stuff. Sam puts emails like this directly into a folder titled “hate mail,” while I let them hurt my feelings, which is something I should work on in therapy or elsewhere. Thin skin over here. Anyways that’s a big windup to the point of this BTB, which is basically talking about how I/we end up prioritizing what we do all day, and how that leads to what you see on the internet and in your inbox. The honest truth is that at bigger publications or even medium-sized publications, what you see on a day-to-day basis is more or less the same. As in, similar mix of newsletters, opinion pieces, reported news, etc. Some days there will be big features or big scoops, but the general “vibe” of what you see on a big outlet is not going to be different from one day to the next. With such a small team, our articles end up being some combination of what we find interesting and important mixed with literally everything else going on in each of our lives. We try to bring you the best we can each day, but the reason you got an election take from me on Wednesday of last week rather than, say, a Flock investigation, is that I was in Europe last week and had a time zone advantage to sort of digest and analyze what happened while most of the United States was sleeping. Every article is more or less like this. Why me, why now. The answer is often “because my eyes are bleeding on the other thing I’m working on and I need to mix things up a bit,” or “because I can’t stop thinking about how bad the All-In podcast is,” or “because I have two hours right now before a doctor’s appointment and Sam is at a conference so when I get back she will be busy so can’t edit.” I wanted to write my take about the All-In podcast because it got me really riled up, but it came when it did because an investigation I’m working on needs a bit more time, and we’re shorthanded this week, with some folks traveling, myself dealing with a bunch of life logistics, reporting for longer term things, a doctor’s appointment that runs longer than expected, whatever. I know 99% of you know this and are here with us but basically: If you’re waiting in line for more of the original reason you subscribed to us, PLEASE STAY IN LINE. I promise we have not drastically changed our editorial remit, our perspectives, or what we care about because we haven’t done an article about surveillance in a week. We are possibly just working on the next big thing in that space, are trying to follow the news or current events to some degree, or, like, one of our moms is visiting us so we had to skip a specific story.We obviously can’t and don’t explain that on every article we do as it is not interesting to the vast majority of people and all of our articles need to stand on their own. But yeah, we do a mix of stuff for all sorts of reasons both philosophical and highly practical and logistical.

item.title: Why the Trump DOJ Is More of a Wreck Than Ever
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.A Two-Tiered Justice DepartmentBefore jumping into the news, I wanted to frame up quickly how to think about the current structure of the Justice Department as we head into the second half of Trump II.The departures of some top political appointees from the Trump DOJ since the GOP was blown out in the midterms has gotten a lot of attention, but it’s been variously miscast, misunderstood, or mischaracterized.The way the Justice Department historically worked was similar to every other department: A slate of political appointees was layered on top of the career employees to run the department and implement the president’s broad policy agenda. Those political appointees varied in terms of skill, professionalism, experience, and willingness to be independent versus do the White House’s bidding.There were outliers — like Attorneys General John Mitchell and Bill Barr — but for the most part, the political appointees could be placed within a range that we might call “normal.” Then along came Trump II, and everything changed.Attorneys General Pam Bondi and Todd Blanche exist far outside the normal range and have redefined what outliers are. They obliterated DOJ independence and participated in using the department as a sword against Trump’s foes and a shield for his friends.They each surrounded themselves with a cadre of like-minded political appointees, but that circle is smaller than usual and has been getting steadily smaller. At this point, it’s down to Blanche, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, and Aakash Singh, the principal associate deputy attorney general. A former DOJer joked to the NYT that the Trump DOJ should be called “Four Guys” — a play on the burger chain’s name — to reflect its tiny leadership cadre.Unlike past administration’s, the Trump II political appointees aren’t layered on top of the career employees in normal hierarchal fashion. They exist outside of that framework and in a posture not just adversarial to career employees but to some of the core functions of the department under the law, like public corruption and civil rights.After the extensive Trump II purges of career employee, the political appointees now oversee a department Swiss-cheesed with a lack of capacity, abandoned units and sections, and absentee management. The only thing that keeps the department running in any recognizable form is that most of the day-to-day functioning of the DOJ happens in the 94 U.S attorney’s offices around the country. But they haven’t been spared either.The rush for the exits among some political appointees post-election hasn’t really changed the core dynamic; it just more clearly reflects what was already going on. The department was already being run by the relative few remaining Trump true believers.So small were there numbers and so preposterous their legal arguments that it’s been left to senior political appointees like Woodward to actually handle cases themselves, appearing in court, and earning the direct ire of federal judges. Woodward is defending inquiries in separate cases in D.C. and Chicago into whether the DOJ misled courts, and Woodward himself has come under withering criticism from judges.The post-election departures have probably zapped some of the manpower that the political appointees have to handle cases directly themselves, although they’ve already shuffled in new attorneys to help. That’s a separate issue from the purges of career employees leaving DOJ beleaguered and under staffed, especially as it contends with a wave of immigrant habeas cases.So when Singh — the conduit between Main Justice and the 94 U.S. attorneys — warned them after the election of firings to come and urged them to be on a “wartime footing,” it looked less like a powerful threat and more like flailing from a position of weakness.While weakened, the Trump DOJ is no less dangerous after the election because it’s probably even more dysfunctional, unpredictable, and subordinate to the Trump White House.Trump DOJ Sanctions AlertA federal judge in the Eastern District of New York this week barred a Trump DOJ attorney from ever again appearing in a particular immigration case in front of him, Just Security reports. Two other DOJ attorneys in the case may suffer the same fate, the judge warned.U.S. District Judge Sanket J. Bulsara said that a letter to the court from Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Price was in “bad faith, a deliberate attempt to mislead the Court, perpetuate a fraud on the tribunal, and violate[s] obligations under Rule 11.”The breach appears fatal to Price’s standing with the judge:Judge Bulsara told Richard Hayes, head of the civil division at the U.S. Attorney’s office, that he should consider removing Price from other cases. “You should think about whether you want to swap him out and have some other lawyer from your office appear in any of his cases before me,” Judge Bulsara warned. “Your office is on notice.”U.S. Attorneys Scheme: WDVA EditionA criminal defendant is trying to disqualify Robert Tracci from acting as the top federal prosecutor in the Western District of Virginia, Bloomberg reports. Tracci’s appointment as first assistant U.S. Attorney came after the U.S. attorney position was already vacant, a circumstance which other courts have found insufficient to lawfully elevate the first assistant into the top post. It is one of the mechanisms that the Trump DOJ has used in its scheme to install loyalists as top federal prosecutors in blue states.Stephen Miller Will Fail ‘Catastrophically’Miles Taylor: “I spent the better part of two-and-a-half years dealing with Stephen Miller almost every day. And his selection [as White House chief of staff] is among the most dangerous, foolish, and self-defeating actions we’ve ever seen an American president take.”Golf Course Case Heats UpAhead of a very contentious hearing this morning in the D.C. golf course case, the Trump DOJ told U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes that it objects to her plan to appoint a special master in the case. Reyes intends to have former D.C. U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu investigate whether the Trump DOJ or other government counsel misled the court in the case as a precursor to a potential contempt of court inquiry.The hearing this morning started HOT — even though the hearing was ostensibly not about either the special master appointment or the DOJ’s alleged misconduct in the case. The immediate issue is that President Trump has ordered the closure of most of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, on Nov. 15, and the National Park Service plans to follow that direction. Plaintiffs are seeking a TRO to keep the park open.Tying Up Some Loose Ends on the Election: “In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election,” ProPublica reports.The Big Lie of Noncitizen Voting: A federal magistrate judge in Wisconsin last week dismissed two voter fraud cases brought by the Trump DOJ. In each instance, the judge adopted a similar reasoning to a federal judge in Florida in a ruling last month. The gist is that the 40-year-old federal ban on noncitizen voting is unconstitutional because the states alone have the power to set voter qualifications in federal elections. The Florida case is on appeal, and there’s a lot more litigation coming over this. But it represents a big threat to Trump’s Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting.Politico: DHS messages back up allegations that Lewandowski operated as shadow secretaryNYT: “A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”Next Week: Changes to Morning MemoTomorrow will mark four years since I took over writing Morning Memo. I assigned myself the task on what I thought would be a temporary basis until I found someone else to do it. It didn’t work out the way I expected.That temporary fill-in ended up being the beginning of one of the most rewarding phases of my time here at TPM. At that point, I hadn’t written regularly in more than a decade, and I discovered how much I enjoyed the chance to do something directly myself rather than overseeing the doing of it by others.Since then my role at TPM has evolved and so has the role of Morning Memo. Those changes accelerated in the first half of 2025 as we sailed into the teeth of the Trump II storm. Given the significance of the historical moment, Morning Memo gradually moved away from being a one-stop shop for all of the day’s essential political news and became instead a chronicle of the depredations of the Trump II presidency, with a special focus on the rule of law.You may have also noticed the publishing time moved back closer to midday as the emphasis of Morning Memo changed from a rundown of the news to developing a taxonomy for and a shared narrative of the budding authoritarianism in America.It became clear well before the election that it was time to repackage Morning Memo to better reflect what it has become. With the election past us, now’s the time to make the change. Beginning next week, “Morning Memo” will be renamed and its promise to you refined and updated.Please welcome “Unsanctioned.”I’ll be writing Unsanctioned every weekday. The substance of it will look very much like the Morning Memo of the past 22 months (which looked a bit different than the pre-Trump II version of Morning Memo that we started with). It will be repackaged and rebranded to reflect the new name and the new emphasis.Among the changes, Unsanctioned will also offer extras exclusively to TPM members. It might be an extra edition on a busy news weekend or holiday. It might be a deeper dive on a topic or story than there’s room for in the standard version of Unsanctioned. It might be access to live interviews, additional news items, special news alerts, and other ways of serving you news and analysis.If you were already receiving Morning Memo via email, you don’t need to do a thing to receive Unsanctioned. It will pop up in your inbox starting next week. If you have liked Morning Memo, you’ll feel right at home with Unsanctioned. And while I want to provide TPM members with additional ways to connect with Unsanctioned, non-members will still have access to what you’ve come to expect from me each weekday.I’m looking forward to embarking together with you on this next phase for the country and for what I do here at TPM. I’m excited by the possibilities.

item.title: Mauricio Pochettino Leaves The USMNT For An Even Bigger Mess
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: After an extended denouement to a doomed tenure, Manchester United finally set manager Michael Carrick loose on Thursday, hoping to put an end to the club's worst league start in 40 years. On Friday, the next era for England's most famous club began, sort of, as United announced that Mauricio Pochettino would be leaving the U.S. men's national team on Nov. 18 in order to become the new boss at Old Trafford.Carrick's departure is no surprise, but Pochettino's arrival counts as a bit of a shock. Pochettino had famously come to international prominence first at Southampton and then in his five-season-plus stint at Tottenham Hotspur, which saw that club's evolution from an also-ran into, well, an also-ran that could actually fight with the big boys. Eventually, his tenure there grew stale and the lack of trophies forced a move, with Tottenham firing him in November of 2019. The Argentine then took a year off before signing on to succeed Thomas Tuchel at Paris Saint-Germain in early 2021; his first half-season there wasn't great, as he oversaw the only PSG squad to not win the Ligue 1 title this decade. He did go on to win the league in his first full season, but PSG let him go in the summer of 2022 anyway. A return to the Premier League with Chelsea followed in 2023, where he finished in sixth place in his only season at Stamford Bridge.That brings us to September 2024, when Pochettino became manager of the USMNT ahead of the 2026 World Cup cycle. His appointment was a big deal, as he became the highest-paid and most accomplished manager in the country's history (Jurgen Klinsmann will quibble with the latter assessment, but whatever) in advance of a home(-ish) World Cup. Pochettino had a rocky start there, but eventually righted the ship enough to guide the USMNT to a Group D first-place finish and a Round of 32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. An embarrassing loss to Belgium in the Round of 16 put a bit of a damper on the run, but overall, Pochettino did what he was hired to do: help the USMNT perform at the World Cup.

item.title: Utah’s Superhero Keeper Will Face Washington’s Attacking Horde
item.author: Abigail Segel
item.content:encoded: Before the NWSL playoffs started, I predicted, like many, that San Diego would go all the way. The second-seeded Wave were so solid, so well-balanced, and with a possession-based style that steamrolled team after team. Making it past the faltering, Mina Tanaka–less Utah Royals in the quarterfinals didn't feel anything close to a question. Where San Diego had earned 25 points in the final 10 matches of the regular season, Utah earned just 11.I've never been so happy to be wrong. In delivering a 1-0 upset in San Diego last Friday, Utah provided a postseason performance that left me, a neutral, pumping with joyful adrenaline. As expected, San Diego dominated in nearly every way: shots, possession, touches in the final third. But the only stat that matters is goals scored, and Utah goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn had something to say about this.

item.title: Sicily and the Family Tree of Citrus
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: The key to the citron’s future—a future that links nearly every aspect of Sicily’s cultural, political and culinary history—lies just outside of urban Palermo. It’s a flat plain that was well watered by three rivers. The Arabs turned it into a fantasyland of fertile agriculture. They dug reservoirs and sank new wells and ran canals out across the valley. They began to see it as paradise—the literal version they knew from Persia. They called it the Conca d’Oro. The Golden Shell.Today, mention of Sicily’s Conca d’Oro symbolizes endless citrus groves. But before miles of orange and lemon trees, it was the citron that proved an Asian mountain fruit could survive a Sicilian August. The answer? Yes, as long as the water keeps moving.Somewhere in one of those shaded Palermo courtyards, a gardener planted a skinny sapling from a land Sicilians would never see. He was just keeping a tree alive. He had no way of knowing he was starting a kingdom.

item.title: Notre Dame Brings Havoc To The CFP Rankings
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Lots of things got chucked in the bin last week: Miami's unbeaten season and Mario Cristobal's muffled rage, Ryan Day's offseason peace of mind, Lane Kiffin's shiny glow in Baton Rouge, the Heisman Trophy projections (now it's Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker and Boise State running back Dylan Riley as the favorites, right?), Nebraska's budget for the next seven years if it fires Matt Rhule and has to pay him $63 million to turn in his sideline credential—in all, it's just getting thicker at this end of the trough.As a result, Georgia is the new badass in residence after stomping Ole Miss, 42-7, and UCLA and Utah are last unbeaten teams in FBS. Texas is back—what, for the third time now?—and there are still five Big Ten coaches who haven't gotten the memo to rip ESPN for jerry-rigging the committee rankings to satisfy their SEC overlords. Remember, children: A conspiracy doesn't have to be proven to be advanced—it only has to sound evil to be convincing—and college football's various hierarchies have been doing Satan's bidding since 1869. But never mind all that; you're already bought in, so enjoy hell. For now, let's dance that ska.

item.title: New in Church & State: Preaching against the Ten Commandments in public schools
item.author: 010001a1d56f134d-9b8bfbb0-8f9e-410e-bcc2-63907759202a-000000@amazonses.com
item.content:encoded: Our cover story highlights why the Rev. Josh Hosler preaches against posting the Ten Commandments in public schools at the Church of the Good Shepherd in Federal Way, Wash. While you’re there, I also encourage you to check out my column examining how church-state separation grounds our national community and widens the path forward for authentic common good; learn why release time for religious instruction programs have threatened the religious freedom of public school students for decades; and hear firsthand how interning at AU reignited one young woman’s patriotism. You can also get a preview into the upcoming high-stakes Supreme Court term; explore how a military spouse’s “agnostic bible” is rewriting the rules to advocate for the separation of church and state; catch up on our recent legal work; and more!

item.title: Let’s all point and laugh at the panicking imbecile in the Oval Bordello
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Pour one out for Preznit Fuckwit. He’s going through some things right now.No, strike that — pour them out for Preznit Fuckwit. He’s going through right now. Donny knows that come January, once the Democratic majorities are sworn in, his life is going to — and he’s having a rather hard time coping.The rabid family of coked-up raccoons that live inside Dear Leader’s fat, waterlogged skull were seriously working overtime yesterday morning, chewing through the wires. Donny was wide awake and panic-posting around 5am, shitting out increasingly-deranged lunacy onto his crappy app. Every grudge and grievance got a good airing out.The Democrat Party, lead by one of the most Corrupt and anti-American groups of political leaders and hacks in the history of our Country, and even the World, is doing everything in their power to get away from MASSIVE BLUE STATE CORRUPTION by saying, over and over again, that the Trump Administration is corrupt. It is a sound bite that they viciously use, over and over again, in order to nullify the TREMENDOUS & UNPRECEDENTED theft that has taken place in our Blue States - Minnesota, California, and others, all over the U.S.A. In any event, THE DEMOCRATS ARE CORRUPT AND EVIL, and I am the exact opposite! Fight hard, Republicans, or you won’t have a Country left! President DONALD J. TRUMPCorrupty McCorruptionface says what?Next year, Democrats are going to have a field day, looking into Dear Leader’s malfeasance. What legal standard are you applying to distinguish what they say and what the president says? BLANCHE: There can come a point when a criticism becomes a threat and when a threat becomes something criminal.Holy shit, Blanche really is the tiny mobster from the Bugs Bunny cartoons. Look at him. All he needs is the clownishly oversized hat.Muggsy Blanche is so fucktacularly terrible at being an enforcer. There’s nothing whatsoever that’s intimidating about him. And he can only dance around the reporter’s question and avoid answering it, because as much as Donny wishes it were true, criticism of Dear Leader is not yet a hate crime in the US.Never bring a Muggsy to a Constitution fight. He’s out of his depth. Just listen to Jamie Raskin serve him up a big slice of Fuck You Pie.“The government cannot intimidate people because they exercise their First Amendment rights in a way that government officials don’t like. That’s ridiculous. Somebody should tell Todd Blanche and his team to get a Supreme Court decision called Steffel v. Thompson, which says it’s legally actionable to bring an injunction action against the government if the government is trying to scare you out of exercising your First Amendment rights and your Constitutional rights. In our case, it’s not just that these members were exercising their Constitutional rights; they were exercising their constitutional duties. We have a duty, as the Article I preeminent branch of government, to conduct oversight operations of the entire government, as well as the economy and other things happening in society.”Jaime, stop it. He’s already dead.Here’s the thing that Donny and his few remaining loyalists haven’t yet figured out: nobody is afraid of him any more. He’s the lamest of ducks. The other day, when he started whining about the election results, it was Megyn Kelly — Little Miss Fear of a Black Santa herself — who told Donny to zip it.Quack fucking quack, Dear Leader. Enjoy your ever-increasing irrelevance. I’m actually referring to your 30,000 stock trades (more than all Members of Congress combined), your Qatari-gifted luxury jet, your crypto scams, your Truth Social pay to play scheme, your billionaire-funded ballroom, your insurrectionist slush fund, and your pardons for big donors—just to name a few. Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted? What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution! President DONALD J. TRUMPThe Seditious Six? Donny is still whining about the six Congresspeople who put out that video reminding U.S. service members they have a duty to refuse illegal orders? That’s one of many bugs that are up Donny ass on this particular morning?I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S. The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters.Wait, seriously? Couchfuck McGee is now Donny’s corruption czar? I’m loving this idea. I would pay good money to watch Couchfuck show up at the Minnesota State Capitol and go ‘so, how long have you been corrupt? HA HA, THAT’S GREAT.’Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the Midterms - I WAS NOT ON THE BALLOT- the INVASION of our Country is taking place again. Huge CARAVANS are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico. Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want - “Send them to America,” they say - But they will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED. MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED. There will be no leniency! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMPHoly shit, he’s off his rocker. This is what happens when you live in a fact-free bubble and get all your information from Nosferatu McGoebbels and the Diaper Nurse. What ‘perceived’ loss in the midterms? What is Donny yammering about? There was nothing ‘perceived’ about the ass-whupping that Donny’s party got. And ? Really? No, Donny, no. You’re supposed to fearmonger about imaginary caravans the election, after. Dear Leader is bugfuck nuts, and he’s just getting worse. All this batshittery is just from the of the investigations that won’t ramp up until next year. What’s going to happen then? He’s going to completely lose his fucking mind, and god knows what he’s dumbfuckery he’s going to get up to. He’ll probably try to nuke the Capitol building.This shit is unsustainable. 25th Amendment, let’s go. I’ll take my chances with the couch fucker.In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call. That’s why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.We need this. It’s time for the Democratic leadership to be younger and more progressive.Yes, I know. Senator Van Hollen is 67 years old. That’s still younger than Chuck Schumer, who’s 75.And he’s definitely more progressive.Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.A friend texted this photo to me last night. I’d never seen it before. It’s Ms Spouse and her bestie Kathy down at our lake on November 12, 2022.Okay, that’s put me in the mood for more Kathy and Claudia pics, so here you go.Have a great Friday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Faking contact sheets with an app
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I don't enjoy making contact sheets in the darkroom, but I love them, so Claude and I made an app for it.I've tried printing "Contact sheets" from apps like Lightroom, etc. but they don't look at all like contact sheets. They're just a boring grid. I wanted something nicer.I know, it's cheating, but in just a couple of hours I had a native macOS app that generates JPG or PDF contact sheets from a collection of film scans. I drag the scans onto the app, enter the roll number, camera, film stock, date, and any notes about the roll and I get a reasonable facsimile of a real contact sheet.I print them on US Letter sized photo paper. There's room on the left to punch holes for the ring binder. Stack them above the matching negative sleeve and it's almost like the real thing, without the hassle.I wish I had the energy to make actual contact sheets in the darkroom, but I don't. I'll take this instead.

item.title: Why is no one talking about this?
item.author: 1axbu94jjhaneq2wl1qmrqxrtbrs0tar9a47fn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Earlier this week, amid all the excitement in Mississippi and uncertainty in Alaska, a federal judge quietly closed the book on the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California. The DOJ had sued to force the state to set aside more than 20,000 ballots it did not want counted.After aggressively litigating the case all the way to the Supreme Court, and losing at every level, the DOJ asked the court to dismiss its own lawsuit. The court obliged.Only two weeks ago, the specter of the DOJ prosecuting election officials for counting ballots hung over the Golden State and elections nationwide. We watched as the Trump administration escalated its lies and demands. We worried that this case might be a prelude to seizing ballots.The order closing the case was a simple one page. But in it, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter offered one last statement explaining what had been at stake:“This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy.”These words echo what conservative Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote six years ago when he sternly rejected the Trump campaign’s challenge to the 2020 presidential election in Pennsylvania:“Free, fair elections are the lifeblood of our democracy. Charges of unfairness are serious. But calling an election unfair does not make it so. Charges require specific allegations and then proof. We have neither here.”The parallels between November 2020 and today are striking. In both instances, Trump’s party lost hotly contested elections. Both involved litigation Trump instigated to try to change the outcome. And both then and now, the courts soundly rejected his outrageous claims.Beneath those similarities, however, lie disturbing differences.The Pennsylvania case in 2020 was litigated by a bumbling Rudy Giuliani on behalf of the Trump campaign. It was the dying gasp of a losing campaign.The California case, by contrast, was filed by the Department of Justice. It was not born of desperation; it was part of a larger, premeditated attack on free and fair elections.And while the Pennsylvania lawsuit sought to throw out lawful votes, the California case went further. It was paired with threats to investigate and prosecute state and local election officials.Perhaps most importantly, the dismissal of the Pennsylvania case was celebrated in the national media as a triumph of democracy over efforts to discredit free and fair elections. The dismissal of the California case this week barely registered outside a handful of outlets.Over the last two years, there have been many instances of Trump’s aberrant and destructive behavior. None has done more damage to the nation’s identity than his ceaseless attacks on our elections.But worse than Trump’s conduct is the way it has been normalized in places that once would have found it outrageous and worthy of unsparing condemnation.If a federal judge can remain judicious while saying the DOJ’s lawsuit “attempted to disrupt an ongoing election,” why can’t the legacy media use similarly direct language? If a court is willing to say the DOJ’s intent was to “create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers,” why can’t our civic leaders say the same?After the 2020 election, for a brief time at least, this was not a problem. After Jan. 6, 2021, the condemnation of Trump was forceful and uncompromising.He was impeached, and a bipartisan majority of the Senate voted to convict him. Media outlets across the spectrum spoke in clear moral terms. Business leaders pledged to support democracy.Yet today, as Democrats celebrate their victories and the GOP nurses its wounds, there is near silence about Trump’s assault on voting and elections. It is as if it were a passing phase, a remnant of the pre-election period that we can now forget.This was the mistake many made after Trump left office the first time. We thought he was gone and his movement discredited. The initial shock and outrage over his behavior wore off. Corporate pledges quietly lapsed. Polite society moved on.How many more elections must we endure in which the threats reach critical levels? How many more times can we ask lawyers and the courts to bail us out?In the coming weeks, Democrats will take power in Congress and in states around the country. They must address the threats we have endured for nearly a decade under Trump and the MAGA Republicans.That means enacting strong new voting laws, protecting voters and election officials from intimidation, and conducting oversight over the executive branch’s unlawful actions.We as citizens must do our part as well.That means calling and writing our representatives and demanding that they use every tool available to them. It means showing up when our legislatures debate election laws. And it means standing up, speaking out and working to defeat Trumpism as an ideology.I understand that there are many other important issues facing our country, from the cost of living to health care. But unless we fix our democracy, none of those other problems will be solved.Over the next few months, I plan to make this a central theme of my writing and advocacy. I hope you will join me. Subscribe to Democracy Docket to follow along.

item.title: The Filibuster Runs Deep. Very Deep.
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I went back and forth with a number of people yesterday about the filibuster and the leadership contest in the Senate Democratic caucus yesterday. You want Van Hollen because among other reasons, some contended, he gets you closer to getting rid of the filibuster. Don’t be so sure of that. I want to show you something that popped up yesterday in my Twitter feed that is a good example of why. TPM alum Sahil Kapur posted this clip of Bernie Sanders getting asked about the filibuster. The answer isn’t great. I’m not picking on Sanders here. I’m flagging this precisely because Sanders is a key player making this leadership contest possible and people imagine, with some good reason, that Sanders is most willing to upend conventions, take on establishment thinking, etc. It’s an example of how deep filibuster thinking runs.
