item.title: Republicans hate our veterans — and no one hates them more than Preznit Fuckwit
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Yesterday was Veterans Day, and we heard a lot of pungent mouth-farting from the Usual Republican Suspects about how much they and our nation’s veterans.There they were, tweeting out the same old boilerplate platitudes about and . It’s all bullshit. The GOP our veterans. As always, watch what they do, not what they say.Veterans are useful props whenever some fuckface wingnut needs to burnish their patriot cred, but when it comes time to supporting our veterans — say, by helping them when they’re in need — it’s a completely different story.Need proof? Let’s go to the video tape, from July 29, 2022:Here we have a bunch of Republican Senators fist-bumping. Why? Because they just blocked a billthat would have expanded healthcare coverage for military veterans exposed to toxic burn pits during their service.Who the fuck that? Put down your fists, and at least have the decency to slink away in silence, embarrassed over your ghoulish treachery. Awesome job, you evil soulless hypocrites — because nothing says ‘we support our heroes’ so much as ‘just fucking die.’Now let’s fast forward to April 2025, when the Space Nazi’s merry band of unfuckable DOGE incels showed up at the Department of Veterans Affairs and said, ‘good news, everyone — you’re all fired.’ They then took a wrecking ball to the place.Listen up, shitwits: you send a person into a war zone and tell them to fight for their country, and when they come back injured and permanently disabled, you fucking well take care of them — forever.It’s basic human decency.The freedoms we enjoy as Americans came at a cost. Generations answered the call to serve, putting their lives on the line to defend our country and way of life. This Veterans Day, join me in honoring and thanking those who served. We owe them a debt we can never repay.Steve, with all due respect, fuck off.You voted against the VA Employee Fairness Act, the Veteran Service Recognition Act, the PACT Act (twice), the Equal Access to Contraception for Veterans Act, and the Ensuring Veterans Smooth Transition Act.For a guy who claims to honor those who made sacrifices, you have a fucked-up way of showing it.“Today we salute the brave men and women who wore our nation’s uniform and defended the homeland. Their sacrifice deserves our gratitude, our respect, and our unwavering support. Never forget those who fought for our freedom. God bless our veterans and the United States of America!”Sit down and shut up, you vapid bobblehead. In your first term in Congress, you made 15 anti-veteran votes. Last year, you voted to cut funding for the 49,000 veterans in your district by supporting a bill that guts their health care.How delicious is it that this complete waste of space was just denied reelection by an actual veteran, the retired Rear Admiral Eileen Laubacher?, Handy. Enjoy fading back into well-deserved obscurity.“God bless our veterans from Ohio and across the country for their service and sacrifice this Veterans Day.”By the way, Jimmy Jords can barely be bothered to commemorate the day. He just shits out the same bare minimum every year. Here’s his post from 2025.“Happy Veterans Day! God Bless all who served. American heroes!”Shove it, Jimmy. you voted against the PACT Act, the Food Security for All Veterans Act, the Veteran Service Recognition Act and the VA Employee Fairness Act.Don’t even get me started on five-time draft-dodging diaperload.I’d love to show you the heartfelt Veterans Day message that Donny posted to his crappy app, but I couldn’t find one. Nothing. Not even a concept of a sketch of one.He couldn’t even be bothered to pretend to give a shit. Yesterday, Preznit Fuckwit traveled to Arlington National Cemetery and laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Who Didn’t Have A Rich Father To Get Him Out Of War By Paying A Quack Doctor To Gin Up A Bullshit Note About Imaginary Bone Spurs.“Soon we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphant arch to our veterans.”Oh, so now we’re supposed to pretend Lord Shitticus is putting up his ginormous arch for ? Oh, please. The fucking abomination is going to plunge the gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery into permanent shadow.Before we move on, it must be noted that what remains of Dear Leader’s pudding-brain has become a neurological superfund toxic cleanup site.“Green Beret Ryan Hendrickson was leading his team through a— Taliban-held village in Afghanistan at— 3 in the morning when he was— stepped on by— enemy? I mean, he was the enemy, the enemy was all over. He made the mistake. A mistake that— people understood when they were in the battles, jungles.”Holy shit. What the fuck was that? Donny completely loses the thread of what he’s reading off the teleprompter, and just starts winging it. Afghanistan doesn’t have any jungles (I checked with the plagiarism robot, just to make sure), but there are jungles in every war movie Donny’s ever seen on TV, so there you go. He can no longer tell fact from the dim, flickering images playing inside his fat, waterlogged head.What an utter fucking embarrassment.Let’s take a look at Donny’s own long history of quote-unquote , because — spoiler alert — .We can start with that lovely incident in 2024 when private citizen (and convicted felon) Donny trespassed his way into Arlington National Cemetery to do a disgraceful thumb’s-up campaign photo-op while trampling over the graves of fallen heroes — and grinning like an asshole the whole time.Let’s also not forget that in November 2018, as world leaders gathered at a cemetery in France to honor the memory of US soldiers killed while fighting in World War One, Donny blew the whole thing off — because it was drizzling lightly, and he didn’t want that weird tangle of piss-colored bullshit on top of his head to get wet. Instead, he spent the day rage-tweeting from his hotel room. Good times, bro, good times.What kind of overgrown grievance-toddler gets mad at a fucking boat?Now I want to repost something I wrote on September 24, 2023 — because of all the shitty episodes regarding Little Donny Fuckface’s callous treatment of our veterans, this one just might be the rock-bottom worst:At his welcome ceremony at Joint Base Myer–Henderson Hall, across the Potomac River from the capital, Milley gained an early, and disturbing, insight into Trump’s attitude toward soldiers. Milley had chosen a severely wounded Army captain, Luis Avila, to sing “God Bless America.” Avila, who had completed five combat tours, had lost a leg in an IED attack in Afghanistan and had suffered two heart attacks, two strokes, and brain damage as a result of his injuries. To Milley, and to four-star generals across the Army, Avila and his wife, Claudia, represented the heroism, sacrifice, and dignity of wounded soldiers.It had rained that day, and the ground was soft; at one point Avila’s wheelchair threatened to topple over. Milley’s wife, Holly­anne, ran to help Avila, as did Vice President Mike Pence. After Avila’s performance, Trump walked over to congratulate him, but then said to Milley, within earshot of several witnesses, “Why do you bring people like that here? No one wants to see that, the wounded.”Never let Avila appear in public again, Trump told Milley. (Recently, Milley invited Avila to sing at his retirement ceremony.)what a cold-hearted dick.“why do you bring people like that here? no one wants to see that, the wounded.”imagine you’re a severely wounded soldier. after five combat tours, sacrificing yourself for your country — you find yourself in a military hospital, minus one leg, your life permanently altered. you live though months of hell — bedridden, undergoing multiple operations and grueling physical therapy — and when finally you’re discharged, you’re confined to a wheelchair for the rest of your life.and what does the President of the United States — your Commander in Chief — say about you?“no one wants to see that, the wounded.”fuck you, Donald Trump. you piece of shit.Donny, Handy Oakley, Scalise, the whole worthless lot of them — the next time any of these grandstanding performative peacocks starts going on and on about how much they love the shit out of our veterans, remember: watch what they do, not what they say.But oh you lucky duckies, I saved the most egregious behavior for last.“Happy Veterans Day — to our best Americans. The Hegseth’s are honored to celebrate our veterans this morning at Arlington with @POTUS, @VP & @SecVetAffairs. Thank God for our warriors, past and present.”Oh, the really? The Hegseths (no apostrophe, brainiac) are ‘honored to celebrate our veterans’? These fuckfaces start laughing it up, in front one of our nation’s most solemn monuments — to the point where the guard on duty literally SCREAMS at them that ‘ALL VISITORS WILL MAINTAIN AN ATMOSPHERE OF SILENCE AND PAY RESPECT AT ALL TIMES!”That’s right, they take this shit seriously at the Tomb. They don’t care if you’re the piss-drunk Secretary of Whatever You’re Calling Yourself This Week. You will keep your fucking mouth shut at all times. This isn’t some open mike. Zip it and keep it zipped.Go laugh it up in front of the Epstein Dance Hall™, if you must.Oh my god, it’s every bit as fucktacularly bad as we suspected it would be. Accountability cannot come soon enough.We really need a little Daily Claudia right about now, don’t we?Here’s a triptych from the Newburgh NY restaurant Blu Pointe on September 18, 2025.Have a great Thursday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: An Expert And A Noob Play ‘Final Fantasy Resonance’
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: While there are many fantastic Japanese role-playing game (JRPG, for short) series out there, and with apologies to and , is the biggest and most important of them all. Every numbered entry in the main series is an event, and since almost every game is its own story (to date, there have been two main games to get direct sequels: got , and inexplicably got two sequels), there are swaths of new gamers dipping in every time a new game releases.Despite that, it's safe to say that has somewhat lost its way, or at least what was once its identity. What started as a turn-based RPG has evolved, first into a more active-style combat system and then more recently into something bordering on an action game. This makes sense for Square Enix, the series's developer, as turn-based combat has mostly, though not entirely, slipped from an important game genre into something more niche. Chasing the action trend that took over turn-based RPG's spot with the games made financial sense, and it kept from growing stale.That said, there's still a hunger for turn-based RPGs, and especially turn-based games; the last mainline game to be strictly turn-based was 2001's . With that in mind, we arrive at , the recently released (and relatively successful) spin-off that is a sort of remake/re-using of assets of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a mobile gacha game. is not asking the player to part with any money besides the initial price tag, and instead is a fully fleshed-out 30-to-40-hour turn-based RPG adventure through time, space, and history.

item.title: The Word of the Day: Accountability
item.author: bounce_a1d1deb5-a5de-f111-91f0-000d3a18e244_prod@bounce.myngp.com
item.content:encoded: Sesame Street once featured a regular segment, , in which Muppet characters and a celebrity guest explained a specific vocabulary word. Their choices evoke nostalgia for words that today are often derided as weakness, for example, diversity, belonging, fairness, and kindness. were applied to this post-election climate, two would dominate: Accountability and Affordability. Which should Congress be working to solve? But this is not a binary choice. If that Sesame Street segment existed today, perhaps the wisdom of Big Bird and Elmo could break through the cacophony to explain how interdependent these concepts actually are.Affordability is built on the rule of law and requires a system of commerce that is fair, predictable, and offers a level playing field for all. If the rules are changed to allow those in power to dole out favors to their friends and supporters while punishing their enemies, affordability for all becomes unachievable. Accountability provides the foundation for affordability. Just as government leaders are accountable to voters, government lawyers are accountable to the Constitution and to rules of professional conduct, the oath they swore when they became lawyers, and the rules of a fair justice system. If government lawyers are dishonest or mislead the court, fail to adhere to the rules that govern our profession, or attack judges personally for decisions they do not agree with, then the public itself is harmed. LDAD has helped pioneer the notion that lawyers in the public sphere must be held accountable when they undermine a free and fair election or ignore rules that apply to government agencies and their leaders.This week, LDAD and 53 scholars and retired judges filed an against three senior Department of Justice officials: Harmeet Dhillon, the former Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; Robert Keenan, Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; and Eric Neff, Acting Chief of the Voting Section. The complaint alleges that Ms. Dhillon, Mr. Keenan, and Mr. Neff violated their professional and ethical obligations by pursuing lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia, jurisdictions that refused to provide the Department of Justice with unredacted voter records containing millions of Americans' sensitive personal information, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, addresses, and voting histories, and continued to pursue claims that courts repeatedly rejected as legally unsupported. As of October 23, 2026, DOJ had lost all 27 cases in which courts issued a ruling, as well as the first appellate decision addressing the DOJ’s demands for this voter information. Yet DOJ continued to pursue the same baseless legal theories rejected by the courts. LDAD also recently sought accountability by filing an against Hugh Evans, a member of the Alabama bar who serves as a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The complaint concerns the sworn affidavit Mr. Evans submitted to a U.S. Magistrate Judge in January 2026 to obtain a search warrant for 2020 election records held by Fulton County, Georgia. The FBI executed that warrant on January 28, 2026, seizing more than 650 boxes of ballots and other election materials. The complaint alleges that the affidavit withheld from the court material information: that Georgia election authorities had already investigated and rejected the very allegations on which it relied.Accountability is a critical . It is the glue that holds the justice system together and the very foundation of the rule of law. It is the pathway to affordability and to all of the rights that we hold dear. For a brief respite from the many harsh words that currently undermine the foundation of our democracy, enjoy these words brought to you by the Muppets -guaranteed to make you smile. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.Lawyers Defending American Democracy

item.title: State Borders Are Hard to Draw From Memory
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Borderline challenges us to draw map borders from memory. The United States version has proven to be quite popular. Drawing each state's borders is not easy when you've never done it before, no matter how well you know the US map. Some people are astonishingly good at it. Then you remember that no one is going to try the game unless they think they can do it. A compilation map of how all players drew those lines is fascinating. Matt Forrest brings us some insights about that map, specifically that the states with the most complicated borders turn out to be the easiest states to place. The hardest are those with simple, straight borders because they are all together in the American West. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: Robyn’s Tiny Desk Concert
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Every choice here is a tender one, down to the teardrop glued to her cheek. Every move is confident, yet comes from a place of vulnerability. Most of these arrangements play up the quiet desperation in her outsized songs, though on “Ever Again,” Robyn pulls off a magic trick by inviting us into the conversation, opening a broken heart to defiant resilience. “Light Up,” in particular, sounds revelatory, a glitchy synth banger reborn as a piano ballad. “I was looking at you like a mirror,” she sings with a catch in her throat, like an old memory surfacing for a split second, as she builds to a moment of emotional release.Robyn was 16 years old when “Show Me Love” appeared on her debut album, Robyn Is Here. “For me, this is where it all started, in a way,” she tells the audience, understating the foundational impact the hit would have on late-’90s pop. Behind the Desk, its lite new jack swing slows to something more spacious and reflective, if no less flirtatious. She lets the music age with her.

item.title: The Honey Trapdoor
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang had sex with multiple partners, but somehow my portfolio got screwed. When it comes to Nvidia, I got in early. And I stayed in. I’m not a promiscuous trader who goes in and out, in and out. And until this week, that loyalty had paid off. Like millions of stock owners, I wish I had pulled out earlier. In fairness, nobody thought the AI’s most engorged bubble would ultimately be popped like a cheap condom by the most human of desires. I still have no idea how a guy at the center of the company at the center of the industry at the center of the global economy had the vigor and spare time to juggle numerous affairs (not to mention Donald Trump’s ego). This guy was managing the most important company in the world while managing multiple romantic partners. I’ve seen 100 megawatt data centers that burn less energy. What was he trying to do, run for president? Seriously, if Huang had any more sex out of wedlock, he’d have to rename his company X. Everyone knows the number one rule in business is that you don’t have more partners than your company. I know this seems like a lot of cheap jokes, but after this week’s hit to my portfolio, I can no longer afford the expensive ones. And I’m not the only one. Everyone had Nvidia in their portfolios. And now the thrill is gone. And so is the trill (several of them, actually). I can’t remember if it was Warren Buffett, Milton Friedman, or John Maynard Keynes who said, “Don’t tap that if it will tap the market cap.” Now, Nvidia board members are left to Purell themselves as they feverishly search for a new leader to replace their supposedly irreplaceable old one, who just issued his resignation (although, I’m guessing the board pressed Ctrl-Shift-Esc before Huang pressed Command-Q).+ Until today, the government was telling us that we can’t drive a Polestar or buy a DJI drone, but it’s fine if Nvidia sells chips to China. And the tech industry that has been telling us that we need to risk our very existence to stay ahead of the Chinese in the AI race initially tried to brush off Huang sharing secrets with a spy as no big deal. Up is down and wrong is right in the age of corruption. Jensen Huang’s resignation means the full story is probably a lot worse than what we already know. It also suggests that there are still lines that can’t be crossed (except when it comes to the administration, whose involvement in this is likely a bigger scandal than the scandal). Now comes the hardest part. Finding a new AI CEO whom people trust when AI CEOs have spent so much time convincing us they’re not to be trusted. Whoever gets the gig is going to have some big shoes — and a lot of little leather jackets — to fill. Trump says that Tim Apple should become Timvidia. But Trump himself is heavily implicated in this disaster. I’d rather see Tim Cook replace him. (If Cook says no to Nvidia, maybe Trump will suggest Dana White for the job.)+ Meanwhile, the Justice Department has launched several investigations into purported honey-trapping spy Alice Huang. But the people at the very top of the administration were warned about her a long time ago.+ “It has been a hard week, even for the thick-skinned. The news that Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence regards as a Chinese spy, has shaken not only Silicon Valley and geopolitics. It also has been an earthquake for the leather-jacket-wearing community.” Jensen Huang Betrayed the Leather Jacket Community. You can run, but you can’t rawhide.There was a joke going around the internet that the reason it was taking so long to get the final election numbers from Mississippi is because they have to count, One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, Three Mississippi. Whatever took so long, it was worth the wait. Scott Colom’s “shocking upset victory in a state where Donald Trump won by 23 points in 2024 is even more remarkable considering Mississippi’s history. This was the state where Jim Crow was the most violent and repressive. It was where Emmett Till was lynched, Evers was assassinated, and the young civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan. There were 581 documented lynchings during the Jim Crow era, more than any other state.” Mississippi Elects Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction. “Before the passage of the Voting Rights Act, only 6.7 percent of eligible Black voters were registered to vote in Mississippi. Now, more than 60 years later, it was Black voters who turned out in record numbers to rewrite the history books, motivated in part by a new struggle to protect voting rights.”+ “It was Mr. Hudson’s father who was initially cast in the campaign ad mocking a suggestion from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, that Mississippi residents pick another type of protein to avoid rising beef prices. When the elder Mr. Hudson balked at a script that would require him to utter profanity on camera, his son volunteered.” The Man at the Center of Scott Colom’s Protein Ad. (And shee-it, that ad helped change history.)“These settlement numbers, reported for the first time, provide a rare glimpse into what the companies are willing to pay to avoid high-profile trials with teen users — and the looming financial risk such cases present. Roughly 9,800 personal injury cases are pending in state and federal court against Meta, Google’s YouTube, Snap Inc. and TikTok Inc.” (Gift Article): The Confidential Payments Meta and TikTok Made to Addicted Teens. “Seven confidential deals with young plaintiffs ranged from $2 million to $2.5 million. And the remaining personal injury lawsuits could expose the companies to billions of dollars in liability.”“Air travel has become so safe in large part because of a profound commitment from the people in charge to learn from tragedies — what aviation experts call ‘lessons written in blood’ … But the Trump administration has displayed an extraordinary unwillingness to learn new lessons, and in some cases it seems to be unlearning the old ones.” James Fallows in the (Gift Article): Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?+ Nothing to Write Home About: “The last time sales were this low was August 2010 when the economy was still reeling from the housing bust and the recession that followed.” (Gift Article): Home Sales in October Plummet to 16-Year Low.+ “Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded the soldier who reprimanded him and members of his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal on Thursday.” (He must have been embarrassed to award someone he’d ordinarily fire.) After hearing voices and laughter, Specialist Iglesias of The Old Guard yelled, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”“​In its glory days, the S.S. United States was fast, luxurious and all but indestructible. As the ocean liner’s designer, William Francis Gibbs, liked to ​say, ‘You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her, and you can’t catch her.’ And he was right, up to a point. On Wednesday one of the greatest ships to sail the seas made its final journey, 180 feet down to the bottom of the ocean.​” The S.S. United States, a Historic Supership, Sinks to the Ocean Floor. But the metaphor doesn’t stop there. It was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico…

item.title: Anita Tatlow (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Anita Tatlow, a British ambient musician based in Hong Kong. She trained classically as a pianist and vocalist and studied piano at university. There she met musician Ben Tatlow, now her husband, with whom she co-founded the label Echoes Blue. She’s collaborated with many artists through the label, and she’s released solo music since 2020. Her latest record, , is an ambient album mainly built from voice and piano. On one track, she told us, “I created a shimmer effect which started out as a piano tremolo that I recorded and then processed through the Strymon Night Sky pedal and reversed it and it becomes inaudible as a piano but a super mystical texture.” We’re also playing , her 2025 collaboration with composer Adi Goldstein. A conversation with Anita follows the streaming links.I’m based in Hong Kong, and there are not many ambient artists over here. Ben, my husband, who I run Echoes Blue with – he’s always been good at connecting with people who are working in similar spaces to us, and he was in touch with Cynthia. I think she did a rework of one of his tracks and vice versa. He told me I should chat with Cynthia so she and I connected on a call.We were just talking and figuring out how we could work together more. That was how the idea for formed. We decided that we wanted the collaboration between our labels Echoes Blue and to be about raising up women in the ambient space through joint releases and compilations. And it just evolved from there.For Echoes Blue, how did that label start and what kind of music do you focus on?From early on, we built it up as a way to release music ourselves. As our own projects grew from one to two to five to lots, Echoes Blue became that umbrella for everything. Over time, we started working with more people. One of the earliest artists whose music we released (that wasn’t me or Ben) was Dear Gravity. Ben and he and some other guys do the all:ambient podcast together.Echoes Blue didn’t initially start out as an ambient-specific label, but with our own ambient projects, and as artists joined the roster, we increasingly leaned into this ambient and ambient-adjacent space. That said, we’ve always evolved in every season – both as musicians and as a label – which may mean broadening our stylistic output further over the coming years.It’s been really cool to see some of the artists who have been with us since they had a few thousand listeners on Spotify to now receiving much greater recognition, and to see how their music has continued to evolve and grow in that time as well.In your Foxy Digitalis conversation you talked about certain milestones and one of those was going into music full-time. We were curious about that.It’s been quite the journey. Long story short: After studying music at university, I trained to become a primary school teacher which I did for several years, while Ben had a corporate job in marketing. Then we both moved from London to Sweden (he had grown up there). We moved there partly to try the music thing. I worked part-time as a church musician in Stockholm, and he had a part time job too – we did that for quite a few years. We were always working around 1-1.5 jobs between us, plus doing music as well. Having the mindset of not giving up on something was really crucial. Having each other for support and encouragement helped too – it’s not easy to start out as a musician and we had to be resilient to continue to build it up, with several setbacks on the way.After five years in Sweden, we moved to Hong Kong. I got a new job as a church musician/ worship leader here. Hong Kong was always on our radar, and we had always been drawn to the place since visiting for the first time in 2009. This opportunity came up and we jumped at the chance, still doing music on the side but at this point Ben was working on it pretty much full time.And then around three years ago we got to a place where we had built up multiple projects, the label – in fact multiple labels: we have and then also , which Ben runs with Marshall Usinger, whose moniker is “Be Still The Earth.” Plus we’ve had other label collaborations and side projects as well – so we had a lot going on.From all of that growth, I really needed to step on board full time, and we were in a position to do that which I’m really thankful for. But that’s only through doing lots and lots of things. If we had only one artist project, there’s no way this would be sustainable. It’s only because we have so many things going on, which keeps us both very busy – especially with two young kids as well.Regarding labels, in recent years our readers have been more specifically drawn to Flow State’s human emphasis, because there’s so much generated music and fake artists. So for our process, we’ve come to rely more on labels as vetters and profilers of the people behind the music. Echoes Blue specifically leans into the humanity of the artists on their roster.Echoes Blue has always been about real humans. Even before the “AI boom,” there was a whole thing around Spotify playlists being filled with tracks that were bought to fill the playlists. We just saw how this was so rubbish for people who are trying to create art. It started there. We try to have a relationship with the people we release with. At least one of us has gotten to know them, we know who they are, and that they’re good people.I also think it goes back to the idea of pivoting. Since we started, we’ve had to navigate big changes in music already, so with AI, we kind of saw it coming. When it happened, we knew we had to double down on the fact that what we’re releasing is human-made, and that’s what listeners are asking for. People want to hear stories through music. The story is super important, and more and more that’s becoming apparent. When people submit demos to us, we’re always asking, “What’s the story behind this?” Because it’s always the deeper stuff that resonates with people.I think AI can have a place as a tool for making systems effective, but not for us in the creative process.For your new album, the title () calls to mind the unpredictability of life and the various forks in the road that led one to where they are. We’re curious what ideas and experiences make up the story of this album.There were a few things that brought to life. This year, we were able to buy a home (after years of renting) and put down roots, which was a pivotal moment because it felt like we finally landed. We have also lived in three different countries and made career and life decisions which go against the grain. And I’m just aware that all of those decisions have led to where we’re at, both physically but also in terms of the people we are becoming – and it’s true for all of us. There’s the poem by Robert Frost that says, “I took the road less traveled by / And that made all the difference.” I feel like there’s something in me that says I’m never going to take the path that’s expected. It’s like the film – the idea that you’re at a crossroads and you could go this way or that way, and the decision could have a huge impact on the rest of your life.I was thinking about this a lot as I was developing the album. I tried to screenshot in my mind various moments that have been pivotal snapshots in time for each of the songs. I also love collaborations and wanted these to feature on the album because none of us walk this journey alone. So I collaborated with Ben (aka Antarctic Wastelandsand Memories of the Forgotten) as someone who’s been on the journey with me for a significant portion of my life. Then I asked Marshall (Be Still the Earth) to collaborate as we’ve known him for several years and work with him closely with him though slow echo. I only metfrogithrough this year so she’s a newer collaborator, and I loved working with her too – to the point that we ended up with two collaborative tracks. I wanted the collaborations to represent the fact that people we meet across different time zones and timeframes are all part of How do these experiences and ideas then manifest in the music itself?All the tracks are made from vocals and piano, because those were important aspects that shaped parts of my life, being classically trained as a pianist and vocalist. All the initial drones and ambient pads were created from my vocals in various ways. I created a Decent Sampler instrument a few years ago, based on my vocals, which I then used to create some of the additional layers. These layers, together with the stories set the tone for each piece. And all the pieces contain piano elements as well but in some these elements are more disguised. For example, in “and that made all the difference” I created a shimmer effect which started out as a piano tremolo that I recorded and then processed through the Strymon Night Sky pedal and reversed it and it becomes inaudible as a piano but a super mystical texture instead that’s integral to the piece almost like a shimmer. So there are lots of details like that in the different songs, which I love.What were other pieces of gear you used on the record?The Night Sky was the main pedal I used for this project. All the vocals went through that so I spent a lot of time learning what it can do, and I’m still not an expert! And I spent a lot of time manipulating the vocals I was creating: stretching, reversing, and layering them to create textures, because I wanted the vocals to be the main instrument alongside the piano across the whole release. I also used Valhalla Supermassive quite a bit to add to the atmospheric, ethereal sound of the vocals.What piano and what software?We have a Nord piano and I also used the Imagiro virtual piano for a lot of the piano parts on . We have a bunch of different ones. For different projects I switch it up. I’m about to start a new project and I think I’m gonna start with vocoder stuff. We just got a microKORG 2 which is super fun.Did any memories of your classical training and growing up playing that music come back?I was doing some tremolo stuff, and I was like I really need to practice. Let’s be fair, I’m not a concert pianist, but I did a couple of years of performance at university level. I’m really glad I had that training – but I don’t think it’s necessary to be an artist. I record the piano using MIDI so I can edit anything afterwards. The classically trained side of things is funny because you catch how you recorded it vs. how it’s to be played, and I definitely hear it and want to go in and edit. It sort of becomes wired into you.What are you working on next?I’m working on a couple of collaborative projects. One is with Lore (Lina Hallberger) from Sweden. She and her husband Max run Silent Sonic Records out of Sweden. They’re really wonderful people. I’m working on a project with her which is about bringing the nature side of our two worlds together, like the Nordics vs. the tropics. Nature ambient isn’t something I’ve done a huge amount of so I’m excited for this.I’m also working on more of my own ambient stuff, but also branching into other genres as well where I sing more. I always find getting the perfect vocal take is harder when more lyrics are involved. Ben and I have a project called Narrow Skies, which has nothing to do with ambient, and we’re working on some new stuff for that. I’m not even sure what genre to call it – it’s somewhere in the downtempo / dreampop world.What’s nice about having multiple projects is when you feel like you’re done with a project writing in a certain style, switching to another creative outlet gives me creative space so I can come back fresh.Cynthia and I are working with a whole roster of incredible women and gender expansive artists for , which will be releasing on Friday March 5, 2027, ahead of International Women’s Day (March 8).Oh, and very excitingly, I’ve got a Christmas ambient (if that’s a thing) release coming out next week on November 17. It’s a three-track vocal ambient release – they’re slightly darker ambient covers of Christmas songs. So very excited to share that with the world this year!

item.title: I spent two years defending these Mississippi ballots
item.author: 1axbxsdl4pgemalky98w4g6g34ie632aghi2eb@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Lawyers like to joke that they went into law to avoid math. But my career has been marked by certain unforgettable numbers.There is 218, the number of seats a party needs to control the U.S. House. And there’s 60, the number of votes it takes to break a Senate filibuster.There is 428, Harry Reid’s margin of victory after his 1998 recount. And there’s 312, Al Franken’s margin over Norm Coleman after months of recounts and litigation following the 2008 election.Today, a new number was burned into my memory: 67. That is how many absentee ballots Hinds County, Mississippi, received, processed and counted in the five business days after Election Day.To be clear, these voters, like thousands of others across the state, did everything right. They filled out and mailed their absentee ballots by Election Day. Through no fault of their own, slow mail service meant county officials did not receive them until afterward.In Hinds County, these ballots were reviewed and processed, and as a result, Scott Colom’s lead grew by a net 58 votes.If Republicans had had their way, these ballots never would have been counted. They would all have been rejected for arriving too late, and the voters who cast them would have been disenfranchised.I do not make this statement lightly or as a generalization. It is a statement of fact.In January 2024, the Republican National Committee sued the state of Mississippi to invalidate its law allowing ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrive within five business days afterward.By then, I had already litigated several cases against Republicans over this very issue. Because these ballots tend to skew Democratic, the RNC and its allies have repeatedly fought to have them discarded. Elias Law Group has fought just as hard to have them counted.The RNC has been candid about its motive. “Late-arriving mail-in ballots that are counted for five additional days,” its lawyers wrote in the Mississippi complaint, “disproportionately break for Democrats.”In a state where race and party are so closely correlated, they might as well have added that counting ballots cast by Black voters would hurt Republicans’ chances of winning. Hinds County itself is more than 70% Black.When the RNC sued Mississippi, it seemed clear to me that it was hoping to find a friendly red state that would either quietly settle or, at the very least, not fight back hard. It did not count on my law firm intervening to defend the Mississippi law.Over the two years that followed, on behalf of Vet Voice Foundation and the Mississippi Alliance for Retired Americans, my firm and I fought the RNC at every level of the federal courts. We won before a conservative federal district judge in Mississippi, only to see that victory reversed by the even more conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.Along with the state, we took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court, though few thought we would succeed. But we did.This past June, the Supreme Court ruled in our favor, 5-4, in Watson v. Republican National Committee.Writing for the majority, Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained that “by default, responsibility for the mechanics of congressional elections belongs to States.” Those words would come to matter not only in Mississippi but in other cases nationwide.At the time of the decision, most of the attention focused on what it would mean for the more than a dozen other states with laws similar to Mississippi’s. Few expected it to matter much in a state as Republican as Mississippi itself.So, when I saw the numbers from Hinds County earlier today and realized what these voters had helped accomplish in the Senate race, I paused. It is not just that these voters would have been disenfranchised for no reason. It is that they would have been denied the chance to be part of history.Over the last several years, Republicans have relied on the courts to advance their disenfranchisement schemes. The Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in Louisiana v. Callais, gutting the Voting Rights Act, remains the most prominent example. But hardly the only one.Republicans thought they would win Watson. As a voting rights lawyer, and as counsel in the case, I was thrilled they did not.But today, my connection to this case grew deeper. It was no longer just an important precedent. It was a lifeline for democracy and free and fair elections in Mississippi.Which is why another number will forever be burned into my mind: 4,669. Scott Colom’s margin of victory over Cindy Hyde-Smith to be elected to the U.S. Senate.

item.title: Paul George Has Turned Out To Be The Ur-Celtic
item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: Get past the unseasoned beef between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in Tuesday's Celtics-Sixers matchup, and reach instead for the real juice: a killer performance by Paul George, the player for whom Brown was traded. Though a single regular-season game in November is no way useful to assess a trade in its entirety, the contrast last night between those two wings was telling: Brown (keyed-up, foul-prone, poor decision-making) sat out much of a game where George (methodical, efficient, at ease in the flow of offense) flourished. Boston won, 123-101. More than anything, George's 36-point outing was a reminder of his eerily slick, timeless style could have plugged into every NBA roster constructed over the last decade, and how it distills Joe Mazzulla's Celtics squad to its spiritual essence.Fair minds were skeptical that a star version of George would ever return. In two years with Philly, he seemed to have receded into a fog of lower-body injuries, mystery drug use, and inconsistent podcasting, playing just 78 total regular-season games. Meanwhile, Brown had just come off a workhorse campaign for the Celtics, logging 71 games while soaking up 36 percent usage on his way to an All-NBA second team. For all the hand-wringing about Brown's true value, both in a vacuum and within the Celtics system, he was clearly the more valuable player at the time of the trade. When swapping two seemingly onerous contracts for one another, each one asking somewhere between 32 and 35 percent of the salary cap for a wing who likely wouldn't live up to that price tag, it was the Sixers who had to sweeten the deal with draft picks. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d7mSyzoPfbk

item.title: Staying Cool at the Airport
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I was in the last boarding group, and when they finally called our zone, there was a bottleneck of people trying to get in line to board. As I stood waiting and shuffling around, I watched as a man took a step forward to get in line and saw him step right in front of a woman who was on her last nerve.She threw her hands up in the air and spoke angrily but passively to the man’s back, “What an ass. Oh, well, I guess you must be sooo important—you should just go right ahead! Don’t worry about the rest of us.”She rolled her eyes and heaved heavy sighs, throwing a little tantrum.The man didn’t realize he’d done anything wrong, and it took him a moment to realize the kerfuffle happening behind him was related to his actions. As he turned around and saw how flustered she was, he reacted with genuine wide-eyed surprise and apology, “Oh, I’m sorry! Please, go ahead.”Hands up, avoiding eye contact, exaggerating sighs, and waving him forward. “No, no, no, go ahead, Mr. Big Shot.”The man paused and turned like he was going to walk forward but then stopped.He took a breath, turned all the way around to face the woman, and gently said, “This feels important to you. Please, I would like for you to go ahead of me.”He stepped to the side and calmly gestured for her to go forward. There was no passive aggression, no sarcasm, no hidden agenda. Those of us watching could feel that he meant it.At this, the woman deflated. Her aggressive energy melted.She began apologizing, “No, I’m sorry, I’ve had such a hard day. That damn delay just put me right over the edge…”“I completely understand,” he responded, smiling and nodding back at her.By then the line was moving forward. I took my place behind them and listened to their amicable conversation about holiday plans as we boarded the plane.This was a small moment in time—an interaction that took maybe ninety seconds in total—that impacted me deeply. I was so impressed by how this man was able to be present to this woman’s aggressive behavior in a tense, public setting without taking it on or responding defensively.He remained calm, present, and genuinely kind, and in doing so helped her regain her own composure, which then resulted in a warm connection between the two of them.His maturity neutralized the tension in the space, making it safer for everyone else in the vicinity, too.

item.title: Two Hard-Up Vikings Fans “Celebrate” The Return Of Kirk Cousins
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Three years ago, after a long but loveless marriage, the Minnesota Vikings let QB Kirk Cousins walk out the door. They felt free. Unburdened. , even. No longer would they have to spend night after night asking themselves, “Where is this relationship going?” They could finally find someone new. They could believe in love again, and maybe even have a bit of fun getting back out there on the scene.That scene, much to the Vikings’ chagrin, turned out to be far less exciting than they’d anticipated. Maybe it was them. Maybe they weren’t quite as charming and attractive as they thought they’d been. Regardless, they eventually found themselves lonely, broken, and frankly hard up. And so, with Taylor Swift’s “Style” playing on a loop in the background, they swallowed their pride, along with a good amount of red wine, and made the call they swore they’d never make. Kirk Cousins is a Viking again, and us Vikings fans feel a little bit ashamed that we let this happen all over again. That’s the subject of this week’s special Trade Deadline Edition of All Ball. https://art19.com/shows/the-distraction/episodes/d0e962b6-9e05-45c6-af98-0b5f8d111e53

item.title: Look Who Came Crawling Back To Kirk Cousins
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Under any other circumstances, in any other year, Kirk Cousins being traded back to the Minnesota Vikings would be universally mocked under the You Can't Make Someone Go Back Home statutes. The story of Kirk and the Vikes is one that had been told all the way through, in no great rush at that, and was on the merits not one that would have had the public demanding or even imagining a reboot. But here, now, in the situation in which the Vikings have placed themselves—well, put it this way: No NFL trade has ever had so many people call their shot ahead of time and then nod with approval after it came to pass.Yes, even though Cousins already titillated and frustrated the Vikings alternately over six years by being Almost That Guy, they brought him back on Tuesday in a desperate admission that they had turned their quarterback room into a lividly radioactive dump site. Cousins, we must presume, went with a song in his heart, because he finally found his nirvana: a place without a young quarterback desperate to make his bones waiting to replace him.A Cousins trade of some kind had been rumored from the moment he landed in Las Vegas to play for the Raiders, primarily because he was so obviously there to hold the place card until No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza was ready to replace him. Minnesota wasn't much of a trade option until the Vikings made themselves one—well, the only one. After Cousins was lured to Atlanta (illegally, as the league eventually ruled), the Vikings fell in and out of love with J.J. McCarthy, fell briefly in like with Kyler Murray and then watched his hamstring explode, watched Carson Wentz melt into a puddle in real time on Monday night, and rejected Max Brosmer as a viable option on the fly.

item.title: Scientists Discovered An ‘Invisible’ Object In Space. It’s Challenging Our Understanding of the Cosmos
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in . Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them. The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star.Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun.The object lurking in J0008+0128 could be up to 2.8 times as massive as the Sun, which “potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes,” according to the new study. The colossal mass, combined with its unusually wide orbit of 1,218 days, challenge our understanding of how these objects form.“We search for compact objects (mainly neutron stars and black holes) using large spectroscopic surveys,” said Song Wang, an associate researcher at the National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who co-authored the study, in an email to 404 Media. “We have found more than 10 neutron stars, and J0008+0128 is the most massive one among them.”Generally speaking, stars that are over 25 times as massive as the Sun will form black holes, while stars that are about 10-to-25 times as massive will become neutron stars. Stars with masses similar to the Sun, meanwhile, are destined to spend their afterlives as white dwarfs, which are much larger and less dense than neutron stars. For instance, neutron stars are mere miles in diameter, whereas white dwarfs are about the size of Earth.Because they are dense pressure cookers, neutron stars are filled with disassembled components of atoms, especially neutrons—hence the name—but also protons and electrons. Supermassive neutron stars like the one in J0008+0128 can shed light on the poorly understood “equation of state” in these objects, which is the relationship between their immense pressures and densities. “The equation of state of neutron stars is a long-standing unsolved problem in astrophysics, and neutron star masses can provide crucial observational tests,” said Wang. “This is particularly true for massive neutron stars: how massive a neutron star can become depends on how ‘stiff’ its internal matter is in resisting gravitational collapse.” “The discovery and measurement of supermassive neutron stars (i.e., those above two solar masses) can place important constraints on the equation of state of matter at extreme densities, helping to identify the theories that truly describe the behavior of matter under such extreme conditions,” he added. In other words, J0008+0128 could open a window into the churning atomic stew within these exotic objects. But the system is weird for reasons beyond the supermassive object lurking in the dark. Indeed, the team ran thousands of simulations but none of them “reproduced physical and orbital properties similar to J0008+0128,” according to the study.The wide orbit between the neutron star and the red giant star is particularly difficult to explain. Neutron stars could become supermassive by gravitationally tugging material off of their stellar companions, but this object is too far away from the red giant for this mechanism to make sense.“In fact, many compact objects discovered in recent years cannot be explained by standard binary evolution models and supernova mechanisms,” Wang noted, citing two other examples, known as Gaia BH2 and G3425. Wang and his colleagues proposed a few alternate scenarios to account for these outliers. It may simply be that supernovas can form supermassive neutron stars within the mass gap in rare cases. The researchers also speculated that this system once contained three objects, and that two of them merged together to form the supermassive neutron star.“There may be two massive stars forming an inner binary,” Wang explained. “They can merge at different stages. For example, a neutron star merges with a normal star, or two neutron stars merge. Either case could produce the supermassive neutron star that we observe today.”“In addition, if J0008+0128 formed through single-star evolution, its discovery would suggest that supernovae can produce massive neutron stars,” he added.Studying systems like J0008+0128 could illuminate the murky limits that determine the afterlives of massive stars. They are also helpful for understanding the dynamics of neutron star mergers, which scientists can detect through gravitational waves, which are ripples in spacetime. Wang and his colleagues were able to make this new discovery with the help of sophisticated sky surveys, including astrometric data from Europe’s Gaia space telescope. The team hopes that the forthcoming data release from Gaia, due out next month, will help to narrow down the possible mass of the unseen object in J0008+0128. “The discovery of J0008+0128, together with other systems discovered in these years (e.g., Gaia BH2 and G3425), suggests that much work remains to be done on binary evolution and supernova explosion theory,” Wang concluded.

item.title: Nick Cousins Sure As Hell Was “Not Doing Great”
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: The Capitals beat the Senators in overtime on Tuesday, but the most impactful play of the night was not a goal. Late in the third, with the score 2-2, Ottawa's Nick Cousins kind of casually gathered the puck in his own corner and started to skate up the ice. Before he could do anything with it, however, Cousins got comprehensively bulldozed by Caps defenseman Jakob Chychrun, who sent his opponent's body into horizontal flight against the boards before it bounced limply to the ice. After a review, the refs deemed the hit clean, but Cousins did not return to action. He didn't go to the hospital, but according to his coach Travis Green, "He’s not doing great.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g3E6wjvAA9M I have complicated thoughts about this play. It is very difficult for me to resist marveling at Chychrun's spectacular force and its devastating aftermath; it's as real an athletic feat as any skillful dangle. The fact that it was perpetrated on Cousins, a pest so annoying that his peers named him the league's most punchable player last year, only makes it easier to ignore the human toll. But it's also hard for me to see it and not think about Claude Lemieux, among other ex-NHL tough guys, whose brain was donated to CTE research after his death by suicide earlier this year.

item.title: Understanding the Scandal/Accountability Conveyor Belt
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: There’s a para-news topic I’d like to discuss with you. It has to do with how scandals do or don’t develop, what catches fire and what peters out. We know that one of the constant themes of the last two years was that anti-bromide “nothing matters.” A mammoth scandal is uncovered. A few pieces are written about it. And then … nothing. It just falls under the waves. There is a key structural reason for this that gets far too little attention. It turns on the incentives reporters, publications and readers have to pay attention.The standard scandal reporting progression goes something like this: Reporters unearth scandal details. Attention shakes free more information and the momentum builds. Eventually public officials announce hearings or law enforcement agencies begin investigations. Sometimes it’s both. Those actions both validate the reality of wrongdoing and create new stories to cover. It’s both the existence and progress of these investigations and the new information they generate. There are things that criminal or legislative investigators — with warrants and subpoenas — can pry loose that reporters almost never can. Eventually you might have resignations or indictments, perhaps reforms.

item.title: Leadership Dispatch: Use positive language
item.author: bounces+38uqqg6p9kfkhr65vo9urh445opwzs7h57lq@ckespa.joshdoody.com
item.content:encoded: This week's Leadership Dispatch is about how to communicate more effectively by using positive language. There are two main reasons you should consider communicating this way: You'll be perceived as more collaborative and easier to work with; when you need to deliver bad news using negative language, you'll get much more attention.Use positive language whenever possible.When you set a positive tone for your conversations you will be perceived as more collaborative than combative or resistant, and people will feel better about working with you. And when you use negative words, they will stand out and get maximum attention.In practice, this means avoiding negative words such as “can’t,” “don’t,” “won’t,” “couldn’t,” and “shouldn’t” and finding alternative ways to convey the same ideas using positive words.Instead of “We can’t do that”, try “What if we tried this?” Instead of “I don’t think that’s a good idea”, you might say, “Let’s keep iterating to see if we can find an even better approach”. The idea is not to be passive-aggressive or evasive, but to be more thoughtful when dismissing ideas, suggesting alternatives, or even delivering bad news.This gives more weight to any negative message that you need to deliver because you’re only using negative language when you must communicate that something is dire or needs a high level of attention.It’s a challenge, but this is a muscle that you can exercise and strengthen over time.

item.title: It's One Banana Michael, What Could It Cost?
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: I went a bit mad watching four hours of the All-In podcast, a thing I definitely do not recommend that you do. If you’re unfamiliar, it’s a podcast run by four venture capitalists that is borderline unlistenable. I do it so you don’t have to! The Silicon Valley besties aren’t doing so well:If you want to watch four billionaire/billionaire wannabes cope with the election results, you could watch the absolutely dreadful hosts of All-In talk across a livestream and a follow-up podcast for four hours, or you could just watch the Lucille Bluth "What could a banana cost, Michael" clip on repeat until your eyes and ears bleed.Throughout their post-election breakdown podcast episode released over the weekend, the All-In bros seem to be on the verge of grasping why Americans are so mad and who they’re mad at, but are still trying to find the guy who did this. They appear to finally grasp that Americans are mad at something called “oligarchs” but largely do not seem to know who they are (it’s them). Populist anger at the oligarchs is a “perception” or “narrative” problem. The four hosts — David Sacks, Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and David Friedberg— spend much of the episode considering whether they are out of touch, or whether the children are wrong. Let’s see how they did. “We lost all the podcast bros,” David Sacks, a Trump sycophant billionaire most famous for leading anti-DEI witch hunts against college administrators and writing interminable, book-length tweets, said on the most recent episode. “We lost a huge part of our base. The Republicans in particular are dependent on the podcast circuit. Let’s call it alternative media. Why? Because the mainstream media hates us. Legacy media hates us.”“And they’re 90 percent left, so it is what it is,” Jason Calacanis, a man who seems singularly focused on discussing how he moved away from California three years ago to move to now-Blue Texas, responds.“Without them, we don’t have any media that supports us,” Sacks says, seemingly unaware of the existence of Fox News, CBS News and 60 Minutes under Bari Weiss, the Paramount-Skydance (and CNN) merger, Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post, the concept of Elon Musk’s X, to say nothing of Democratic pseudo-scandals being ginned up by the New York Times.The podcast, like their election night coverage last week (which features, among other guests, Ted Cruz and the CEO of Polymarket explaining at length how little he knows about elections), goes on and on like this. In the aftermath of last week’s election, the schadenfreude of watching right-wing figures crash out as they realize just how unpopular Trump’s policies have become has been particularly satisfying. But there’s something special about watching smarmy Silicon Valley weirdos who sound like they haven’t spoken to anyone who hasn’t founded a startup in several decades advance their theory of the case about what just happened, and what Trump could do next to “save his legacy.” Calacanis, for example, suggested a policy of “no taxes on people under a certain revenue, uhh, income threshold.” He catches himself, perhaps realizing that most people don’t think of their paychecks as their “revenue” because they are not businesses. Palihapitiya says something must be done to “allow the wage earning class to feel more ownership of the United States economy.” Calacanis has come to the realization that “the bottom half of non-equity holders” are mad about the state of the country. Sacks says the wave happened because of “this narrative around affordability plus the perception of the lack of affordability” that has put the public “in a very ornery mood.” “It doesn’t matter how good the economy actually is,” he says. “It matters how good people perceive it to be,” adding that “the economy is not that bad. I mean, in fact it’s quite good.” In fact, data shows this is deeply out of touch with what people across the country are experiencing: More than half of Americans can’t afford to have an emergency fund or save for the future, and most Americans report having to cut back on their lifestyles to afford to live. Housing affordability is at crisis levels. This week’s episode of the podcast is out, which features Matt and I commandeering the ship to rant about how X is a filter bubble, the right’s memes don’t work anymore, and a bit about the All-In podcast. We also talk about how I was wrong about Reverse Engineer Anything. In the subscriber section, we do a deep dive on all the different types of porn the United Kingdom just criminalized. I haven’t been able to find the full context of this because I pay for journalism but draw the line at Politico, which is reporting that Palantir CEO Alex Karp says “all of our products are essentially progressive” and that “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet.” The Torment Nexus promises to do better. It’s no surprise tech CEOs are trying to pretend the last few years didn’t happen, but it’s particularly galling for Palantir, which runs Trump’s surveillance-powered immigration crackdown regime, to pretend like this is the case. Even if you ignore its ImmigrationOS, which you cannot, the company’s entire reason for being is not “progressive” in any way. Last year, Karp published “The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the West, a book that one of his own employees called “absolutely unhinged” in an interview with Joseph last year. The messed up thing about Karp pretending he’s a Democrat is that he’s done this before, and the Democratic establishment, including House leader Hakeem Jeffries, is happy to take money connected to Palantir. You can see more about this on The Palantir Payroll, a site designed to track Palantir-connected political donations. Anyways, bleak stuff. I missed this investigation by the site InfoHawk into a network of more than 800 scam websites that are impersonating chain restaurants by cloning their website, menu, and order process, but inserting a fake payment portal that captures a customer’s credit card information and takes their money (but doesn’t send them food because the order is not real). A lot of these were ranking above the actual restaurant’s website by purchasing Google Ads. Shout out to a reader for sending this our way. Please subscribe to my podcast: I think the way this article is written is infuriating, especially because it “interviews” the AI and is confusing to read, but the tldr is that Pod News found an AI-generated podcast being run through Muse that publishes 23 hours of content per day. That gives you one hour to sleep and interact with your loved ones. Enjoy! Simon Willison, an OG open source developer and blogger who graciously links to us pretty often (thank you!) wrote a little blog about how he used Claude to find a mysterious beeping noise in his house that had been going on for weeks. As someone who has driven myself to near madness looking for a cricket and a fire alarm I hid once, this was a fascinating read/quite creative. He had various devices with microphones on them listen for the beep and then played a game of hot-and-cold, which eventually led him into a box that had “an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.”
