item.title: Bury Me At Camp Blood
item.author: Joshua Rivera
item.content:encoded: The 2009 remake of is, by most conceivable metrics, a bad movie. Cacophonous, slapdash, and dutifully uninspired in its pursuit of tits and guts, the movie is a chore even in the forgiving eyes of horror gorehounds. But on the southwestern edge of Pennsylvania's Pocono Mountains, on the giant screen of The Mahoning Drive-In—the largest still showing movies on 35mm film—it's intoxicating. Not because of some magical idyllic drive-in experience, but for the deep, strange siren song of drive-in, and the Gathering of the Juggalos–esque events it hosts every year. There are lawn games, costume contests, and raffles. People pitch tents and set up campers, they unfold card tables and have potlucks, spread out blankets and camp chairs and spooky lamps to make it easy for friends to find them in the dark between movies. Almost everyone here is from somewhere else, and none of them care how bad the movie is. They like the movies, sure, but they love The Mahoning.People are lured to this place. That's how most encounter it—someone brings you, serves as a guide, an evangelist. Something makes visitors want to share it with others immediately, in no small part thanks to the spectacle of events like Camp Blood, an annual celebration of slasher movies. This is my third Camp Blood; I first came here because a friend brought me, and this time I want to know how others found their way to this unremarkable patch of the Poconos. I speak to a gaggle of friends, many of which are connected by a man from New Hampshire named Keith. He united a bunch of movie fans from Boston and Ohio, and inspired them to make the long drive down to Lehighton for the Mahoning. I was eager to meet Keith, but unfortunately he was busy mainlining triple feature at another repertory house, The Gap Theatre in Wind Gap, Penn., a 48-minute drive from the triple feature that began here at sunset."[Keith] was like, 'The programming at this drive-in is incredible," one of the friends, a man named Desmond, tells me. "And then one year I had to go because they played , which is a dinosaur movie I'm quite fond of from the '60s … that got me out here, and it's the first drive-in I've ever been to."

item.title: Silicon Valley Podcast Hosts Try to Understand Why Regular People Are Mad
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: If you want to watch four billionaire/billionaire wannabes cope with the election results, you could watch the absolutely dreadful hosts of All-In talk across a livestream and a follow-up podcast for four hours, or you could just watch the Lucille Bluth “What could a banana cost, Michael,” on repeat until your eyes and ears bleed.Throughout their post-election breakdown podcast episode released over the weekend, the All-In bros seem to be on the verge of grasping why Americans are so mad and who they’re mad at, but are still trying to find the guy who did this. They appear to finally grasp that Americans are mad at something called “oligarchs” but largely do not seem to know who they are (it’s them). Populist anger at the oligarchs is a “perception” or “narrative” problem. The four hosts — David Sacks, Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and David Friedberg— spend much of the episode considering whether they are out of touch, or whether the children are wrong. Let’s see how they did.“We lost all the podcast bros,” David Sacks, a Trump sycophant billionaire most famous for leading anti-DEI witch hunts against college administrators and writing interminable, book-length tweets, said on the most recent episode. “We lost a huge part of our base. The Republicans in particular are dependent on the podcast circuit. Let’s call it alternative media. Why? Because the mainstream media hates us. Legacy media hates us.”“And they’re 90 percent left, so it is what it is,” Jason Calacanis, a man who seems singularly focused on discussing how he moved away from California three years ago to move to , responds.“Without them, we don’t have any media that supports us,” Sacks says, seemingly unaware of the existence of Fox News, CBS News and 60 Minutes under Bari Weiss, the Paramount-Skydance (and CNN) merger, Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post, the , to say nothing of Democratic pseudo-scandals being ginned up by the The podcast, like their election night coverage last week (which features, among other guests, Ted Cruz and the CEO of Polymarket explaining at length how little he knows about elections), goes on and on like this. In the aftermath of last week’s election, the schadenfreude of watching right-wing figures crash out as they realize just how unpopular Trump’s policies have become has been particularly satisfying. But there’s something special about watching smarmy Silicon Valley weirdos who sound like they haven’t spoken to anyone who hasn’t founded a startup in several decades advance their theory of the case about what just happened, and what Trump could do next to “save his legacy.” Calacanis, for example, suggested a policy of “no taxes on people under a certain revenue, uhh, income threshold.” He catches himself, perhaps realizing that most people don’t think of their paychecks as their “revenue” because they are not businesses. Palihapitiya says something must be done to “allow the wage earning class to feel more ownership of the United States economy.” Calacanis has come to the realization that “the bottom half of non-equity holders” are mad about the state of the country. Sacks says the wave happened because of “this narrative around affordability plus the perception of the lack of affordability” that has put the public “in a very ornery mood.” “It doesn’t matter how good the economy actually is,” he says. “It matters how good people perceive it to be,” adding that “the economy is not that bad. I mean, in fact it’s quite good.” In fact, this is deeply out of touch with what people across the country are experiencing: More than half of Americans can’t afford to have an emergency fund or save for the future, and most Americans report having to cut back on their lifestyles to afford to live. Housing affordability is . Friedberg says “there’s this idea of this oligarchy,” and that AI “made it really easy to attack with this oligarch narrative,” which have led not to people “choosing socialism as an ideology or as a set of principles, [but] socialist outcomes arise from the policies that people think are going to solve their cost issues.” Aside from pretending the tech oligarchy isn’t real—even as we watched an unelected Elon Musk ransack the government as his companies collect billions in contracts, for just one example—people are mad at AI because it threatens their livelihoods, superpowers surveillance, has made the price of gadgets and computers skyrocket, is built on stolen content, has rotted people’s brains, the list goes on. Palihapitiya appears shocked that trickle-down economics, a widely disproven economic theory, yet again did not work (but did serve to make everyone on the podcast far richer): “I thought top down economics can still work. I thought that when you had asset owners building assets and investing in the economy, these things can get to everybody else. It’s clearly not happening.” He, too, believes that at least some of this is a perception problem rather than a real problem. He brings up a viral video of SpaceX employees pitching a data center to Cochise County, Arizona, where the employees explain the potential benefits of a data center. “They [the SpaceX employees] should be proud of how they conducted themselves. But they were getting run over,” he says. “This is an emotional issue that is not tethered to the facts. It represents a totem around the oligarchy and the economic fissure that exists in the U.S. economy.” Calacanis suggests the “data center stuff is performative” and suggested that Trump could work with Democrats to raise the minimum wage to $15 because “it would counter this narrative that we don’t care about the bottom half of society. In fact, there’s only 10-15 million people who are under $15 an hour, so it’s an easy thing to do.” The “emotional issue” is, in fact, a well-documented and factual one: data centers don’t deliver on the job growth they promise communities, are of manipulating air pollution permitting processes, and damage and disrupt the places where they’re put up, and are driving a new fossil fuel boom.Friedberg appears obsessed with the idea of “socialism” and government spending, and says that the end result of people being mad about oligarchy is “voting in more of these kinds of socialist principles, socialist policies, socialist politicians.” Sacks has convinced himself that we must not give the people what they have voted for, which is accountability, but sees the Democrats as a huge danger. “I believe that Democrats want to create a surveillance and censorship state that’s turbocharged by super intelligence. I mean, that’s ultimately the end state.” Flock CEO Garrett Langley, who is actively building the “super intelligence” powered surveillance state, was a recent All-In guest, where he got to talk at length about to the hundreds of communities across the country that do not want it, with little pushback from the hosts. There is not so much to analyze here, exactly, other than to point out how wildly out of touch the oligarchs are, how extremely weirdly they look at the world, and how little they think about or interact with the average person. They are not to be taken seriously, save for the fact that they have lots of money and have a close relationship with this current administration. It is hard to hand out gold stars to this lot, but Palihapitiya does, at one point, come close to actually getting it. “They are shouting a broad-based belief that the economy has completely decoupled from reality and is broken. The economic reality in America is broken. There is a small percentage of people—the four of us on this podcast and our friends—who are the asset owners of America,” he says. “We have benefitted in every weather condition. When rates were zero, we benefitted because we were able to build our businesses with very cheap capital. When rates were high, we benefitted because we had pricing power.”

item.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

item.title: The Dying Minutes of World War One
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Canadian soldier George Lawrence Price, from Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, was serving with the 28th Infantry Battalion on November 11. The 26-year-old was part of a five-man patrol that was checking buildings beside the canal at Ville-sur-Haine, in Mons, for signs of the enemy.Unfortunately, they found them – a group of German soldiers in the process of setting up machine guns on a wall overlooking the canal. There was an exchange of fire; both sides took cover and the Germans retreated.The Canadians began to follow, but just as George stepped out onto the street he was shot in the chest by a German sniper. Dragged into a nearby house, he was treated by a local nurse, but there was little she could do.George Price died soon after, at 10.58am… just two minutes before the armistice.

item.title: House Republicans reveal their 2027 plan: to be unserious, obstructionist shitwits
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Last week’s midterm elections should have been the perfect teachable moment for Republicans. Had they bothered to listen to what We the People were saying, they would have very clearly heard, ‘we’re tired of this shit. Clean up your fucking act, or get used to permanent irrelevance.’But, of course, Republicans don’t know how to listen — . They proved it yesterday by choosing as their House Leader the huge, steaming pantload, Jim Jordan.What even is a Jim Jordan? We’ve all seen him strutting around like some fucked-up barnyard banty rooster, shouty, half-dressed, pointing his finger while he excitedly squawks about who the fuck even knows or cares.Shirt-Sleeve Jimmy has no interest in . He has no interest in reaching across the aisle, and He’s just a weapon. He’s a blunt instrument. He’s a heat-seeking moron.I swear, Republicans just keep getting worse. Three years ago, the House GOP rejected Jimmy’s attempt to replace Feckless Kevin McCarthy as Speaker of the House. Back then, they wanted no part of Jordan’s unserious clown act. Now, they’re embracing him with open arms.And then, as if naming the shouty, half-dressed degenerate wrestling coach to be their Leader weren’t already enough, House Republicans then doubled down on the dumbfuckery, sending Tom Emmer to the podium to make infantile, impotent threats.“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase because, come January 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot… This Republican leadership team will expose the Democrats’ lies and show the American people their true colors as the radical communists that they are.”Bro, what the fuck are you gibbering about? That’s now how this works. That’s not how any of this works.Homie, your party’s in the minority. You hold no power. What ‘lies’ do you imagine you’re going to expose? And what’s all this bullshit about Democrats being ?You stupid fuck, the midterms were a rejection of all the dumb shit you’ve been pulling, and this is your answer? To promise to dole out more of it? Do House Republicans have some sort of political death wish? What kind of party watches themselves lose (as of this counting) 43 seats and goes, ‘oh yeah, we’re totally crushing it. Let’s do more of the same.’Dude, read the room. Voters are sick of idiotic red-baiting, and moronic culture wars. They want someone who’ll fix all the shit you broke. That’s why so many of your former colleagues are now out of jobs. You want to join them? Just keep on doing what you’re doing. Now let’s move on to asshole, Piss-Drunk Pete Kegstand. Pete weaseled out of getting impeached yesterday, but not before holding some yappy little vanity press conference during which he preened, defiantly flapping his gin-soaked gums in defense of his own lawless self.“Was die Artikel selbst betrifft: Iran, die Kartelle, Maduro, Jemen. Jede einzelne Operation war rechtmäßig und wurde vom Führer angeordnet.”In case you don’t speak German, I should probably provide an English translation.“As for the articles themselves. Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen. Every one was a lawful operation ordered by the Commander-in-Chief.”Got that? Piss-Drunk Pete was just following orders. Now, where have we all heard that excuse before?Continuing to write these daily posts has been for me an essential part of my grieving process. But every now and then, the profound sadness of it all becomes just too overwhelming — and so today, I’m going to cut this post short and give myself a bit of a necessary mental health break.I still feel adrift and unmoored, and I still miss Claudia so much.Let me once again take a moment to say thank you to the thousands of people who have posted, commented, private messaged, texted, and phoned to offer support and condolences. I am blessed to be surrounded by an amazing, caring community.Thank you for hanging in there with me. See you tomorrow.And with that, let’s have us our Daily Claudia.Today, I want to repost the very first photo I took of Ms Spouse, forty-six-and-a-half years ago, in the spring of 1980, on MacDougal Street in Manhattan.And I also want to repost Claudia’s final photo, taken on her birthday last February, four days before her passing.Sigh. I miss her so much.That’s it for today, I’m outta here. Again, thanks again for hanging in there with me. I promise you that I am taking my own advice: practicing self-care and doing everything I need to do to keep sane. See you tomorrow.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: For and against
item.content:encoded: Early in my career, I was web performance and accessibility and building cool things.But as JavaScript frameworks became increasingly ubiquitous, we saw the things I was start to degrade rapidly. Sites got slower and harder to use.The web took on a boring sameness.I spent increasing amounts of my time and energy being JS-heavy tooling like React and abstracting away writing code to NPM modules.More recently, I’ve been AI. Like the JS libraries of yore, it’s making the web shittier… for the same reasons as JS frameworks, and many new reasons, too.Friends, I’m so fucking sick of being things.I want to be things again, but the current state of the web and the tech industry more broadly has made that relatively impossible for me when it comes to web developer topics.That’s not to say there’s not still good things happening to the web. CSS is having a renaissance!But the joy is gone .They knew how. It wasn’t that they didn’t care or didn’t want to. They wanted. They still loved… what it had been.But as they tried to connect to what had once been so captivating, they felt nothing but yawning absence. A void where they’d once been filled.That’s essentially how I feel about dev more broadly right now.I can do the work. I enjoy the rote feeling of wielding an experts tools to practice my craft. It’s meditative, when I get into the coding zone.But that captivating spark? It’s gone.I’m writing here a lot less lately because I’ve been finding meaning outside of the web.I’ve been feeding people through a community farm stand I started out of my home. I’ve been doing outreach to unhoused folks in my area.I’ve been talking to strangers and reading books and riding my bike and exploring the little nooks and crannies of the new town I call home now.I should probably write more about those things.

item.title: Jayson Tatum And Jaylen Brown’s Beef Is Severely Undercooked
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: The weightlessness of the early season and the ever-increasing rate of injuries can make it hard to sell a weeknight NBA game in November. There remains, however, a reliable shortcut between "box score I'll check in the morning" and "game I gotta watch live," and it is a route lined with beef. Beef was not promised in the leadup to Tuesday night's game between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which pit former teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum against each other for the first time since Brown was traded in the offseason, but a savory aroma was in the air. Brown's trade brought with it all sorts of thinly sourced reports about he and Tatum having a contentious relationship, and those suspicions were more or less confirmed a few weeks ago. On Oct. 22, Tatum posted on YouTube another episode of his self-produced documentary series. A clip of this episode, in which Tatum recounts the shock he felt when he found out that Brown had been traded—"You traded him down the street?" he says to the person who broke the news—was posted on Instagram, and in the comments section of that post, Brown responded with the "cap" emoji.Brown was calling Tatum a liar, which was enough to elicit some direct questions about their relationship from reporters. ​"Jayson's a great guy," Brown said. "Like I said, great family, hell of a basketball player, hell of a PR team. There's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chops, and some gravy, you know what I mean? He should stay ready at all times."

item.title: Five Species That Harness Wildfires
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: For most animals, plants, and other life forms, fire is the worst thing that can happen. It's deadly, and even if you escape, your environment is ruined. But wildfires have always been a part of earth's activities, and some species have evolved to use it to their benefit. For example, the fire lily bulb stays dormant in the ground until after a wildfire rages through. Then it grows and blooms without competition from other plants! Plants that grow in the ashes of a wildfire attracts bugs, which attract birds. It's almost as if there's a system to heal and renew the environment after its devastated by fire. There are other species that are attracted to wildfires, and even one that actively spreads a fire. SciScow introduces us to how all this works. This video has a skippable ad from 6:00 to 6:48.

item.title: Miss Cellania's Links
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Celebrate the Nation’s Veterans With These 20 Stirring Photographs of American Military Heroes. Veterans Day Was Originally Called Armistice Day. And still is, in many parts of the world. Remaking Despite All the Reasons Not to Do That. I thought the 1998 version was tragically regressive. Thanksgiving Trends: What America Cooked, Forgot, and Ordered on DoorDash. (via Mental Floss) Here's an explanation of how Trump made billions off the presidency in the last two years. It doesn't even take direct bribes or pardon payments into account. (via MetaFilter) Unsettling True Stories That Belong In A Horror Movie Or Netflix Documentary. smell so bad? A microbiologist explains the odors brewing in your gut. (via Damn Interesting) 8 Bakers Failing At Ridiculously Simple Tasks. She was Arrested for Riding Astride a Horse in Central Park. item.title: rustel
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: rustel is a terminal studio and TUI for live-coding music with the Strudel pattern language.The studio features a live strudel code editor, a mixer, synths and sample playback, with Csound orchestras and support for VST3 instruments and effects. It shows the notes being played and graphs of the sound and you can edit the code while the music plays. It also includes a sample browser for previewing sounds if you're curious about the sample library.This tool also supports MIDI and OSC output, Ableton Link synchronization with other music software, themes, WAV or MP3 export and edit recovery. If an edit fails, rustel keeps playing the previous version. Its session tapes record applied code changes and their timing for replay. File watching reloads code saved from external editors during playback.rustel is ideal for programmers, musicians and hobbyists interested in live coding and algorithmic music. It is practical for composing tracks, experimenting with sound and performing sets in a terminal environment.

item.title: adbtop
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: adbtop is both CLI and TUI for monitoring Android app performance through Android Debug Bridge (adb) in the terminal.It can chart CPU and memory use for one app running on the device or the whole phone, alongside device statistics such as battery level and temperature. The CPU view shows activity for each core and thread and for individual apps, it reports frame rates and frames that take too long to draw.Users can launch or stop apps, measure startup times and test power-saving settings. The CLI saves JSON reports and CSV samples, including measurements taken after actions such as opening a screen. It also can be used to purposefully set limits on automated checks at runtime when properties such as memory, hangs or response time exceed certain limits set by the user.For Android developers, testers and QA engineers, adbtop is useful for investigating resource usage during app interactions, checking for memory leaks and testing performance issues before a release.

item.title: rumdl
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: rumdl is a high performance command-line tool for linting and formatting Markdown files.It checks for the headings, lists, links and code blocks content of a markdown file and reports rule names in the MDXXX format. A diff mode previews fixes before files change or applied and formatting, applies available fixes and may succeed with unresolved issues. Check mode returns a exit code for remaining violations in the document.This tool discovers common markdownlint configuration files and adjusts rules for Markdown flavors such as MkDocs and MDX. Its language server applies configured checks inside editors, and pre-commit hooks or CI integrations run them against repository changes.For developers, technical writers and documentation maintainers, rumdl helps keep Markdown files cleanly formatted and consistent across a project. It it is also useful for pre-commit checks after editing, before committing changes and catching formatting errors in the CI.

item.title: tidemail
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: tidemail is a CLI and TUI for reading, writing and managing email from several accounts.It supports Gmail, iCloud, Yahoo, Outlook and custom IMAP/SMTP providers and its interface shows accounts, folders, message lists and can open emails on one screen. Users can view all accounts in one inbox, search downloaded mail, add labels, archive and move or delete several messages together with bulk actions. It can preview pictures inside of emails in a supported terminal with Kitty graphics such as Ghostty, Rio or WezTerm, and only loads pictures from websites with permission from the user.Other features include support for file attachments, automatic draft saving, saved replies, optional spell checking and custom themes. It waits five seconds by default before sending an email, so users have a change to cancel it. It also reads downloaded mail, prepares drafts and sends messages with JSON results for optional scripting use-cases.For those who prefer handling email in the terminal, tidemail is ideal if you are looking for a unified inbox for multiple accounts without needing to use configuration files.

item.title: rat-commander
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: rat-commander is an all-in-one two-panel terminal file manager for browsing and manipulating local and remote files.Its interface is heavily inspired by midnight-commander with a two-pane window setting which you can copy, move or delete files between panels, and transfers files across storage devices in a progress window with a graphical speed chart. It can connect to remote hosts and mount directories via SFTP, SCP, FTP locations into the same panels and transfers normal file operations.What differentiates rat-commander is its command palette with over 100+ available operations, alongside several built-in tools such as a disk explorer showing the largest files indexed on disk, network connections inspector for active connections and a process explorer showing the list of all running processes on the machine. This tool has multiple preview views including a detail, tree, 3D view and a thumbnail view when showing the selected file or directory.Ideal for system administrators, software engineers and developers used to mc, rat-commander provides a similar two-panel file management across local folders and remote servers, whilst providing more built-in useful utilities included.

item.title: dasel
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: dasel is a command-line tool for querying, modifying and converting structured data.It uses the same selector syntax across JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV and other formats. Queries traverse nested objects or search for values matching a condition, and separate input and output formats enable composability uses in shell pipelines, CI/CD builds and in scripting use-cases for automation. dasel goes further than jq by having a built-in environment that allows for testing multiple dataset formats with a rapid feedback and response loop in the live preview in the query. Assignments in dasel change selected values, including values derived from each item in a collection.This tool is very useful towards developers, data engineers and system administrators who already use jq for JSON but need an alternative that supports multiple formats including JSON but also handle YAML or TOML, CSV and more for scripting and automation.

item.title: Everybody's Working for the Weakened
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: The new Dem majority hasn’t even been sworn in and the White House is already threatening to investigate the investigators. “The White House’s top lawyer is threatening a criminal investigation of Democrats for conducting what he alleges are illegitimate investigations into the executive branch — a stark escalation from the Trump administration as congressional Democrats prepare to launch an oversight onslaught when they assume the majority in January.” So the lawbreakers are threatening to go after the lawmakers. That doesn’t seem like the way it’s supposed to work, especially after an election when voters made it pretty clear that they are tired of the corruption. But while the Congress has the backing of a massive election win, the White House has something in its gold-leafed corner. A thoroughly decimated and corrupted Justice Department. And sadly, that’s a pretty big card to be able to play. “When the Justice Department has inserted itself between citizens denied their equal rights and the forces denying those rights, it has been a potent use of the U.S. government. Equally, though, when the Justice Department has inserted itself on the side of those denying others their rights, it has been a force multiplier for powerful interests. Short of the U.S. military, there is no greater coercive power that is brought to bear by the government against its citizens.” Rachel Maddow in (Gift Article): The Collapse of America’s Most Consequential Institution. “Over the course of its century and a half of existence, the Justice Department has been noble; it has been feckless; it has been corrupt. But now, in the midst of a full-fledged authoritarian challenge to the constitutional republic, the Justice Department has entered a whole new phase it has not been through before. It’s a phase you might call ‘gone’: missing, presumed dead.” Of course, a little more than a week ago, we could have made the same pronouncement about Congress.+ The White House and the Justice Department will make it as difficult as possible to investigate the nefarious behavior that took place in broad daylight. Jim Himes is the point person when it comes to uncovering what took place (way) behind the scenes. (Gift Article): Top Democrat Vows Oversight of C.I.A.’s Use of Covert Action. “The incoming Democratic chairman of the House Intelligence Committee is promising to scrutinize the C.I.A.’s ‘extremely aggressive’ use of covert actions since President Trump returned to office, part of a broader effort to conduct renewed oversight of American spy agencies next year … His committee, he added, will also examine donations to Mr. Trump’s various construction projects in Washington from defense and intelligence contractors, and investigate whether intelligence analysts have been pressured to write reports that align with the objectives of senior officials in the Trump administration.” In other words, Jim Himes and his committee are going to be awfully busy digging through what could be a sea of awfulness. (Full disclosure: I know Jim Himes. He’s exactly the person you want on the job.)“There will be parades and marching bands. Flag-waving and wreath-laying. Politicians will make speeches, friends will raise glasses and civilians will observe moments of silence. All to honor America’s service members, now and forever. But for those who have lost loved ones overseas in the Iran war, which has been waged since Feb. 28, this Veterans Day comes with a heaviness that only military families can fathom, and that will grow only more difficult as they face their first holiday season without their sons and daughters, siblings and spouses.” For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss. “Military families are navigating feelings of grief, pride and anger, as well as seeking answers about the deaths of their loved ones.”+ We don’t usually associate casualties of war with the people working on the frontlines of our cyber agencies. But it turns out that job is proving to be increasingly deadly. (Gift Article): More Suicides at Spy, Cyber Agencies Scrutinized by Congress. “There is a lot of stress that a lot of us overlook because we think cyber is away from the front, and physically that’s accurate but intellectually and emotionally it’s inaccurate.”“‘This was an audience we always thought might be lost to their small screens,’ said Paul Dergarabedian, head analyst of marketplace trends at Rentrak, a box-office data service. ‘But I think younger Gen Z audiences are particularly interested in those more handmade, tactile experiences, and going out to the movies is one of them. I think this is going to build on itself … The whole idea of moviegoing has become so cool.” (Gift Article): The Rise of the Gen Z Cinephile. “In states that have seen reproductive access drastically curtailed since the end of Roe v. Wade, newly empowered Democratic governors and lawmakers could repeal abortion restrictions, codify new protections, and work toward enshrining reproductive freedom in state constitutions. Democratic attorneys general could stop enforcing draconian laws that threaten abortion providers and helpers with prosecution and reject efforts to criminalize pregnancy loss.” The Democratic Tsunami Is a ‘Sea Change’ for Reproductive Rights.+ “Trump saw Russian diesel as a way to lower sky-high prices for the fuel, which contributed to rising consumer costs in the U.S. in the run-up to the midterm elections. But the diverted ships show U.S. oil companies are reluctant to handle the cargoes of Russian diesel because of the potential legal and reputational consequences.” (Gift Article): Trump’s Plan to Import Russian Diesel Stalls on the High Seas.+ “Ollie Ballinger, an open-source researcher and lecturer, uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts around the world. But he says pressure from the government has prompted private companies to restrict access to images of places it may not want the public to see.” An video report: The View From Space the U.S. Government Doesn’t Want You to See.+ “While Mr. al-Saadi is being held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, his communications with outsiders have been severely restricted. He has been shackled and held in a special housing unit often reserved for high-profile inmates … But while speaking by phone with his mother and sister over the summer, Mr. al-Saadi delivered coded messages about a forthcoming plot.” Failed Plot to Attack U.K. Base Used by U.S. Was Directed From New York Jail. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest official to be forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety.+ Chipping Away at the Story: “A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington’s efforts to curb China’s access to advanced technology.” Plus, tracking how Jensen Huang changed his stance on China. Huang should be investigated. But so should the people (including the top person) in the White House who enabled him.+ “The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.”Well, well, well, it looks like we finally picked the week to stop sniffing glue. “Doctors in Belgium detailed a man in his 40s who developed a strange lesion in his lungs after accidentally inhaling superglue. Thankfully, the lesion wasn’t cancerous as originally feared and appears to have caused no harm, but it’s stuck around in his lungs for at least nine years.”

item.title: The three names I never forget
item.author: 1axcf6uvpmg4upxuykvh5tibie5q5bh4qw0n9v@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: As a child growing up in New York, I knew very little about Mississippi. Other than trips to see my grandparents in Florida and a visit to Arlington National Cemetery, I had never been to the South.Most of what I knew about Mississippi came from learning about the civil rights era. Even then, to a young boy who had barely traveled outside his own neighborhood, it was mostly a blur of places I had little context to understand.There was, however, one place and three names I knew well.Philadelphia, Mississippi, is where three civil rights workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, were abducted and murdered in 1964 by members of the Ku Klux Klan, aided by local law enforcement.Like me, Goodman and Schwerner were white, Jewish New Yorkers. Chaney was a 21-year-old Black Mississippian from Meridian who had grown up under the very system the three were working to dismantle.The three men were part of Freedom Summer, the 1964 effort to register Black voters across Mississippi. Growing up, they were held up as examples of the importance of standing up for others' rights, even at great risk and sacrifice.They also sparked my interest in voting rights and shaped my view of politics.In 1980, when I was 11, Ronald Reagan campaigned at the Neshoba County Fair, just a few miles from where the three men were killed. Without any mention of them, he told the crowd, “I believe in states’ rights.” Weeks later, he stood in New Jersey and promised to “make America great again.”Eight years later, when I was in college, the movie “Mississippi Burning” was released. It was loosely based on the events surrounding the murders of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner.As I built my legal career, these three men and the cause they championed were never far from my mind. Ahead of the 2020 election, I had the opportunity to work with the Andrew Goodman Foundation on critical litigation to protect young voters.I will admit that until this year, I did not expect to see a Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state where Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner were murdered. Mississippi has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, and it has not had a Black senator since Reconstruction.But then again, I had never seen a candidate like Scott Colom.Colom is an extraordinary public figure: a prosecutor with compassion and an activist who knows how to achieve real change. He is truly a man for this moment.Last week, when Colom and his campaign needed a law firm to protect his lead, I jumped at the chance, not only because of Mississippi’s past but because of what Colom’s victory would mean for its future.In the days since, his lead has grown and so has my respect for him.I am 57 years old now. The stories of the civil rights struggle of the 1960s still linger in my mind. But in addition to being a lawyer, I am now the founder of Democracy Docket, an independent pro-democracy media outlet.So when the vote counting began in Mississippi, it was clear that Democracy Docket needed to be there to report on and document history in the making.For the first time, Democracy Docket sent journalists to cover the hour-by-hour, day-by-day developments in a close election. I have also done near-daily livestreams explaining what is happening and why.While the legacy media has treated this as a horse-race story between a Democrat and a Republican, Democracy Docket has covered it as what it fundamentally is: a story about democracy and free and fair elections.In the days ahead, I expect Scott Colom to be declared the winner and his election certified. When he takes office in January, I have every reason to believe he will become a critical voice in the fight for voting rights for all.Donald Trump and his cronies will continue to attack free and fair elections. I will return to the courtroom to stop voter suppression and election subversion.As I do, I will keep in mind the legacy of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner and what they fought and died for.That is the spirit I have tried to instill in Democracy Docket. I hope it shows every day.If you appreciate this work and share Democracy Docket’s commitment to telling the stories that matter most to voters and democracy, please join now. A premium membership gives you access to all of Democracy Docket’s exclusive content. More importantly, it makes possible the kind of coverage this moment demands.I have come a long way from the young boy growing up in New York learning about Philadelphia, Mississippi, and so has our country. I am proud to be in this fight for Scott Colom and Mississippi voters.

item.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 74: Jeffrey Silverstein
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, host Bob Holmes of the band SUSS is joined by one of the leading practitioners of a style of music that might best be called "cosmic country”: the Portland, Oregon-based artist Jeffrey Silverstein. Bob and Jeffrey discuss some of the roots of this genre with music by Bobby Lee, Joe Harvey-Whyte, Six Organs of Admittance, and more. They also explore the backstories of Jeffrey's latest release, , on the label Full Time Hobby.For Flow State we’re listening to two of Silverstein’s records, beginning with . Described as “loner-folk” and “kraut-laden choogle,” the album was recorded with a full band including pedal steel and saxophone (on “Patchouli”). There are occasional half-sung, half-spoken vocals, but as Silverstein says on the podcast those are more like the musician briefly checking in with the listener rather than being the centerpiece of the song. We’re also playing from 2023, which shows the country influences and features William Tyler on track two.

item.title: It turns out Jensen Huang is just as awful as the other tech overlords
item.content:encoded: A few days ago, you were minding your own business, unconcerned about Jensen Huang or his penis. Perhaps you were still celebrating last week’s election results, and the mild improvement to civilization those results portended. When suddenly, out of nowhere, the name JENSEN HUANG was all over your internet, your nightly news, perhaps even your group text chains. Now you can’t stop hearing about this man, or about how he and his libido got trapped in a byzantine web of international intrigue that involves multitrillion-dollar companies, Silicon Valley, China, the president of the United States, and the growing scourge of artificial intelligence. Who is this Jensen Huang fella, and what exactly has he gotten America into?Reader, fear not. I am a licensed journaltician, and I have a penis of my own. That makes me the most qualified man in America to answer all of your questions regarding this, the juiciest tech scandal since Lizzy Holmes tried to suck cancer patients’ blood using a busted Texas Instruments calculator. Let’s get to the tea.Huang is a Taiwanese American Stanford grad who currently serves as CEO of Nvidia, a hardware company that has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.Article continues below this adQ: How did Nvidia get so big?Because it produces the chips that virtually every American AI company uses to power their now ubiquitous large language models. When the introduction of ChatGPT launched the AI boom a couple of years ago, it was Huang’s chips providing virtually all of the hardware underneath that technology’s infrastructure. As a result, the company’s stock price increased by orders of magnitude, growing Huang’s billions and making Nvidia itself worth trillions. Along the way, Huang got the familiar kid glove treatment from the tech press, who lavished the baron with photo shoots of him clad in his beloved leather jacket, and portraying him as a different breed of cat from all of the other Stanford grads.Q: What made him different?Huang famously eschewed normal, snooty CEO practices in favor of having his employees email him directly. Specifically, he has them outline the “Top 5” things they’re working on at any given moment, which gives him a clearer idea of what’s happening at Nvidia, rather than just relying on a few yes-men to feed him daily rations of bulls—t. Tesla CEO Elon Musk would later steal the “five things” format as a means of having his DOGE goons hollow out the federal government.Article continues below this adWhy yes.Q: OK, enough of the background stuff. Get to the sexy business.Hold up, I still have a bit more pre-explaining to do.I deserved that. Now, the American AI market is a tangle of self-dealing that, as with all financial boondoggles, is deliberately opaque. The less regular folks understand about what these entities are doing, the more they can get away with. But Huang apparently wasn’t satisfied with his company merely dominating the American AI marketplace through such chicanery. He wanted the Chinese market, too. But since the U.S. and China are economic rivals, selling Nvidia’s wares to the People’s Republic of China was a bit of a no-no. Now, Huang did a bit of ring-kissing at the White House to get official approval to do business across the Pacific. But Huang appears to have done a bit of illicit, and mildly erotic, back-channeling to enter the Chinese market before getting that blessing.Article continues below this adThis is where a woman named Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) enters the picture.The honeypot. Huang is a managing director at a Singapore-based tech firm called Megaspeed. According to indispensable tech blogger Ed Zitron, in 2023 Megaspeed launched a subsidiary company named SpeedMatrix, which then purchased over $4 billion in Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs). The facts get murky from here, but the suspicion is that those GPUs were then smuggled into China. Meantime, Huang and Huang reportedly decide to mix business with pleasure. This was a bad move on Jensen Huang’s part, as he’s already a married man. Even thornier, the New York Times reported that as early as a year ago, U.S. lawmakers had reason to believe that Alice Huang was an operative for the Chinese government, had been working to evade U.S. export controls, and had developed a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang. With access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, China could pose an even larger security threat to the U.S. Mission accomplished, ma’am.Q: Do we think the sex was good?It better have been.Article continues below this adQ: What’s the fallout been?Still ongoing. Huang issued the standard public apology to his wife and kids, writing in a statement published Sunday, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” although he did not specify whom he had an affair with (if I were Lori Mills, the wife, I’d take his ass to the cleaners). The company also announced its own internal investigation. Meantime, someone in President Lame Duck’s administration may have deliberately quashed a federal investigation into Megaspeed that could have given us a clearer picture of the f—kery at hand. And the president himself, no stranger to using his penis in malevolent fashion, came to his new best buddy’s defense: “He had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. And I really believe him.” If you share a taco salad with Trump and say nice things about him, he’ll believe anything you say.Q: Do you think Huang was duped?In my opinion, it doesn’t matter. Whether or not Huang deliberately conspired with the Chinese or was an unwitting abettor, he’s still guilty as all hell. But don’t worry. Trump has already informed the nation that the FBI will be investigating the matter further.The same. Trump already told Huang that he has nothing to fear from Patel’s FBI. So that was a fun waste of all of our time.Article continues below this adQ: What does this mean for me?If you hold Nvidia stock (DISCLOSURE: My wife and I own some of this stock as part of our retirement nest egg), you’re probably not too happy about Jensen Huang’s dalliances. Since news of his possible entrapment broke in October, the company stock price has cratered from a high of $243.37 a share to, as of this writing, $168.18. Even worse, the company’s stranglehold on AI hardware threatens to hurt the value of every other major tech company, because all of these corporations have invested literal trillions of dollars into AI. If those companies tank, then suddenly there goes a hefty portion of your 401(k), your IRA, your pension, your everything.You are not alone. Nvidia shareholders are filing lawsuits against Huang, and Democrats poised to take control of the federal government after the New Year are sure to conduct a much more thorough inquiry into the saga than sorry-ass Kash Patel will. Also, even though Huang is the CEO of Nvidia, he, unlike the likes of Elon Musk, does not hold enough personal stake in his company to block Nvidia’s board from removing him. He can be fired. The problem is that no one at his company seems all that keen on pulling the trigger. Huang’s cult of personality at Nvidia is so strong that no one else there appears to believe that it can survive without him. And if that’s truly the case, do you guys REALLY want the second largest company in America to go down? Because there’s a chance that the implications from its demise could reverberate down to you, even if you don’t own any stock of any sort. Trump may be done and dusted, but the too-big-to-fail dilemma here in America is not. In other words, Huang is probably gonna get away with it.Q: I hate this man! And his penis!So do I, my friend. So do I.Article continues below this ad

item.title: Will Schumer Be Leader? Should He Be?
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: A few thoughts on Chuck Schumer and whether he’ll continue as leader in the Senate. One important detail. Senate leadership works differently from House leadership. Majority Leader isn’t a constitutional position. So unlike the House where it’s a public vote and you need a majority of the body, in the Senate, it’s a secret ballot and Schumer needs only a majority of his caucus. So a handful of defections won’t settle this.I said multiple times over the last two years that while I think highly of Schumer, he’s not characterologically or generationally suited to the moment. The big question that faces us today isn’t ideological, “centrists” vs. progressives, it’s fight vs. accommodation. Or, put differently, are we in a normal period of American history in which regular order should prevail or are we in an ongoing national emergency? Schumer thinks in terms of the first and not the second.

item.title: Institute Corporal Punishment For Democratic Strategists
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: Here is a thing that Republicans do not do when they sweep into power: They do not bother brainstorming ways that they can signal a values match with the people who oppose them, and whom they have just defeated. They do not look around, blinking, from the hilltop they have just won, and fret about appealing to the vanquished foes lying half-dead at their feet. When Republicans win, they set about changing the laws, or using the existing laws to their advantage. That is the job. Republican lawmakers express their values through the laws that they make and enforce. They do not get sidetracked by the idea that they can make friends with progressives, and not only because they know that their voters do not want them to do that. They perceive an authentic mismatch of values, and their solution to that is to make progressives eat shit.You will say that this is a weakness of their politics. You will point to their long-dwindling popularity and last week's electoral bloodbath, and say that their reflexive and idiotic tribalism is a terminal illness, and that Democrats should learn from it only that it is self-defeating. You fool. Here you have done them the favor of flattening the actual, substantive, qualitative differences between the goals of the right and the left.You shouldn't do that, because those differences are important. People on the left want things—actual tangible things: laws and institutions and structures—that make sense, that arise from active, curious, engaged minds thinking deeply about how to run a community of any size or complexity. Those things are aimed at the goal of making society more equitable and less brutal, and making life more dignified and less degrading.

item.title: USPS Announces Mythical Creatures Stamps for 2027
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: The legend of Mothman has endured for more than six decades, but of the creatures encountered on these stamps, this flying, man-sized, red-eyed being emerged the most recently. The cryptid was first reported in West Virginia in 1966. Several nights after a gravedigger reported a winged, human-sized creature swooping above, two couples on a midnight drive in the rural outskirts of Point Pleasant reported being chased from overhead at great speed as they fled back to town. Newspapers dubbed the creature “Mothman.” After a year of eerie sightings was followed by a local tragedy, some interpreted the appearances as harbingers of disaster. In the years since, a lighter side of Mothman has been embraced by festival attendees, many in “spooky-cute” costumes that evoke this increasingly popular cryptid.Unlike most of the creatures on these stamps, the Jackalope has been spotted by a great many Americans. It has multiplied rapidly, especially in the West, since first appearing in the 1930s in Douglas, Wyoming. This antlered rabbit was the creation of two young brothers studying taxidermy by mail who, in a moment of inspiration after a hunting trip, crafted the hoax. When the masterful mashup was displayed at a local inn, the Jackalope quickly sprang into regional folklore. Today, Jackalopes are found in gift shops in the Great Plains and Western states — on postcards, stickers, and T-shirts, and as plush toys and mounted specimens. The fanciful hybrid endlessly inspires the imaginations of those who encounter it, and who add to its lore with their own stories, songs, and artworks.The Squonk hides away in northern Pennsylvania’s dense hemlock forests, so distressed by its own appearance that it cries constantly. This piglike animal, wrinkled, blemished, and self-conscious, was first described in print in a 1910 collection of lumberjack folklore, Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods. The book — recounting tales often spun and re-spun by the fireside in remote logging encampments of the 19th and early 20th centuries — relates an episode of a Squonk captured in a bag: As the hunter carried his prey, its weeping faded and the sack grew lighter. Investigation revealed that the Squonk had melted into “nothing but tears and bubbles.” In recent years, the melancholy character has been revived as a darling mascot of introverts and anyone else who relates to the Squonk’s social anxiety.Sasquatch captures the American imagination like no other cryptid. Nobody, though, has captured Bigfoot, as this large hairy hominid is commonly called, nor even retrieved a confirmed strand of hair from its notoriously stinky, shaggy fur. In the Pacific Northwest, ancient Indigenous tales of mysterious, hairy humanoids encouraged caution in the wild and mindful custodianship of forest habitat. By the late 20th century, reported sightings of Sasquatch and similar regional creatures had taken hold and spanned the nation. In fact, tales of huge bipeds are told worldwide, almost anywhere shadowy terrain could conceivably conceal such elusive beings. Hoaxes abound, including blurry films and casts of outsized human-like footprints, but the most notable impression Sasquatch makes is its lasting mark on American popular culture. Even if our most famous mythical creature is nowhere to be found, Sasquatch is everywhere.Champ, as the Lake Champlain monster is affectionately known, is said to dwell within the nation’s sixth largest lake, which defines more than 100 miles of the New York–Vermont border. A glacial lake reaching 400 feet deep and 14 miles wide is bound to contain mysteries — over the last few centuries, hundreds have claimed to see the serpentine organism. Cryptozoologists have tried to determine what it could be: perhaps a descendant of an aquatic, dinosaur-era reptile or whale, as found in fossils? Skeptics point to more mundane possibilities: sturgeon and other large fish that inhabit the lake, swimming deer, waves, mirages, and tree trunks riding currents. While a living specimen has proven elusive, Champ is ever-present as a beloved mascot of the region, celebrated in business logos, and in festivals and museum exhibits.

item.title: Harrison Butker’s PAC Is Going About As Well As His Kicking
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: Harrison Butker is having the worst season of his NFL career. And if that weren't good enough news, his financial foray into politics is basically dead.Butker, placekicker for the Kansas City Chiefs, has hit only 63.2 percent of his field goals this season. He's missed at least one field goal in six of his eight games, and his accuracy from long range has escaped him: He's 2-for-8 on field goals attempted from 50 or more yards. In Sunday's 35-12 win over the New York Jets, Butker made all five of his extra point attempts, but whiffed on a 51-yarder right before halftime. That doesn't matter much against the Jets, but against a more competitive opponent, in a game that might be decided by only three points, Butker isn't as reliable as he once was. Instead of trying to restore masculine values, he should worry more about trying to restore his mechanics.Andy Reid remained vague on whether Butker would keep kicking for Kansas City this coming weekend. "I'll address that as we go throughout the week," the head coach said after Sunday's win. If the Chiefs were to make a change, they would likely look to the practice squad and elevate Justin Tucker, who hasn't seen NFL action since the 2024 season, and was cut by the Baltimore Ravens in 2025 after numerous massage therapists in the area accused him of sexual misconduct. K.C.'s special teams has the roster depth and moral fiber of the White House press secretary pool.

item.title: Jim Jordan and The Ohio State Student Athlete Sex Abuse Cover Up
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: With Jim Jordan elected GOP leader, let’s remember that Jordan is part of a longstanding coverup of sexual abuse of student athletes at Ohio State by Dr. Richard Strauss. The story got a lot of attention a few years ago and it briefly seemed possible that it might derail Jordan’s position in the House GOP caucus. But he stonewalled, refused to credibly address the allegations and eventually his colleagues and conservative media gave him a pass. He’s never come clean about any of it. As recently as last year there was a whole new documentary about it. Multiple ex-wrestlers and even a ref describe how Jordan knew about it, turned a blind eye and has been lying about it ever since. “To say that (Jordan) knew nothing, that nothing ever happened, it’s a flat out lie,” said former Ohio State Wrestler Dan Ritchie in the documentary. You’d think House Republicans would be stung enough by Donald Trump’s main character status in the Epstein Files. But memories are short. Jordan was never the caucus leader until now. Democrats need to be certain everyone knows that his colleagues know about his stonewalling and the coverup and are fine with it.

item.title: The History of Salt
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: We all need salt to function, so animals evolved to seek it out. Lucky for us, the salty seas have left deposits of salt everywhere, if we can find them. Humans, however, sought salt so much that today our doctors tell us to lay off the salty snacks and put away the shaker because it can lead to high blood pressure. It wasn't always this way, because salt was not always so easy to get. the quest for salt as a commodity goes all the way back to the beginning of agriculture. Those who had it became rich selling it, although it wasn't easy- that's why working in the salt mines became a metaphor for backbreaking, unpleasant labor. Getting salt to those who had less became one of the reasons we developed global trade. This TED-Ed lesson brings us a short history of sale, but try to resist the urge to grab some chips while watching it.

item.title: Cooper Flagg Makes It All Make Sense
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: The best players make basketball look simple. The effect is mostly illusory, a byproduct of their size and skill warping a complex game, though there's something to the idea. In essence, what a star does is make the game easier for their team and more difficult for the opponent. It's not rendering anything simple, exactly, more like adding to or subtracting from the bevy of available options for, respectively, one's team or one's opponents. You can only do simple stuff if you have the best players.Cooper Flagg is one such player. Watching him dominate the Indiana Pacers Monday night, I was struck by how simple it all looked for the 19-year-old. With his Dallas Mavericks trailing by 10 coming out of halftime, Flagg made a point of taking and nailing three straight midrange jumpers, shots he can get to anytime he wants. Three times, the cockroach (complimentary) Pacers dodged getting squished and made their way back into one-possession range; with the game on the line, Flagg calmly got the rock and went to work.Flagg wound up with 43 points on 25 shots in 39 minutes, 10 rebounds, six assists, and four stocks, all on the second night of a back-to-back. He played the entire fourth quarter and hit all eight of his free throws. He turns 20 next week, and is at most a few months older than the youngest draftees in the rookie class after his. He's taken to munching PB-and-Js at all times because he's still a young growing boy. Something interesting is happening in Dallas, somehow, which all comes down to Flagg's undeniable superstardom.

item.title: How Much Wealth Does It Take to be Safe in the United States?
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Pulitzer Prize winning journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s new book is about wealth inequality in America. Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (Amazon) follows ten people with ten different incomes, from the bottom 10% to the top 10% and everything in-between:For five years, data journalist Mona Chalabi followed them all, documenting how wealth shaped their feelings, their choices, their identities, and their insecurities. She researched the data behind their taxes, groceries, inheritances, and so much more to understand the systems that keep people stuck. But then, she too found herself facing the same fears, when her mother’s sudden illness and subsequent medical bills threatened her own financial safety and made the questions she had been writing about all too real. How much money is enough? To live a “good” life? To protect the people you love in an emergency?Part of the message of the book is that class doesn’t show up enough in our intersectional identities, and that that’s fundamentally dishonest. I would hope that people read the book and then get much more fluent and comfortable with describing their current wealth and income, as well as the one that they grew up in. I think that’s kind of ambitious, but you never know.

item.title: Jonathan Abrams Writes About NBA Players In Three Dimensions
item.author: Owen Lewis
item.content:encoded: From 2007 to 2009, Oklahoma City Thunder general manager Sam Presti selected future NBA MVPs Kevin Durant, Russell Westbrook, and James Harden in three consecutive drafts, securing the fledgling team an otherworldly core. The results were brilliant and tumultuous. The Thunder started out 3-29 in 2008, but within a couple of years rounded into a fearsome squad that gave the 2010 Lakers a scare, and eventually reached the 2012 NBA Finals, where they went toe to toe with LeBron James's Miami Heat and lost. Then Presti traded Harden, setting in motion a future that would scatter the trio around the league. As they broke apart, they'd help mold the league into its modern shape.Jonathan Abrams, a culture reporter who began his career covering the NBA and has written about it extensively at the , Grantland, and Bleacher Report's magazine, is out with a new book, , about these players and their importance in modern NBA history. At Grantland, Abrams wrote longform profiles and oral histories, in which you could relive the Malice at the Palace, become familiar with the particulars of how an almost-dynasty fell apart, or learn that the Orlando Magic came disturbingly close to being called the "Juice."It's that style of dedicated reporting and patient storytelling that enlivens all three of the book's protagonists, whom Abrams refers to only by their first names. When We Were Young and Fearless leaves the reader with a fascinating image of what the 2010s Thunder could have been, but its greatest feat is perhaps the sympathy and complexity with which it imbues three of the greatest players of the 21st century.

item.title: Why This Trump Lame-Duck Judicial Nomination Could be a Self-Own for the Ages
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: At Stake: Secret OLC MemosThe worst of the Trump II foreign misadventures were sanctioned by still-secret memoranda produced by the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel — and now President Trump is poised to nominate the head of that office to fill a federal judgeship in Texas.An Ohio native, Gaiser fits the mold for a Trump judge. He graduated from conservative Christian Hillsdale College and the University of Chicago School of Law. He clerked for diehard MAGA conservative judges Edith Jones on the 5th Circuit (his one notable connection to Texas), Neomi Rao on the D.C. Circuit, and Justice Samuel Alito. Gaiser was the solicitor general of Ohio before he joined the Justice Department last year.Gaiser will now face a confirmation process in the Senate even as the House is moving toward a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — let this sink in — for overseeing military operations that the OLC under Gaiser blessed with some of its most controversial and still-secret memos.Against that backdrop, nominating Gaiser to the bench is an especially aggressive move. It gives senators newfound leverage to obtain the still-secret (or partially redacted) OLC memos which are suspected of having blessed (i) usurping Congress’ war powers; (ii) a boat-strike campaign that is viewed nearly universally by legal experts as a violation of international law and the rules of war; and (iii) the capture of Venezuela’s Maduro as a “law enforcement operation.”“The nomination of Gaiser for a judgeship is also likely to be, in significant part, a self-own,” NYU law professor Ryan Goodman noted yesterday. “It will very likely yield the public release of Gaiser/OLC opinions on (a) the boat strikes and (b) whatever convoluted magic the OLC concocted to say the Iran war was legal.”As Goodman pointed out, there is fairly recent precedent for senators using the leverage of a confirmation hearing to extract an OLC memo from an administration. Back in 2014, President Obama’s nomination of David J. Barron to the 1st Circuit gave a group of senators the chance to demand a secret OLC memo that justified drone strikes in Yemen that had killed four suspected terrorists who were U.S. citizens, including Anwar al-Awlaki. Barron had authored the memo while serving as the acting head of OLC. The Obama-era memo was turned over on the eve of Barron’s confirmation vote.Impeaching and even convicting Hegseth only gets you so much so long as Donald Trump remains president. Trump selects the next defense secretary, and the Pentagon — like the rest of the administration — is run out of the Trump White House.But a federal judgeship is different.Confirming Gaiser, just 37 years old, puts him on the federal bench for life. It potentially insulates him from further scrutiny for his conduct while at DOJ — in the same way that former acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove was safely ensconced on the Third Circuit Court of Appeals. Perhaps senators have learned a lesson since that fiasco. Perhaps not.: This item initially misidentified the circuit court on which Judge Barron sits.The Purges: Hegseth Google EditionDefense Secretary Hegseth’s office used Google searches for evidence of wokeness to weed out senior officers recommended for promotion as he purged the upper ranks of the military, MS Now reports:The senior official described to MS NOW how Hegseth’s executive office led a planned and deliberate process that involved creating paper-only files filled with printouts from internet searches that were inaccessible to the officers under consideration. Hegseth’s office gave instructions about the new criteria over the phone instead of in writing.The senior official described to MS NOW what was in the paper files for more than a dozen of the senior officers whose promotions were withheld. Some of the findings put into the paper-only files included officers who allowed a celebration that included rainbow flags, a Pride Month event and stood up a diversity committee and task force on the USS Kearsarge to combat discrimination.: On U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s watch, D.C. grand juries have refused to return indictments in three different cases in the past two weeks, the NYT reports. Two of the cases involved alleged voting fraud; one was the politicized prosecution of Trump I White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson.: The Trump DOJ is asserting various privileges rather than turn over some internal communications to U.S. District Judge April Perry in her inquiry into whether she was misled by DOJ attorneys in the since-abandoned prosecution of Operation Midway Blitz protesters. Or as Chicago Sun-Times reporter Jon Seidel wryly put it:Chicago U.S. Attorney’s office in March: “There are no communications … with anyone outside the [U.S. attorney’s office].”Main Justice today: “Please find a privilege log asserting privileges applicable to these communications.”: Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd of Seattle, installed as part of President Trump’s U.S. attorney scheme, made a remarkable admission to the federal judges in the Western District of Washington. In a letter last week, Floyd said that his office is too overwhelmed to continue to contest each of the immigrant habeas cases filed in the flood of such cases unleashed by Trump’s mass deportation operation.US Aircraft Flee RAF Base AgainFor the second time in the last five weeks, the U.S. military has evacuated aircraft from a Royal Air Force base in the U.K. under potential threat from Iran.How the April car crash in Mexico that killed two CIA operatives blew the agency’s cover, triggered a national scandal south of the border, and sent the man who helped the CIA on the run.Lame-duck Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) — a pariah in her own party after she endorsed (losing) GOP nominee Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race — was hard to find when Congress returned to Capitol yesterday. But she was eventually spotted hanging out in the Republican cloakroom.
