item.title: Whining whiner whines about a stolen election. The entire world tells him to shut the fuck up.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: It’s certainly been a perfectly goddamned delightful week, hasn’t it?One by one, the worst shitheads in the world lost their elections. Corruption-factory Ken Paxton. Political tourist Darline Graham. Barrel-bottom slimeball Vivek Ramaswamy. All gone , replaced by actual, fundamentally decent people. Pinch us, we must be dreaming, am I right?But one thing’s been missing, through this entire week. One familiar noise that’s been conspicuously absent from the national discourse. What could it be?Does anybody really believe that this “Election” was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJTWait a minute. Hold on, what in the actual fuck is this half-baked, weak-tea bullshit?Donny, you’ve had to work yourself up into a thermonuclear lather, and this is the pathetic mewling you end up farting out? Come on. This is a stolen election, man — it’s right in your wheelhouse. This is the shit you live for.Couldn’t you have put more effort into this post? Where’s the all-caps hysteria? Where are the multiple exclamation points? This is so low-energy. is that what you want us to call you now? Bro, did you fall asleep in the middle of writing this? Did the Diaper Nurse have to finish it for you, and click ‘send’? Where are the clownish misspellings? Remember “RIGGED AND STOLLEN” from 2020? Six years later, we’re still pissing ourselves with laughter at that dumbfuckery. Come on, dude. Give us something to work with here. You didn’t even bother to thank us for our attention.And why just post? Why not a dozen, each one that much more hysterical than the last? Come on, bro. This is the best you can do? I’m so fucking disappointed in you, Donny. I expected so much better. We all did.Actually, the best part of Donny’s post was the reaction from the rest of the world, which pretty much rose up as one to tell him to shut the fuck up.This is getting so old, so fast. You lost. Get over it.Rep McGovern is right. Donny lost, and he really needs to stick a fucking sock in it.The first stage of grief is denial, Donald.Even MAGA’s reaction to Dear Leader’s post was muted. Everyone’s so tired of this shit. MAGA the election wasn’t RIGGED. Nor was it STOLLEN. They themselves voted for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa and Annie Andrews and Abdul El-Sayed, and on and on. No one has time for any of Donny’s clownfuckery right now. We all just want it to end. January 3rd can’t come fast enough.Oh, but Donny wasn’t finished with us, after his whiny ‘stolen election’ post. He had lots more crazy left in the tank. At around four in the afternoon, he summoned the media for a hastily-thrown-together, unscheduled press conference starring none other than The Wrong Dana White™.The premise of this slapdash dog-and-pony show? That Donny, irrepressible madcap scamp that he is, was just funning with us, when he claimed to have offered the job of White House Press Secretary to the Wrong Dana.Dana White: “I don’t tell brothers ‘no’ to anything, I know. I didn’t say no. I literally— everybody— every media outlet was calling me, and I didn’t want to be disrespectful and say anything until he— he— he, uh, said something first, so—”Donny: “We were having a very bad press day. And I said— I don’t know why— I thought of his name. Been my friend for a long time. I said, ‘you know, I think I’m going to get— DANA WHITE to be my new press secretary, sent it to a group of— of— press. And that was it. I sent it to them. And then, they wrote the story as if I wasn’t kidding. And you were INUNDATED and I was inundated. He was here anyway, with— we thought we would have a little fun, and we brought Dana in. He would be— fantastic.” I have two words. Bull and shit.Oh please. That’s not what happened at all. I will go to my final resting place convinced that the actual story played out as I wrote it up the other day. Someone in the White House suggested naming the actual trained media spokesperson Dana White be the new Press Sec, and dumb demented Donny got it wrong and mistakenly offered the job to his crony Dana White, the dude who arranges human cockfights for money.That’s what happened, I’m sure of it. Donny doesn’t make jokes. He has no sense of humor. Yesterday’s unscheduled presser was a face-saving operation. The Wrong Dana™ had been in London, and they flew him all the way across the ocean so just he could stand at that podium and pretend to have been joking right along with Donny. An actual joke doesn’t need that much explaining attached to it.The fact that Donny’s handlers put this much time and effort into denying that Donny was making a serious offer is all the proof you need that Donny was in fact making a serious offer.And look at all the worthless scribblers of the corporate-controlled press, falling for it and laughing. How fucking embarrassing for everyone involved.But wait — the crazy lasted all the way into the evening.What the hell? Did you notice that? As Geerges takes the call, a woman is heard giggling in the background, followed by the grating sound of Dear Leader’s voice.What the fuck was going on? Were Donny and his diaper nurse tickling each other, going, ‘No, YOU call C-SPAN. TEE HEE HEE’? Where are the adults? What if it hadn’t been C-SPAN? What if Donny and Natty had been daring each other to phone in the nuclear launch codes? Don’t laugh, you know damned well it could happen. Donny then proceeds to ramble incoherently for eight entire minutes, his putrefying brain pinballing from immigration, to Piss-Drunk Pete Kegstand, to Venezuela, to Iran, and back and forth and back and forth. Mimi Geerges keeps trying to interject and steer the conversation, and he just barrels right over her. Eventually, Donny exhausts himself, and Geerges manages to get him off the phone.It’s fucking batshit. What in god’s name is going on? Donny and Natty should not be left alone, unsupervised. Who knows what they’ll get up to next? Let’s palate cleanse with some Thomas Massie.“The Secretary has scheduled his own press conference, that they’re going to let him deliver a rebuttal. And to that point, I hope he addresses the eight articles, and doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion, and do some pull-ups, and, you know, call everybody fat and gay. I may have just given you half his speech, I don't know.”Look, let’s be clear-eyed. Thomas Massie is not our friend. He’s against most of the things we’re for. The Heritage Foundation gives him a 96% rating. Reporter: “Have you spoken to Sen. McConnell about this effort?”Massie: “I have not, but if it were possible to have a conversation with McConnell...”Oh man. I only wish Mitch McConnell had been alive to hear himself dissed like that.And now it’s time for our Daily Claudia. Here’s a triptych from our living room on December 31, 2021.Have a great Tuesday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Come and Take It
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: AI companies are trying to take the only cool thing their tech has ever done, making me vaguely interested for the first time ever in the concept of open weight models, local AI, etc. Time to take out a second mortgage on the house I don't have to finance a graphics card. Anyways, let's get into it:It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs. Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account banned for violating its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts restricted. A project called Decomp.wtf that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior. The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most. Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted. But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails. “My general experience about reverse-engineering getting blocked has been more or less 100% correlated with the ‘cyber’ category blocks I have received. My take is that the lab[s] are probably under pressure to not have their models take part in some kind of criminal hacking activities and their cyber guardrails are erring on the side of being too strict,” Matt Brown, principal consultant at Brown Fine Security and someone who has been using AI to reverse-engineer devices, told 404 Media. “I am investing in hardware and trying to stay up to speed because the frontier labs guardrails will randomly change without warning on the same model. For my security research and pentesting work I really don’t want to invest tooling and energy into an ecosystem that will eventually lock me out. These guardrails on the frontier side have come at the same time as open weight models from (mostly) China are getting better and better.” According to a police incident report obtained by 404 Media, a father in South Carolina asked his six-year-old daughter if she “had the gun” before he left her alone at Target for more than an hour in the middle of the night so “he could maintain his place in line” to buy Pokémon cards. The Department of Justice said that it no longer has enough attorneys available to respond to every habeas corpus challenge, and will begin letting judges rule on cases with no government opposition. Basically this suggests that ICE has detained so many people illegally that it no longer has enough attorneys to argue in these cases. Alarming, but also means that enough people are challenging their detentions that ICE is beginning to cry uncle. Also, I would normally never suggest you go watch a Bari Weiss x Ross Douthat joint, but parts of the interview with Trump were SO WILD. Perhaps this guy doesn’t really stand for anything? Hmm. Our friends over at Court Watch are doing a subscriber drive. Court Watch grabs court records off the notoriously expensive PACER document system and makes them available for free and finds extremely interesting and important cases all the time. We partner with them on a bunch of stories so go check/help them out. The best Raspberry Pi on the market now costs $385. I remember when the whole point of a Raspberry Pi was that it cost, like, $20. This is, of course, due to the RAM/memory/everything shortage caused by AI data center buildout. If you know what people are doing with these top-end Raspberry Pis, let me know?Actors alarmed to learn that they had been replaced by AI in the Return of the Living Dead sequel they were set to star in. The surveillance state, now for kids: The Atlantic has a deep dive on what constant surveillance is doing to children. I haven’t had time to read the full thing yet, but have been waiting for a piece like this for a long time.

item.title: Royals free agent targets: The position players
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: A little over a week since the start of free agency and there's been little movement. Not surprising, but to me, that first large free agent signing...that’s the official start of the offseason. As noted previously in this space, the specter of the owners locking out the players at the start of December means the next several weeks should see a flurry of activity. Already, agent Scott Boras who represents the consensus top free agent Tarik Skubal, is predicting his lefty will sign sometime this month. If that's happening, the whole market could hit frenzy status in the next couple of weeks.With that in mind, it’s time to focus on the players currently on the market who could help the Royals when they finally play ball in 2027.The Royals need to be bold this offseason. I mean . If they deem a player on their current roster is simply “good enough,” then they should probably be looking for an upgrade at that particular position. While left field and center field are obvious positions of need for the Royals, I would proffer second base into that mix. Michael Massey had a fine 2026, producing 2.3 fWAR on the back of stellar defense at the keystone. Offensively, he hit .274/.305/.430 which, with a 100 wRC+, was dead-on league average. But this year’s class at second base is deep. There are possibilities there.As for center, I am intrigued by the presence of Carson Roccaforte in the Royals prospect pipeline. He won a minor league gold glove and went 30/30 with 35 bombs and 32 bags split between stops in Double-A Northwest Arkansas and Triple-A Omaha. He earned that bump to the Storm Chasers later in the season and ended up with 118 PAs over 28 games. That is to say, with such limited exposure to the top of the minors, he probably needs a bit more seasoning to be ready for the show. A stop-gap option in center should remain on the free agent shopping list, although the pickings at that position are extremely slim. And left field has kind of been a disaster since Alex Gordon went south after 2015. Where have you gone, Andrew Benintendi? Royals nation turns it’s lonely eyes to you.We know the Royals are set at short, third and catcher. First base could probably use an upgrade if you don’t have strong feelings in favor of Vinnie Pasquantino, but free agency is the worst place to look to upgrade that position. Right field is settled for the moment as well. That leaves second (possibly) along with left and center as areas where the Royals could see improvement.I’ve compiled some names the Royals should be checking on as the free agent market begins to take shape. The names below are not endorsements. Merely, they are players of interest. As such, I'm ignoring the top end of the position player class. Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are going to be out of the Royals comfort zone. That's not necessarily a bad thing as I'm not sure either one will live up to a four-year (or more) deal. Same for Brandon Lowe. All three received a qualifying offer as well, which would make them even less attractive to a team like the Royals. Those players of interest I have identified for the Royals are listed with their three-year averages in batting average, on base percentage and slugging. Also noted are their three-year averages in wRC+ and fWAR, along with walk and strikeout rates. And finally, I've posted their initial Steamer projections for the 2027 season from FanGraphs. 2027 Steamer Projection: .304/.344/.406, 110 wRC+, 2.8 fWARNobody finds fewer barrels, swings a slower bat and has a lower hard-hit rate than Luis Arraez. Yet, it somehow just works. That’s because the contact he does make is square…and there’s a lot of it. Just look at those walk and strikeout rates!Last year he worked with infield guru Ron Washington in San Francisco. The result: An eye-catching turnaround on Arraez’s defense, one of the biggest year-to-year improvements in Statcast history, going from a -11 Run Value to a +10 RV. That’s insane. Granted, most of his number last year came from first base, but he was there because his defense at second was so abysmal. The last time he played primarily second base prior to 2026 was in 2023 when he also finished with a -11 Run Value. Amazing.Mix the massively improved defense with the steady offense and Arraez experienced a career year at the perfect time. Teams that believe his defensive improvement is sticky, will inflate the price. Even if the glove regresses, there’s value in a .340 OBP with the occasional double down the line.He's suited up for five teams over the last four years because his skill set isn't valued the way it was 50 years ago. Last year, he had to settle for a one-year, $12 million deal. He will get more this winter, but I'd be leery of getting too carried away. 2027 Steamer Projection: .234/.317/.408, 101 wRC+, 2.3 fWARBefore you delete this email, hear me out. Jazz Chisholm Jr. is, at his best, a dynamic player. He went for 30/30 in 2025 and, while none of the five tools scream elite, they’re more than good enough to be an above average player and an upgrade for the Royals at second base.He did slump in 2026, with his home run total dropping to 19 and his strikeout rate ballooning to almost 30 percent because he chased out of the zone more than he had ever before.The problem is, Chisholm doesn’t always seem to be at his best. In fact, he seemed to wear out his welcome in New York. The Yankees didn’t extend a qualifying offer, so he doesn’t come with that baggage. That makes Chisholm an ideal candidate for a short-term “prove it” contract. Dangle two years at $40 million with an opt out and the opportunity to pair with Bobby Witt Jr. up the middle. See if that will motivate him. I think it will. 2027 Steamer Projection: .265/.310/.383, 92 wRC+, 1.2 fWARWe know how much Matt Quatraro and the Royals value defensive versatility. Sometimes, like with Nick Loftin, it works. Other times, like with Jonathan India in left, it absolutely does not. Mauricio Dubón is the top utility player on the market this winter. He logged time last year at second, third, short, left and center. He last played first and right field in 2025.He’s below-average offensively. Last summer, he posted 619 plate appearances, his career high by about 125. Honestly, if a team signs Dubón, they’re looking for the lower end of playing time. He put up 2.2 fWAR in 133 games for Houston in 2024 while posting an 80 wRC+. Last year was one of the better offensive seasons of his career. He should be available for a one-year deal. Two years at $16 million would be the ceiling. 2027 Steamer Projection: .225/.331/.407, 107 wRC+, 1.9 fWARTrent Grisham broke out in a big way in 2025, hitting .235/.348/.464 with a 128 wRC+. Great timing on his part as the Yankees tossed a qualifying option his direction that he immediately gobbled up. The encore wasn’t as fun for either Grisham or the Yankees as the center fielder hit just .211/.308/.395 with a 98 wRC+ as he sold out his contact for power more power. He’s also not a great defender in center, but I imagine a team could grab him and drop him in left.He seems like a guy without a plan at the plate. His swing rate on pitches in the heart of the zone was 67 percent. He doesn’t chase, which is good, but he’s letting a lot of good pitches go by. Hmmmm, I wonder if the Royals have a new hitting coach who is all about planning out plate appearances. Throw him a one-year deal and see if he clicks with Hunter Mense and the rest of the coaching staff to get his offensive mojo back. 2027 Steamer Projection: .230/.336/.406, 108 wRC+, 1.7 fWARIf I were writing a scouting report on Ian Happ, it would read “a solid regular.” That may be damning with faint praise, particularly for a corner outfielder, but that’s who Happ is as a player.A switch-hitter who is better from the left side of the plate, he really struggled when hitting right-handed in 2026, batting .145/.217/.267 against southpaws. Yikes. That may be enough to deter the Royals (and other teams) as they search for a good right-handed bat, but you can’t always get what you want unless you’re willing to pay the premium. Again, the question that I return to over and over again in this exercise is, “would this player be an upgrade at his position if the Royals signed him?” That answer feels obvious.His defense is like his hitting. Good arm. Decent range. Solid, if unspectacular. That’s all you need in left.A two-year deal around $34 million doesn’t seem out of order. I would not be willing to go three. 2027 Steamer Projection: .236/.302/.415, 97 wRC+, 1.4 fWARLook! These aren't endorsements. Merely options. Luis Robert Jr. can’t stay on the field and when he has been on the field the last couple of seasons, he’s been underwhelming. He went for 38 home runs and 20 steals in 2023 and hasn’t been above-average offensively since, so a signing club is rolling the dice that he can tap back in to whatever made him successful just four years ago. To be fair, a lot of his shortcomings can be chalked up to injury. He spent three months on the IL last summer and was a post-trade deadline waiver claim when the Orioles were willing to gamble that he could catch fire the last couple months of the season. He did not catch fire and he’s on this list because the Orioles declined a $20 million option for 2026.The tools continue to tantalize, but the reality is far different. Maybe worth a flier if you can get him on a one-year deal where he has something to prove. Or you take that flier and get frustrated and let him go for a c-level prospect at the trading deadline. It's probably the latter. 2027 Steamer Projection: .251/.350/.384, 108 wRC+, 2.0 fWARTo me, Gleyber Torres represents a gamble in the Jonathan India vein. You can squint and see the upside, but odds are against you. Always limited defensively at second, he’s fluxuated between above-average to just plain average at the plate for his entire career. He’s settled more into the latter over the last three years.Hampered by an oblique injury this year, Torres saw a big decline in his average exit velocity and hard-hit rate and saw his power numbers tumble.This is his third dip into the free agent pool in as many seasons. He initially signed a one-year, $15 million deal in a move from the Yankees to the Tigers. Last winter, the Tigers dangled the qualifying offer and he accepted. And now he’s back on the open market, looking at yet another one-year deal. He could be a platoon partner with the left-handed hitting Massey at second with Massey also serving as a late-inning defensive replacement. That could be some maximizing. 2027 Steamer Projection: .221/.293/.406, 92 wRC+, 1.1 fWARCould I interest you in a project? After hitting 20 home runs in 71 games in 2025 for the Jays, Daulton Varsho had a brutal 2026 campaign where he hit .243/.307/.375 with a 91 wRC+ with the Blue Jays. Dealt to Houston at the trade deadline, he was even worse offensively for the Astros, hitting a brutal .172/.224/.311 over 161 PAs. Turns out, he was dealing with wrist inflammation for most of the year and had surgery at the end of the season to remove a pair of cysts from said wrist. He should be good to go for 2027, which means he’s a candidate for a short-term deal.He’s made his living in center field, but his arm has never been a strong point and has only declined since he had shoulder surgery a couple of years ago. He’s lost a step (or two) as well. At this point, he’s better suited to left field.I’m less than enthusiastic about Varsho as an option in Kansas City. The Royals have taken several fliers on alleged bounce-back candidates over the last couple of years and come up completely empty. Varsho gives off those vibes.Dangle a year at whatever the market rate is; hope for the best and prepare for the worst. 2027 Steamer Projection: .233/.339/.393, 107 wRC+, 1.4 fWARIt seems like the Royals have been connected to Taylor Ward for three or four years now. If the Royals were going to get him, it was via a trade. Now, he’s on the open market, available for the price of a contract. And maybe some burnt ends as a little bonus.Traded to Baltimore last winter, Ward was having another one of his solid offensive seasons, although his power numbers took a nosedive. Yet he transformed into something of an on-base machine. Ok…fine. Shipped to Seattle at the trade deadline he went completely south. Totally gone. Like a 117 wRC+ for the Orioles compared to a 23 wRC+ for the Mariners. Some bad luck in the Pacific Northwest with a .180 BABIP, but his Statcast metrics also took a turn. The power remained AWOL and then so did the on base percentage. If you’re going to revamp your offensive game, you should probably make sure the new one sticks.Ward is also a guy, like Grisholm, who has adjusted his approach at the plate the last couple of seasons where he's much more reluctant to swing. Sure, it's a good thing he's not lurking around the shadow zone, but he's also letting far to many hittable pitches pass by. Again, with the changes the Royals made to their hitting coaching staff the last two seasons, I wonder if there's something there that can be unlocked.Maybe those last couple of months will drop his price and the Royals can pick him up on a one-year deal. His 2026 season was so weird, I don’t know if I trust him to fully recover.

item.title: 'Reverse Engineer Anything': AI Companies Crack Down on the Coolest Thing People Were Doing With AI
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs. Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account for its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts . A project that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior. The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most. Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted. But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails. “My general experience about reverse-engineering getting blocked has been more or less 100% correlated with the ‘cyber’ category blocks I have received. My take is that the lab[s] are probably under pressure to not have their models take part in some kind of criminal hacking activities and their cyber guardrails are erring on the side of being too strict,” Matt Brown, principal consultant at Brown Fine Security and someone who has been using AI to reverse-engineer devices, told 404 Media. “I am investing in hardware and trying to stay up to speed because the frontier labs guardrails will randomly change without warning on the same model. For my security research and pentesting work I really don’t want to invest tooling and energy into an ecosystem that will eventually lock me out. These guardrails on the frontier side have come at the same time as open weight models from (mostly) China are getting better and better.” AI-powered reverse-engineering isn’t going anywhere, but it does look like it’s going to become much harder to use the most popular frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic for it. It’s unclear how much longer it will be possible for you to open an OpenAI Codex window, ask it to find a smart TV hooked up to your network, and tell it to install a new operating system on it. Moving forward, it looks like this type of work will be best done with open source, open weight, uncensored, and local models. That’s a bummer, because one of the things that was so exciting about the Reverse Engineer-Anything trend was how easily accessible it had become.Last month, researchers and law professors at Cornell Tech, Columbia University, and New York University about how cheap, AI-assisted reverse-engineering is challenging big manufacturers’ dominance over the devices their make, and is challenging existing intellectual property law. “AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract,” they write. “The law of reverse engineering was built for a world where opening a device took time, tools, and rare expertise. That friction is vanishing as agents whittle endless, precise picks for the many little locks that fill our digital lives.”In recent days, people have started modifying older digital cameras with new, vibe-coded operating systems. In a video about hacking old cameras, the YouTuber Breno Loves Cameras explains why it’s such a big deal and why camera companies don’t like it; that same logic can be applied to any device manufacturer.“Camera companies have this practice of keeping features to release on newer cameras, and having distinctions [in features] in camera lines,” the YouTuber Breno said in one video. “This is breaking that from those big companies, which are going to lose a lot of money if this becomes a big thing.” Through that lens, it’s easy to see why big companies are protecting other big companies. People finally found a thing to do with AI tools that gives consumers a bit more control over the devices they bought; it must be immediately stamped out.“This vibe-code hacking is only called ‘reverse’ when somebody who lacks a trillion dollars is doing it,” the science fiction author Bruce Sterling tweeted. “When you ‘reverse engineer’ the entire Internet Common Crawl, you just built a nice AI model.”

item.title: What Use Is Kevin O’Connell?
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: There are times when a team can lose a primetime game and feel hard done-by. A good squad can have an off night, or run into a particularly bad matchup, and suddenly millions of viewers have incorrectly concluded that those fellas are bad at football. The Minnesota Vikings, who came into Monday's game against the Buffalo Bills with a 6-1 record, offered no such misrepresentation. Anyone who watched that game came away with a precise understanding of who the Vikings are: a team that can't move the ball to save its life.I shudder to think of the hypothetical casual fan who was excited to tune into a game between two six-win teams, only to be treated to a game that, despite being close in a technical sense, never really offered any drama. The Vikings are to blame for that, as they managed to lose 23-6 while putting yet another inept offensive performance on tape. Minnesota finished the game with 178 total yards and nine first downs, and possessed the ball for 17:28, their lowest mark in franchise history. That was somehow all they could manage against the 30th-ranked pass defense in the league.The star of this horrible show was Carson Wentz, who was forced into starting quarterback duty thanks to Kyler Murray's hamstring injury. Wentz completed eight of his 25 passes for 81 yards, and threw two interceptions. It was a historically bad performance, one so vivid in its awful particulars that Joe Buck and Troy Aikman were able to set aside any hard feelings they might currently have for each other and join in channeling their disgust at the field:

item.title: "Feeling Good" (Nina Simone, 1965)

item.title: Atomic Chicken
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: A flock of chickens seem to be living an idyllic life in the shadow of a nuclear power plant, because they are birdbrains and have no concept of the possible danger. Then one day something goes wrong, and the farm is showered with radioactive fallout. The effects are the ridiculous extremes we saw in 1950s B-movies, like immediate mutant growth and unexplainable super powers. The chickens are still birdbrains, but they have an idea of how to stop the nuclear plant from contaminating their environment. Atomic Chicken is a student film from the French art school Ecole des Nouvelles, specifically the 2023 graduation film for animation students. I like the animated fabric textures, but was a little surprised at one point. "Hey, we can see this chicken's cloaca!" There's a reason for that, since a hen's main talent is laying eggs, and that's important to the story, although what they do with that talent is surprising. (via Kuriositas)

item.title: God and the Big Bang
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: I was tasked with selecting a new stain color for my house shingles, which was relatively traumatic because I have a history of spending an inordinate amount of time making decisions; a process that tends to be followed by a lifetime of regret. I recently spent about 30 hours researching a power adapter and dongle system to simultaneously charge my MacBook and Kindle. How was I going to choose a color for the entire exterior of my house before El Niño hits? I did what most modern internet users would have done. I used AI. I took photos of my house and then had AI show me how it would look stained in the various sample colors my painter suggested. Like many AI experiences, this one was pretty fulfilling and even delightful. But when I think about the AI industry, like millions of other Americans, I have almost exclusively negative vibes. Why does this technology cause such a disconnect between our experiences and our feelings? As I’ve mentioned, I think this is partly due to a broad and growing disconnect between what people want and what AI CEOs think people want. But even more than that, there’s a disconnect between how consumers think of AI (as a new form of super-powered search that finally brings the promise of AskJeeves to fruition) and how AI leaders think of it: As a god. Jaron Lanier explains the disconnect. “This disapproval is unfortunate and unnecessary. It does not arise from the technology itself. It is a reaction to the insular culture surrounding A.I., a culture that is dictating how this innovation is packaged, how it is sold and how it is understood. Words have a way of filtering into actions, as when some of us in Silicon Valley callously treat places where we want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. We technologists are sabotaging ourselves, but it is hard to find a sane focus from inside the intensity and elite isolation of this bubble. Americans are not rejecting A.I. They are rejecting the way Silicon Valley is defining it for them.” (Gift Article): I Am a Silicon Valley Pioneer. We Are Sabotaging Ourselves. (The irony here is that the thing consumers really dislike the most about this new technology is the people. And you can’t really blame them.) “There is an explanation for why some tech leaders, so seemingly worried about an extinction-level event, are plunging ahead with A.I. development: Mankind’s survival, while important to many of them, is less critical than building something they believe to be not only conscious but godlike. A substantial portion of the A.I. community, in celebrating this belief, is quick to support any action or statement that reinforces the idea that the technology is like a deity. They might call for regulation, but only in specific ways — perhaps by deploying more A.I. to control A.I. — that adore the technology’s powers. It is that adoration that is nonnegotiable.” I don’t know about you, but I’m not about to bow down at the altar of a new technological overlord. At least not until I see how my shingles turn out.+ Which brings us to AI’s big bang… (Gift Article): The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? The stock is way down, the FBI and the newly empowered Dems are looking into the issue, and the Information reported that “CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with alleged spy Alice Huang dates back to 2023 and enabled Chinese companies to acquire $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips.” Here’s the latest. God only knows how this shakes out.+ As I wrote yesterday: The enduring stamina of the notion that the carnal is greater than the kernel, that ramming overides the ram, and that the dong is greater than the dongle, provides yet another reminder that the key risk factors presented by the AI boom are the humans behind it. And, in this case, it’s a human in the center of a circular economy. Circular Jerk.Pete Hegseth has declared war on those who want him impeached. That said, he tends to lose wars. “Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday cast the impeachment effort against him as a slanderous attempt by a single disgruntled Republican to damage President Trump, as House G.O.P. leaders said a procedural vote would come in a matter of hours. Democrats are expected to support removing him from office, and there may be enough Republican backing to imperil his leadership of the Pentagon.” It doesn’t help to be bad at your job and deeply hated. “Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral who won a seat in Congress last week after being fired by Pete Hegseth, has lent her support to lawmakers attempting to impeach the defense secretary, saying that he had committed ‘probably plenty’ of offenses to warrant his ouster.” Meanwhile, “Trump posted on social media that he gives Hegseth an ‘A’ PLUS PLUS PLUS’ for his remarks.” (I wonder if Hegseth can bring a Plus Plus Plus One to his impeachment…)While we’re on the topic of grade inflation, the (Gift Article) has a piece on The Parents Suing Schools Because Their Kids Got Bad Grades. “Time was when parents disciplined children for bringing home bad marks. Today, they often take a more adversarial approach, educators say, leaning on teachers and administrators to change grades in disputes that can even spill into court. Ever since remote learning brought classrooms into living rooms during the pandemic, U.S. parents have grown more involved in and less enchanted with schools, according to numerous surveys. That includes scrutinizing how teachers evaluate their children. Four in 10 American teachers report facing pressure from moms and dads to change grades.”“President Claudia Sheinbaum drew a firm line barring U.S. forces from operating on Mexican soil. But in a northern border state, one local partner quietly helped the agency build a foothold.” From life imitating art to life imitating a Netflix series. (Gift Article): The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico. “For more than six months, Mr. Zuany shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations, according to nine officials and law enforcement officers in Mexico and the United States. In return, officials said, Mr. Zuany’s U.S. visa was reinstated. Then, in April, a truck carrying two C.I.A. officers drove off a cliff, killing all four passengers. The crash blew the C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua and set off a national scandal.” “After years of economic turmoil and droughts, the U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to its smallest level in 75 years. The supply shock is driving up steak and hamburger prices at grocery stores and restaurants to record highs—conditions that could last well into the next decade, given how long it takes to replenish a herd.” (Gift Article): Why High Beef Prices Are Here to Stay. (It will be interesting to see how the beef price crisis impacts public health.)+ “For nearly a century, the United States has been the global leader in cultivating young scientists, training them at the nation’s vast network of universities and harnessing their talents to ensure American dominance in research and innovation. But now that Ph.D. pipeline is in turmoil.” Young Talent Fueled American Scientific Dominance. Now It’s Disappearing. (The midterms were great. But it will take years and years to undo the damage of Trumpism across many sectors.)+ “At a time when the rich are walling themselves off from both society and ­reality—building apocalypse bunkers in New Zealand, buying gated homes in Miami and Newport Beach—there’s one major problem with their escapist fantasies: other rich people.” An insane, multi-year drama between billionaires that revolves around the person who was working in a tennis pro shop. This is, at least in part, a story about people who live for conflict. : Clash of the Titans.+ “British writer M. John Harrison won the Booker Prize for fiction on late Monday for ‘The End of Everything,’ a satirical dystopian novel whose themes of ‘catastrophe and apocalypse’ chime with our uneasy times. It’s the first work of science fiction to take the prestigious $67,000 literary award.”+ With So Much New Blood in the Senate, the Average Age Is Falling… To 63.

item.title: 8Ball & MJG – Comin’ Out Hard (August 17, 1993)
item.author: deedub77
item.content:encoded: Since the mid-nineties, I’ve known about 8Ball & MJG, but I never dug into the Memphis duo’s catalog. In my defense, a ton of great hip-hop albums were released almost weekly during that era. This was years before you had access to every album at your fingertips via your smartphone, and the only way to access the music was to purchase physical copies (i.e., CD, cassette, and vinyl) or rip or burn a copy from a friend who already purchased a copy of the album. Whatever the reason, I missed the entire 8Ball & MJG run from ‘93 until 2010. But there is no time like the present.I may have breezed through a couple of 8Ball & MJG records on the radio or seen one or two of their videos back in the day, but I never really paid attention to them. In the back of my mind, 8Ball & MJG seemed to be run-of-the-mill rappers spewing the same redundant pimp shit that a thousand other southern rappers were. Then I reviewed the compilation album for the blog and heard “Listen To Me Now,” and my opinion started to change. Over a slick and funky bass guitar riff, 8Ball & MJG brilliantly issued a PSA on AIDS, rapping from the perspective of HIV for the first half of the record. The shit was fire. I later discovered cameos from the duo on The Almighty RSO’s album and Mase’s debut project, . They weren’t as creative or as conscious as their performance on “Listen To Me Now,” but they were impressive enough to get me to track down physical copies of their catalog, starting with their debut album, . was the first album released on Suave House Records, founded by Tony Draper. Draper is also credited with producing all nine tracks on the album. never received an official RIAA certification, but according to Suave House and the streets, it sold over 500,000 units, building a solid foundation for the label.I usually don’t pay more than ten bucks for a used CD. But the collector in me and my intrigue with 8Ball & MJG’s music made me pay much more than ten bones for my copy. This review marks my first time listening to . Hopefully, it’s worth the investment. – Over eerie, slo-mo, lean-influenced chords and drums, Satan himself (played by MJG) stops by to welcome the listener to Memphis and the album, and he introduces the players for the evening. What the hell (no pun) is up with that hideous laugh at the end of his monologue? It sounds like Alvin Seville is getting an exorcism. – After several listens to this record, I believe that “9 little millimeta boys” has a dual meaning. It’s Memphis slang for a sucka or a chump, but it also describes a killer, which is the persona 8Ball & MJG adopt throughout this song. The Memphis duo threatens to kill every “9 little millimeta boy” in sight, and according to 8Ball, women can get a taste of the heat as well (would that make their female victims 9 little millimeta girls?). The “thick as Heinz” bass line, combined with exhilarating HBCU marching band-like horns, is the audio double Dutch ropes 8Ball & MJG jump in between, quickly finding their rhythm, and completely smoke this shit. Both figuratively and literally. – Tony Draper whips up a production that’s as spooky as it is funky, as 8 and M give the listener a glimpse into the underworld of pimpin’ and drug dealing. As usual, 8Ball delivers solid bars, but MJG shines the brightest on this track, providing intricate detail about the key players in his drug ring and his prominent prostitution clientele. He even lists his prostitutes’ price menu (I don’t solicit hookers, but $200 for her to jack you off sounds extremely overpriced, even by 2026 standards). – Draper’s instrumental was clearly inspired by the theme song, making for the perfect cinematic soundtrack to back 8Ball & MJG’s thrilling bank-robbery script. There are a few holes in their storyline, but overall, I was entertained. – TD chops up Womack & Womack’s reworking of Teddy Pendergrass’ “Love T.K.O.” and turns it into a beautifully soothing musical canvas (I love the soulful Cecil Womack vocal looped up for the hook). Our hosts paint it with high levels of pimpology and misogyny, and some of the content was uncomfortable to listen to (mainly 8Ball’s persistent mention of beating women). I hope the domestic violence portion was just a bit and not their truth; and if it was their truth, I hope they’ve put that dark side of their lives behind them.– For the title track, our hosts give us more of what we’ve heard from them on the previous four tracks. Mr. Draper mashes up Simply Red with Rufus, creating a soulful groove for 8Ball & MJG’s gangsta/pimp propaganda to breathe on. – 8Ball gets the first solo joint of the evening, jumping back into storytelling mode as he details his rise from lowly Mickey D’s worker to drug kingpin. The bars are engaging, and Draper scores the affair with Casio keyboard-esque chords, spiced up by a monster bassline and sleek 808 drums. This was fire.– The beat and rhymes on this one sound like they were recorded a few years before the rest of the album. This is easily the weakest track on the project. And by the way, blowing up nigga’s cars for calling you fat is crazy, 8Ball. – ends with an MJG solo joint. The title might lead you to believe this is more of the same pimp promo we’ve gotten on the rest of the album. It is partially, but MJG also examines how the concept of pimps and hoes reaches beyond the streets into politics, government, and the world. The bass line sounds like a muscle-bound dude’s getting ready to kick your ass, accompanied by slithering 808s and discrete wah-wahs. It doesn’t stand up to 8Ball’s solo record, but it’s still decent.If you read this blog regularly, you know is my favorite hip-hop album of all time (and if you’re new to the blog or didn’t know, the blog name is an obvious breadcrumb). is full of stellar production and masterful hood poetry from a youthful and hungry Nasir Jones. The combination was magical, but just as important as the music and bars on was its conciseness. At nine tracks, left no room for fluff, and each track was packed with appetizing, well-conceived content. Like , was truncated to nine tracks. But that might be the only thing the two albums have in common.On their debut album, 8Ball & MJG spend the entire forty-two-minute runtime slangin’, killin’, and getting high. None of it is original, even by 1993 standards, and it gets redundant (and at times cringeworthy, specifically when 8Ball gets into his domestic violence bag on “Pimps” and “Niggas Like Us”). Yet for most of , the duo makes the regurgitated subject matter their own, dressing it up with their unique Memphis diction, slang, and southernly soulful cadences that keep you engaged.While 8Ball & MJG hold court with their performance on , I was even more impressed by the Tony Draper-led production. TD maestro’s the affair, blending sleek 808 drums, tough bass lines, funky synth sounds, and a few soul samples (see “Pimps” and the title track). A couple of his instrumentals fall short, but overall, Draper’s southern-fried production sounds great underneath 8 and G’s Memphis-influenced street soliloquies.On second thought, there are a couple more things and have in common. On “Mr. Big,” 8Ball raps about grabbin’ his “TEC from the dresser.” On “Represent,” Nas raps about “Pulling his TEC out the dresser.” lived up to its title. does likewise.-DeedubFollow me on Instagram @damontimeisillmatic

item.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is at $8/$40.The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

item.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked.If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it.

item.title: “60 Minutes” found zero minutes for Trump’s new Big Lie
item.author: 1axboacd0cf9o1fnfu0ms74722xavqooe338gz@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest?” Donald Trump posted on Truth Social this morning. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT”With that post, Trump went all in on a new Big Lie, this time about the 2026 midterms. None of this should come as a surprise. I warned about it on my podcast on Sunday.But you wouldn’t have known it from watching “60 Minutes” that same night.I spent the better part of an hour on my podcast walking viewers through Trump’s growing embrace of election denialism. The signs were obvious to anyone who bothered to pay attention. Trump had been sharing conspiracy theories and making threats about elections in Alaska. The legacy media ignored them.I timed the episode to end just before “60 Minutes” began. Trump was being interviewed by Ross Douthat, one of the program’s new conservative correspondents, and I wanted to see whether election denialism would come up.Douthat asked Trump about UFOs, death and religion. They chatted about forgiveness and about a potential successor to lead the MAGA movement. Yet, he did not ask a single question about Trump’s election denialism.The only reference to Trump’s attacks on elections came in the segment’s introduction, and, ironically, it falsely credited Trump with having set election denialism aside:“In the past, this president has met defeat with claims of fraud and the effort to overturn the 2020 election. But when we met with him in the White House on Friday for his first sit-down interview since the midterms, we found him in a surprisingly reflective mood, and seemingly accepting of defeat.”Trump was less than 24 hours away from proving that claim wrong, but “60 Minutes” still found zero minutes to press him on election denialism. Instead, it vouched for him.I was disappointed but not surprised.Under its new ownership and its editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, CBS News has a track record of going easy on Trump. An interview conducted by Douthat, with Weiss in tow, was never going to be combative or challenge Trump on election denialism — the core of his movement’s ideology.So how did I see what the legacy media missed?To start with, I listened to what Trump was saying. I read what he was posting. I took him literally and seriously.Just as important, I had seen this pattern before. Less than a week after the GOP’s stinging defeat, Trump’s messaging was slowly but surely shifting from “I lost” to “Republicans lost” to “maybe Republicans didn’t lose at all.”Donald Trump was never going to let an election loss pass without a lie. From the birther conspiracy about Barack Obama to the 2020 Big Lie and his ongoing efforts to relitigate that loss, election denialism has become the one requirement for membership in the MAGA movement.Most importantly, I have no reason to look away.This is the ethos I have infused in Democracy Docket. It has no corporate overlords and no other businesses that depend on access to the White House or favors from government officials. It doesn’t need to stay in Trump’s good graces.That independence, and our commitment to democracy, allow Democracy Docket to tell the truth about Trump’s attacks on elections while other pundits and commentators stay silent.And this is only the beginning. Trump’s post took aim at voting machines and early votes. It’s worth watching where that leads.Officials may face pressure to delay or refuse certification. Early and mail voting may come under new attacks. There may be a push to change how votes are cast and counted before 2028.Democracy Docket will be tracking and exposing every step.That’s why Democracy Docket’s reach and influence keep growing. Most recently, it has added regular live podcasts to its free offerings to serve those in our community who prefer to hear from me on video.For $10 a month or $120 a year, you’ll get my premium newsletters with analysis you won’t find anywhere else. You’ll also get members-only live events and access to our members-only community.Most importantly, you’ll help keep Democracy Docket independent, so we can keep covering the stories the legacy media is ignoring.The midterms may be over, but the fight to save democracy is only beginning. I’m proud to have you by my side.

item.title: Are Tighter Export Controls Coming for NVIDIA Processors?
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: The Information is reporting (paywall) that regardless of what multiple investigations unearth about NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the scandal is likely to spur Congress to impose tighter export controls on the advanced processors used in AI data centers. There’s been a big bipartisan push for this in Congress for a while but it’s largely been headed off by White House resistance. That resistance seems to center on Trump himself and the small coterie of Silicon Valley advisors who run AI policy at the White House. As I noted in this post, the argument for tight export controls seems pretty strong to me, certainly if we’re operating on the premise that U.S. superiority in AI development is a critical national security interest.

item.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solveThere is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find itI want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes fromThere needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server appIdeally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.The research looked good, so I told it:Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something elseThat got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening make live changes to the software as it ran.This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurateThis gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beepsThat added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestampThat made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay playsNow I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking forThen the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it isAt this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.And since I had one spare device, I then said:add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so farI think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to .Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

Now outgoing Speaker Johnson says he may not send the impeachment article to the Senate? What stands out most is what’s happening. There’s no real defense from the White House or anyone else in the GOP/MAGA sound machine. The White House posted a couple videos on social media. Obviously they’re on record saying they don’t support it. But that’s really about it. You can imagine the thermonuclear (maybe literally) response to anything like this at almost any point in the last two years. But now? The vibe here is something like “rough what happened to Pete. I guess not everyone makes it after a rough midterm like that.” Oh well …

item.title: The Free Press Deletes Video In Which Reporter Is Scared Of The Word “Habibi”
item.author: Brandy Jensen
item.content:encoded: Olivia Reingold might be the most notably embarrassing employee at the Free Press, but her coworkers won't let her take that title without a fight. Last Wednesday, following the midterm elections the outlet posted a video by a different staffer who characterized Abdul El-Sayed's victory speech, which he gave almost entirely in English, as being delivered in Arabic. By Sunday, that video was deleted. The publication announced the decision, which apparently needed four days of deliberation, with the following note:We deleted an opinion video about the use of foreign languages in election night speeches. The post contained a factual error and its tone fell short of what we believe advances healthy public discourse. The rigorous editorial process that produces the work that appears on our website and in our newsletters must apply to everything we post on social media. We’ll be updating how we do things to achieve just that. We regret the error.The video in question was by reporter Maya Sulkin, whose accompanying caption was as follows: “Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed gave his victory speech in Arabic last night. Rep. Ilhan Omar addressed her victory party in Somali. And this morning, Iran’s supreme leader posted that America’s collapse ‘has accelerated.’ What should we make of these acceptance speeches?” The blue wave has resulted in some unlikely victories, but I didn't know that included the supreme leader of Iran.

item.title: Dad Asked 6-Year-Old Daughter if ‘She Had the Gun’ Before He Left Her in Line for Pokémon Cards
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Pokémon released its Mega Evolution Delta Region cards this week and one man in Charleston, South Carolina wanted them so badly that he left his 6-year-old daughter in line at Target at 1 am with a pillow and a blanket. According to the incident report obtained by 404 Media, the person next to the little girl in line heard the father ask if his daughter “had the gun” before he left her alone at Target for more than an hour. Later, the father he left his daughter behind so “he could maintain his place in line and avoid missing the opportunity to purchase the cards.”Pokémon cards are and people will wait to go to wild lengths to secure them. Waiting in line outside of a store for days before a new release is routine. John-Michael Dooley was waiting in line outside of a Target in Charleston, South Carolina with his 6-year-old daughter on the morning of November 6 when he decided to run home. He didn’t want to lose his place in line so he left his daughter behind “sleeping on the concrete,” according to a record of 911 calls obtained by 404 Media.Other people waiting for Pokémon cards watched Dooley drive away and called the cops when he didn’t return. One guy on the scene started a timer on his phone when Dooley left and called the cops once it hit 45 minutes. “[He] advised later that he continued the timer on his phone, and the point in which the father returned to target showed 1 hour and 6 minutes,” according to an incident report obtained by 404 Media.The person in line next to the 6-year-old “recalled the father waking his daughter up before he left and advised her he was ‘taking the dogs home,’” the report said. “Following this, [he] recalled hearing the father ask the daughter if ‘she had the gun’ before leaving.’ All parties on scene advised that the offender did not ask anyone to care or look after his daughter, and all stated the offender simply left her there by herself.”The cops woke the girl up and she told them “she was at Target in line to get Pokémon cards with her father when the store opened,” according to the incident report. The police didn’t find a gun. “The only items the juvenile had in her possession when she was located was a pillow and a green blanket.”Dooley returned to the line to find police talking to his daughter. “The juvenile still was unsure to the whereabouts of her father at this time,” the report said. “Several minutes after this, I could hear and see a dark colored SUV driving in the parking lot of Target in our direction. As the vehicle got closer, the [person who called 911] yelled out ‘That`s him.’”Dooley got out of his car and police arrested him. “The offender was brought back to my patrol vehicle at which point he continued to say that he had only left to bring his dogs home,” the report said. “The offender reiterated this several times while also confirming that he left his 6-year-old daughter unattended for a period of time.” Dooley has been charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.Pokémon card collecting has been at the center of a few strange crimes over the past few years. Fights broke out in multiple Target parking lots earlier this year when a set dropped.
