item.title: Florida State Stares Into The Abyss
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Mike Norvell is finally, officially out of my life. I am ecstatic, but I am also left completely cold. The good thing about having a hatable figure looming large over your school is that they absorb all the problems that exist, in that program and everywhere else. My opinion about his coaching is a matter of public record, but I'll say this: Norvell and that dumb face of his made for a good lightning rod, all things considered.But now he's gone. Athletic director Michael Alford was gone in September. Thanks to an approximately $50 million buyout for Norvell and the general changing landscape of college football, the future of FSU football is more uncertain than it has ever been.

item.title: We Have Star Wars at Home
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: This is cool: Evan Puschak looks at the rush of cheapo knockoff space operas that came out in the wake of Star Wars, a once-in-a-generation film that refashioned the entire movie business. Even the names are kooky: Starcrash, War of the Planets, Battle of the Stars, The Humanoid, Message From Space, Battle Beyond the Stars, The Man Who Saved the World, Star Odyssey, and The Beast in Space — although tbh, Star Wars is a goofy name as well. Some of the movies even had lightsabers and anxious robots.Certainly what was so exhilarating to many about these films was not simply the experience of a new kind of realism. Perhaps even more important was the intensified density of effects in films of the era, which many at the time understood as a thrillingly new and vividly somatic technologized experience. This book aims to recover the excitement that not just ticket-buyers but also many academics, critics, and journalists felt upon experiencing the special effects-heavy films of the 1970s, in particular Star Wars and Close Encounters, and further grant historical dimension and context to that experience. It may be surprising for many to realize that in the 1970s George Lucas and Steven Spielberg were considered among the most interesting, ambitious, and exciting filmmakers of the era, alongside more canonized American filmmakers like Stanley Kubrick, Francis Ford Coppola, Peter Bogdanovich, and Martin Scorsese. What critics praised most often about Lucas and Spielberg as filmmakers was their grasp of specifically cinematic visual dynamics that lent their films both greater visceral and sensual engagement and an extra layer of expressive and intellectual potential. While many critics have (often rightly) condemned the aggressive, pummeling blockbuster style that has arisen in the wake of the two successes of 1977, it is incumbent upon scholars to recover the creative process that made them so stimulating and exhilarating to the likes of Pauline Kael, Stanley Kauffmann, Roger Ebert, and other prominent critics of the era, as well as so popular with audiences. A renewed interest in special effects technology by influential auteurist filmmakers certainly made this historical development possible. However, even more strongly, auteurist filmmakers went to the considerable and painstaking effort to promote and develop complex special effects technology, precisely in order to realize aesthetic filmmaking goals they designed to rouse and provoke the sensorium. They called this approach variously “visual storytelling,’ “visceral engagement,’ or “graphic dynamics.”Moreover, so-called New Hollywood filmmakers in the 1970s reinterpreted the role of cinematic aesthetics to suggest a purposeful relation between sensual and intellectual impact. In other words, filmmakers sought to stimulate the senses. This was not to numb the viewer but to activate him or her — not unlike the notion of drug-induced mind expansion. Intensified color schemes, beams of light, fast-moving objects, and quick editing first penetrate the body and then engage the mind with the films’ ideas about technology, kineticism, power structures, liberty, etc.I am firmly in the camp of those who enjoy filmmakers that engage the senses like this — among contemporary filmmakers, Christopher Nolan and Denis Villeneuve come to mind as continuing the legacy of Lucas et al. in this way.

item.title: The Iran War Dodge Spreads
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Yesterday, I wrote about JD Vance’s push to make the 2026 midterm a referendum solely about the Iran War. Things were going great, he claims, substantively and politically, until the Iran War brought everything crashing down. We’re seeing that a number of Democrats, albeit for different reasons, want to push this line too. Yesterday Eric Levitz at Vox interviewed data guy David Shor who said something similar. If you’re not familiar with him, Shor’s in the group who argue that Democrats need to jettison hot-button social and cultural issues that make them unviable with big parts of the electorate — immigration, gender and sexuality, guns, policing, etc. This is one of these claims that is demonstrably accurate to a significant degree in electoral terms, but more complicated when it comes down to applying it to the practicalities, commitments and mutabilities of the actual world. In this case it leaves him wanting to place overwhelming emphasis on the Iran War since Democrats put up the biggest midterm landslide in half a century and mostly didn’t avoid hot-button issues, or at least not as much as people with this viewpoint said was required, for most of the 2026 campaign.Here’s the discussion of this issue …

item.title: The Tide Finally Turned Against the Depredations of the Trump II Presidency
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: We, the lucky ones, emerged this week from one of the darkest stretches in American history. The jubilation, the relief, the exhilaration are heartfelt and genuine and real and understandable. But not everyone who began this arduous journey with us was still around to celebrate its climactic conclusion.Over the past 22 months, there have been innumerable tangible real world victims of the Trump II rampage: the millions of abandoned beneficiaries of USAID; the sick and dying betrayed by MAHA’s perverse notions of public health; the countless families ripped apart by indiscriminate mass deportation; the hundreds of immigrants dumped in countries with which they had no prior connection; the forgotten souls shipped off to foreign gulags; Renee Good and Alex Pretti.There is no minimizing or excusing it. What they have lost is not recoverable. There is no making them whole again.The COVID pandemic taught those of us who didn’t already know it the cruel lesson of how quickly humans forget and move on. Down deep, it may be a biological imperative, but we have refined it with a culture of short attention spans, a cultivated urgency to be always looking ahead, and an infinite ability to tell ourselves soothing and self-congratulatory stories about our own greatness.Moments in history like these, when America redeems her lost promise, are uplifting and tantalizing with possibility — for those who survived what came before. The toils of slavery, the carnage of a civil war, the dehumanization of Jim Crow exacted extreme tolls in human misery and suffering, and the harrowing accounts of all but a very few individual victims are lost to history. There were in fact few happy endings.In a culture that worships heroes, our stories are so full of them that I grew up internalizing that heroes were everywhere in every story and that all of us should be poised to be heroes in our own stories. It was only during COVID and the depredations of the Trump era that I finally came to see how rare heroes actually are and to understand that we are obsessed with heroes and with neat tidy Hollywood endings precisely because they are so rare in real life.The heroes of the past nearly two years are not the people you’ve seen on TV or the pundits you’ve read or those who have delivered the loudest smackdowns of Trump. They weren’t posturing or preening. They were doing thankless tedious work that is neither glamorous nor lucrative. The work of democracy is boring, bureaucratic, and procedural — but essential all the same.The heroes have been court staffs, paralegals, clerks, and junior associates working all night in emergency proceedings. They’ve been public interest lawyers, solo immigration attorneys, and immigrant advocates who were already familiar with the Kafkaesque immigration system even before Trump returned to office and made it infinitely worse.Widening the circle, they’ve been health care providers, NGO workers, and arts administrators tirelessly endeavoring to preserve public services while fending off attacks. They’ve been parents struggling to provide normal childhoods to children who have been targeted because they’re brown or trans or disabled.We, too, will move on in due course. But I didn’t want to do it yet without acknowledging who and what we’ve lost along the way.I am deeply grateful that you have stuck with Morning Memo over the past two years. I did not make it easy on you.I vowed not to sugarcoat the reality of Trump II but to chronicle it unstintingly. When things were at their most bewildering and hard to categorize in familiar ways, I threw enormous amounts of information at you. It was often raw and unsorted as I felt my way towards making sense of it all.I refused, maybe stubbornly, to cast events in hopeful or optimistic terms unless they truly deserved it. I didn’t try to stuff events into artificial framings that fed the earnest desire for comeuppance, the hero’s revenge, or the villain’s fall.It was a hard slog for readers. Many of you told me so. Morning Memo was difficult to read, hard to stomach, and relentless day after day for months on end.Politics was grim. People wanted to avert their eyes. Many tuned politics outs or hit pause.After a dramatic upswing in readership during the initial wave of Trump II atrocities in February and March 2025, it became hard to grow the audience for Morning Memo. The audience plateaued, but it didn’t shrink.I feel a fierce pride in you for riding it out with me.Trump II is not over yet. But we’ve clearly entered a new phase, with dramatically different power dynamics and a chance finally to move from a defensive crouch trying to protect what precious ground could be saved to taking the offensive and beginning to reclaim vast areas of American public life.I look forward to navigating this next phase with you.The Remaining Senate Races Edge Blue: Scott Colom (D) has widened his lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R). The latest AP tally has him up by 1,936 votes, as the legal fight over the super-close election begins to take shape.: The NYT projects that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) is likely to sustain her narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) even if she falls short of an outright majority and the election is decided on ranked choice. Meanwhile, President Trump wildly claimed that Sullivan should declare the winner.Straight Into My Veins: Southern GainsWSJ: The Red Wall Falls: Democrats Shatter Decades of GOP Dominance Across the SouthStraight Into My Veins: Texas SweepPolitico: Democratic Attorneys General Just Took Texas Off the Board: “We took the head of the snake.”Texas Tribune: How schools could change for millions of students.Politico: How Dems’ sweep in Texas blows up the 2028 map.”I am not going to answer that question because that is a stupid question.”—longtime voter fraud bamboozler and election denier Cleta Mitchell, when asked by the NYT if she would join with President Trump in accepting the results of the 2026 electionSher-ROD! I Will Never Unhear This ...Trump DOJ Watch: Personnel Shuffle EditionSome notable departures post-election from the Trump DOJ:Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who was overseeing the bogus investigation of the so-called “grand conspiracy” against Trump by the Deep StateHenry C. Whitaker, counselor to the attorney general, who among other things was handling the appeals in the James Comey and Letitia James prosecutions.Be careful: No clear through line connects all of these departures, and there are often post-election personnel shuffles.A Grim But Essential ReadPerhaps as a reminder that our struggles to preserve democracy have been more modest than we might like to admit: An incredible survival tale of one Ukrainian infantryman hunkered down alone on the front line against Russia as his body slowly disintegrated.

And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better.— Nilay Patel, The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election

item.title: Behind the Blog: Dam's Bursting
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss election outcomes and code as a human endeavor.This week I got a real wave of ‘oh man this fucking sucks’ regarding AI. I won’t link to it because it’s just a rando person, but scrolling Reddit I saw someone who said they used Claude to build stuff with Max. Max, or Max/MSP, is a visual programming language that is heavily used in the world of music and visual art. It is the foundation of a lot of electronic music. You can build essentially anything in it, if you put in the work to understand how to put it together. And that can be a lot of work.I’ve built various little things in Max. I made a tool that takes a drum break and generates new, random drum and bass style breaks from it. I am a big, big fan of generative music (both listening and making) where you create rules and parameters, press play, and let the rules decide what comes out. I made another that has various synthesizers, and from scratch manipulates the audio so they sound like Tibetan singing bowls, with their harmonies and individual melodies morphing over time. I also started working on the visual part of Max, called Jitter, to take audio output from Max and generate visuals.These were deeply difficult to make, at least for me. I can code in Python, but this was of course learning an entirely new language, and one whose syntax (and everything really) is entirely different. It took lots of long nights of figuring out, okay, this device connects to this one, this thing goes here, okay, I’ve figured it out. Code is a human endeavor. It can be for a lot of people a creative pursuit (it was for me for a while). But Max coding is human. It is code to create music. And now here was someone using Claude to bypass all of that. To cheat themselves out of the satisfaction of learning an instrument, or in this case a new musical language. I have no idea if they understand what Claude made, or whether they care. But this one was a real gut punch to me.Music creation is one of the areas I do not want AI to touch at all (at least unless it is some very specific use case with the artist’s own data, or something similar). For years as a musician, I simply would not use other peoples’ samples because it felt like a shortcut, it didn’t feel like mine (I know this is an extreme position, and I love lots of sample based music, I just don’t want to make it). This is now even further: you want AI to not only make the music (like Suno), but also the tools that can help you create it in the first place. I dunno man, it just fucking sucks.I held a few articles I’ve written this week back for next week because the election became the story this week, and rightly so. The main thing I published this week was my analysis of the election, which lots of you have said you liked and which a lot of people suggested I must have had fun writing. I did have fun writing it, thank you v much, but I also had a great time this week consuming the memes, the livestreams, the podcasts. Great week for content. If you’ll remember, after Trump got elected a second time, we started to see a handful of people cancel their subscriptions with us not because they said they didn’t like our work, but because they didn’t see what the point was. They figured it was all over, that journalism was useless, that there was not much that could be done to stem fascism in the country. The last two years have been brutal, about as bad as I thought they could be and in many ways worse. A day or two after his election, we all cowrote a piece called “Why the Work Still Matters.” If I’m being honest, I think we wrote it in part because we were scared that people would just mass unsubscribe from us because they felt greater despair, and we wanted to maybe convince ourselves a bit that we could still do this work under Trump. I’m going to quote from that piece at length for a second: “We cannot and will not make false promises to you about the power of journalism—especially at a small publication—to stop the country’s knowing march into authoritarianism. But we can explain our approach to the work and we can demonstrate to you why it matters,” we wrote. “We cannot set the bar for our success at the systemic saving of democracy. Instead, we have found that our work can and does make incremental positive change at the local, state, and federal level, and that, over time, these small improvements become increasingly important. “Our work is populist in that we recognize that many of the problems plaguing the United States today and which are factors that have laid the groundwork for Trump’s return—income inequality, a lack of affordable housing, unstable work, the widespread inability to tell what is real and what is fake—are being at least partially driven by technology and/or the immense wealth of the people who own tech companies,” we added. “Most of our articles tell the stories of hyperspecific communities of people who are using technology or are impacted by it in some way. By focusing on how technology impacts people, we have found that we can impact technology and make the world slightly better, regardless of who the president is.”There’s lots more there. This was published basically exactly two years ago. Since then we have seen many terrible things happen; you’ve read about them on our website and elsewhere. I am too tired at the moment to dig through our archives or rack my brain for more about the horrors of the last two years. But we have also seen, as we hoped but couldn’t know for sure, people organize to support each other, grassroots movements against AI-powered surveillance, ICE’s brutality, Silicon Valley’s excesses, AI data centers, inequality, and more. We know for a fact that a lot of our work has led directly to incremental progress over the last two years. I don’t propose that our blogs created the wave we saw Tuesday, but we’ve heard directly from people who said our reporting inspired them to, for example, get an anti-ALPR license plate regulation put on their town’s ballot. Their town overwhelmingly voted to ban the tech. There are so many things that everyone who has been working for a better future has done over the last two years (and long before that), that made these election results possible, and that made Tuesday feel so satisfying.It’s like the coin pusher game at the arcade. You diligently put quarter after quarter in and maybe it feels like nothing happens. I leave the arcade and you put some quarters in. Every once in a while, a few quarters come out the bottom that make you feel like maybe the game isn’t as rigged as you think it is. Eventually, something like Tuesday happens and zillions of quarters come out. Maybe a few of our quarters helped out. I don’t know if that metaphor makes any sense whatsoever, but it feels like Tuesday was something of a dam bursting. I’ve heard it described as the collective exhale after a decade of misery that has created the space for progress. There is so much more work to be done!One thing I am really excited to see come of this week is the wholesale rejection of data centers specifically. Matthew Gault wrote a great writeup of how this played out across the country, so I don’t want to repeat it too much. But in the last year or so, the explosion of data center projects (and yes, everyone’s calling them “compute campuses” now, which a bunch of overly online people noticed this week too — they’ve been pulling that shit for a while now, but I don’t think the phrase is actually any more palatable than “data center” anyway so, who cares) have bummed me massively. They’re a huge, destructive, ugly, extractive symbol of what the tech industry has become, but instead of remaining concentrated in Palo Alto or in an Apple Store as physically cursed places, they’re taking up miles of land around the country, sucking dry everything around them, returning nothing but bullshit. In 10 years these warehouses will stand abandoned by all stakeholders and we’ll all get nothing but shitty tap water in return. Combined with Flock’s presence around the country, they’ve infiltrated our physical spaces in ways that make Big Tech’s impact on our lives impossible to ignore. And I wonder if that’s part of what we’re seeing in these election results. As Gault wrote: "These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress, told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”

item.title: Final exam for that 1966 American literature college exam
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: Several days ago I posted a reading list from 1968 for a college course on Twentieth Century [American] Southern Writers. The course required reading 16 works from 9 authors. The final exam begins by asking the source for eight excerpted extended quotations, followed by writing an essay comparing the approaches of three of these authors on the subject of love relationships, followed by a second essay comparing/contrasting three of these authors with regard to the style and tone of "southern writers." The final embedded page has some notes I scribbled down while trying to organize my thoughts.The exam booklets were not returned to us, so I have no record (or memory) of what my answers were. My transcript shows a B- for the course, which was quite satisfactory for my pre-med needs. I wonder how I would do today were I to re-read the same books and re-take the exam (an interesting thought experiment which I don't plan to implement). (But I may still re-read some of the books, many of which have left vague pleasant memories in my head).

item.title: What Harmeet Dhillon left out of her resignation letter
item.author: 1axckhtfz27exyoh2ko4cl96s1n5gdibde0yxv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: As the Department of Justice filed a flurry of lawsuits in the final weeks before the election to derail vote counting and certification, something was off. On my daily podcasts, I repeatedly asked: Where is Harmeet Dhillon?Dhillon was the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights and a former Republican election lawyer. She was the architect of DOJ’s failed lawsuits to gain access to state voter files. And yet, in the homestretch, she was missing from the biggest cases.Finally, the mystery has been solved.We now know that in early October, Dhillon told the White House she planned to leave after the election. Yesterday, she formally resigned.Now the question is, what happened to one of Donald Trump’s staunchest promoters of disenfranchisement?When Donald Trump prepared to take office for the second time, he made clear that he wanted the Department of Justice to serve his personal agenda. And nothing was more important to him than vindicating his discredited theory of election denialism.This required transforming the Civil Rights Division into an attack dog that would limit voting rights rather than protect them. The person he chose to lead this effort was Dhillon.When he nominated her in December 2024, he described her as “one of the top Election lawyers in the Country, fighting to ensure that all, and ONLY, legal votes are counted.” While Trump may have overstated her reputation slightly, there is no question that Dhillon lent an air of respectability to the election-denier cause.A California lawyer with strong Republican Party credentials, she carried less baggage than those closely associated with Trump’s 2020 post-election debacle. For a while, Dhillon seemed perfectly positioned to succeed in the new MAGA administration.Yet from the beginning, Dhillon ran into problems.Her signature legal effort was obtaining complete voter data from every state. When 30 states and the District of Columbia refused, she sued them. These cases did not go well for her.By Election Day, DOJ had lost 27 of those cases in district court and won none. It also lost the only appeals court ruling. The losses included more than a dozen defeats before Republican-appointed federal judges, nine of them appointed by Trump himself. DOJ was having scarcely more luck defending against lawsuits challenging the administration’s efforts to restrict voting by executive order.Taken together, DOJ’s voting litigation resembled the same failed scheme Trump’s private lawyers launched after the 2020 election. As the defeats mounted, it seemed clear that something would have to change.It seems that “something” was Dhillon.Yesterday, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that he had accepted her resignation. Dhillon’s letter to Trump, which lists her achievements, makes no mention of the voter roll lawsuits.The only election-related accomplishment she cites is her deployment of election monitors. After much excitement, this too seemed to have fizzled in the end.With Dhillon’s resignation made public, attention immediately turned to the reason for her exit.Some suggested she might have jumped off a sinking ship of increasingly desperate, losing voting cases demanded by the White House. As I noted above, her name was conspicuously absent from the pleadings filed in California seeking to set aside 20,000 ballots, and in Alaska, where DOJ wanted to dictate certification.The other possibility was that she was pushed out for leading a failed legal effort to achieve Trump’s election goals. Given her dismal record in court, this too seemed plausible.Then, late in the day, CBS News reported a third possibility: that Trump demanded she be fired after watching her brief appearance on “60 Minutes” in mid-October, feeling she had not been forceful enough.In most respects, the interview was standard fare. Dhillon toed the White House line on distrust in elections and noncitizen voting. While Trump may have wanted something more conspiratorial, she suggested that unspecified “irregularities” had marred past elections.What I suspect landed her in trouble was this exchange: What I’m hearing you say is that you think it’s very unlikely that a vote, a state vote, will be challenged. But people worry about that. Can you rule it out? Well, I don’t know what is going to happen, but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states.The problem for Dhillon is that by the time the interview aired, DOJ had already sued California to force an “interruption in the usual course of counting” ballots in that state. Indeed, DOJ was insisting that state and local officials ignore state law and set aside ballots from 20,000 people the administration had identified as potential noncitizens.Meanwhile, DOJ was on the verge of filing an even more outrageous lawsuit that sought to block Alaska from certifying its Senate results if Trump’s preferred candidate lost.In Trump’s orbit, it is impossible to know what really motivates hirings and firings. Dhillon, for her part, told Fox News she was not asked to resign. The truth may lie somewhere in between.Dhillon may have been less effective than Trump wanted and more principled than he would tolerate. She may have had red lines she would not cross, in public or in private.Either way, her legacy will be that of someone who came to DOJ to do Trump’s bidding and fell out of favor when she failed. In that, she joins a long list of others who have learned that with Trump, loyalty is a one-way street.

item.title: Farewell To The Cybertruck, A Total Failure
item.author: Albert Burneko
item.content:encoded: The Tesla car company "will be winding down production of the Cybertruck" in 2027, according to a tweet from Elon Musk. Like everything else Musk says, ever, this must be treated as having essentially no truth value whatsoever and at best a coincidental relationship to anything that later happens with or to Cybertruck production. It's noteworthy as an index of what Musk wants people to believe—it's noteworthy, then, that Musk wants people to believe that the era of Cybertruck production is coming to an end.And by "noteworthy," I mean: fucking hilarious!Few vehicles live on in history as metonyms for failure and embarrassment. Edsel, DeLorean, whatever poor beleaguered machine ferries the Sacramento Kings to a given road game instead of doing them the favor of exploding along the way. Add to these the Cybertruck, one of the most hyped vehicles of all time; Tesla's production capacity for the Cybertruck reportedly was something like 250,000 units , and, should the end of its production in fact come in 2027, it will wrap up its four-year run certainly having sold, in total, worldwide, under half of that number. Given the ballooning demand for electric vehicles, the relative lack of competition among all-electric trucks, Tesla's huge head-start in EV production, the unparalleled hype around the Cybertruck's release, and its flowering into a rolling emblem of Musk's personal toxicity, the Cybertruck deserves to endure in history as among the most embarrassing mass-produced products ever available for purchase by human beings. I'd rather carry a battery-powered Big Mouth Billy Bass around under my arm for a year than be seen, by any single person, climbing into or out of a Cybertruck once.

item.title: UK Sex Workers Wake Up to Sites Purging Their Content Following Porn Ban
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Immediately after the of porn fantasies involving choking, breath-restriction, and relative roleplay, adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all.Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure.” Some creators who’ve contacted Clips4Sale to appeal these removals have shared screenshots online of the reply the platform sends: “At this time, we have implemented a general restriction on content availability in the UK to ensure compliance with applicable regulatory requirements,” Clips4Sale support replies, according to these screenshots, viewed by 404 Media. “This is a precautionary measure and does not necessarily indicate that your clips contain prohibited content or violate our policies. We are continuing to review affected content, and additional clips will be made available to UK buyers as they are reviewed and cleared.” Updates to the UK’s Crime and Policing Act went into force on Friday. The law criminalizes a list of sexual acts, including downloading or publishing choking and incest roleplay content. The law is vague and overbroad, criminalizing “strangulation or suffocation” and “certain types” of incest roleplay. There's a lot of confusion among sex workers and fans about what this encompasses, and seemingly could include various kinds of gagging, face sitting, and roleplay. Violating this law, either as someone in possession of noncompliant content or publishing it, carries a risk of up to five years in prison. UK-based creator Sophia Truee told me that Clips4Sale removed more than 75 percent of her content — 392 out of 506 videos — with the platform flagging it as requiring edits without noting what needed to change. Truee makes POV content where she’s alone talking to the camera. Many more creators have shared on social media that content that shouldn’t be in violation of the law has been caught in the crossfire on Clips4Sale specifically. In an email sent to creators on Thursday, the day before the law went into force, Clips4Sale said it would be reviewing “both the video content and its details, including titles, tags, keywords, and descriptions” of content that creators have uploaded to the site. It told creators no action was required. “Affected clips will be hidden automatically starting November 6. If you'd like to make a clip available in the UK again, you can edit the content or its details as needed and submit the changes for compliance review.” Approved content would go back up, the company said.Another message from Clips4Sale on creators’ dashboards said: “As we gain further clarity on the regulatory requirements, we expect to be able to make additional content available again to UK users, wherever permitted. These restrictions apply only to the UK and will not affect your content's availability in other markets where it is permitted.” According to the law, however, if creators based in the UK possess that content, they’re still facing jail time. “Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.” Madame Caramel, another UK-based creator using Clips4Sale, that out of 900 clips she had available on the platform, she now has 198 left. Another creator, that the platform restricted 931 of her clips from UK audiences. “All of them [had] utterly NOTHING to do with the UK laws,” she wrote. There are many, many more creators across social media reporting that they’ve woken up to their clip sites gutted with no warning, even though their content wasn’t non-compliant by the letter of the law.With the speed at which content has been purged en masse, and with some creators reporting instant rejections of content that should actually be compliant with the law, Clips4Sale may be auto-moderating with a very wide net, and sifting through reviews creators are now forced to send for legal content. This is something most social media platforms do to try to comply whenever over-broad laws or payment processor regulations hit. Other platforms are also attempting to comply now that the law is in effect. LoyalFans has a notice on its homepage for fans addressing the new law. It says: “These changes may also apply to content you've purchased, downloaded, or saved privately on your devices. Non-compliant content in your Loyalfans account will be removed on November 5, with no further action required from your side. We encourage you to understand the new law and review any affected content you have downloaded, or stored privately, whether on your phone, computer, or cloud storage.” LoyalFans updated its terms of use on Thursday to include strangulation or suffocation, in its unacceptable content list, “including any content, whether real or simulated, that explicitly and realistically depicts a person strangling or suffocating another person, such as applying pressure to the neck or obstructing the nose or mouth,” the terms now say. “This content is prohibited regardless of whether the participants consent, and even if it is fantasy-based, roleplay, or digitally created.” Several creators using LoyalFans have posted on social media saying they’ve had hundreds of videos removed from their accounts on that platform, too.JustForFans, an LGBTQ and kink content site, posted on X earlier this week that creators should review their content and use its new “restrict this content” option to keep it from being viewed by users in the UK. The platform also said that it would be scanning every new video upload for consent requirements and content restrictions. “If we find content that should be restricted in the UK, we will restrict it and you can review it in a new section of your Media Center called Restricted Content. The page will tell you what we found and give you options right on that page to fix it: re-word a post, replace a video with another video, delete the video, or tell us we are wrong, and why you believe we are wrong. A staff member will review your changes,” it said. “The UK's new pornography restrictions are creating a lot of uncertainty for adult creators, and we want to give our models options rather than simply take away their work. We're reviewing new and old content for potentially restricted material, blocking flagged content from UK viewers and giving models the ability to correct or challenge those decisions. Creators can also restrict individual videos themselves or block access from the UK entirely," JustForFans founder Dominic Ford said in a statement. “The law is nuanced and not particularly well-adapted to gay content. The spirit of the law is about protecting women, but some things don't translate directly to gay culture. For example, 'daddy' is an archetype, not a claim that someone is your actual father, so we're not treating those scenes as automatically prohibited. Our priority is to comply with the law without unnecessarily restricting content elsewhere. We also want models in England and Wales to understand that the law covers possession, not just publication, so they need to take extra precautions.”The vagueness of the law, combined with the use of auto-moderation on sites like Clips4Sale, have come together to create a nightmare for creators. “This highlights the lack of protection sex workers and content creators have when laws aren't properly researched and clearly written. We do our very best to stay compliant and ensure everyone's safety by following the rules,” Truee said. “This highlights the unprecedented use of AI in moderation and the lack of clear instructions from the government.” Clips4Sale told 404 Media in a statement: "The UK law carries criminal penalties for possessing or distributing consensual kink and fetish content made by consenting adults, meaning our creators risk arrest if we allow them to distribute banned content in the UK. Unfortunately, there’s no good guidance as to what content might or might not now be illegal. As a result, we’re being aggressive for the time being when it comes to limiting content. We know this is not what creators want, and it’s not what we want. Over the coming weeks, we hope to be able to clear clips that were limited during this precautionary period, after we’ve had a chance to review them more closely. This law is impacting an already marginalized community, mostly women, mostly queer or gender-nonconforming, heavily stigmatized and discriminated against. As with most sex censorship, the burden falls heavily on communities with the least amount of power. We will work with the UK government to comply with the law and our creators to keep them safe."Updated Friday, November 6 1:03 p.m. EST with comment from Clips4Sale.Updated 3:08 a.m. EST with comment from JustForFans.

item.title: Losing loser won’t ever erase the stain of losing the midterms
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Imagine, if you will, that you are United States President Chucklefuck McDingleberry.Your second term in office has been such a shittacular disaster that your own party has just taken a historic drubbing in the midterms. You’re radioactive right now. The voters have pantsed you. You’ve now been outed as a loser. The rats are leaving your sinking ship. Everyone loathes you. Even your most die-hard cultists are all, History will remember you as a failure. The worst of the worst.Given all that, what do you do for an encore?“When you look at that White House, you know, I hear Obama, but he— Obama doesn’t know about dirt and filth. And he doesn’t know about cracked stones. And he doesn’t know about broken windows. He’s probably fine with them. But I’m not. I’m not fine with them.”Holy fuck, Obama’s tossed-off crack about how Donny’s Oval Bordello ‘looks like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory’ really really got under Donny’s supernaturally-thin skin. He’s still shitting himself raw over it, a week later.Meet the new Donny, same as the old Donny.Any competent leader, after being handed such a humiliating loss, would be meeting with staff, and going, ‘how do we fix this? How do we rebuild the trust of the people?’ But not Donny. He is fundamentally incapable of reflection, introspection, or change. He never has been, and he never will be. So he’s going to pretend it never happened. He’s going to blunder right ahead, doing the same old shit, telling the same old lies, boasting about the same old imaginary accomplishments, building the same old useless monuments to himself — and nursing the same old grievances and grudges.Oh, and Donny has a cunning plan to force everyone to ‘enjoy’ his Oval Bordello in perpetuity.Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.See you in court, if you think that’s ever going to happen, fuckface. Every president gets to decorate their own Oval Office. It’s historical precedent.I have a better idea. Instead of deeming Dear Leader’s vulgar monuments to himself to be worthy of preservation, how about creating a National Registry of Fucking Eyesores To Be Demolished? Because that’s what Donny’s really leaving behind. Fucking eyesores, to be demolished.The Epstein Dance Hall where the East Wing used to be.The Epstein Parking Lot where the Rose Garden used to be.The Epstein Trough of Rancid Water where the Reflecting Pool used to be.The Epstein Helipad where the South Lawn used to be.And, of course, the Saddam Hussein Cheesecake Experience where the Oval Office used to be.But it’s not just judge who blocked that shit. It’s a judge we already know and love.U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan blocked work on the arch for two weeks while the court considers challenges to its legality. Three Vietnam War veterans, a historic preservationist, the D.C. government and the Commonwealth of Virginia sued to halt construction.That’s right, it’s She’s the judge who was presiding over Donny’s Big January 6th Insurrection Fuckery Trial, until his reelection put the kibosh on that. She has no patience for any of Dear Leader’s bullshit, once literally ruling ‘presidents are not kings,’ in a judgement against Donny. It’s heartening to see that she’s still out here, fighting all the good fights, and still getting in Donny’s way.We thank you for your service.But it doesn’t matter how man shitty monuments this pathetic dipshit erects in his own fragile, needy honor. He’s never going to erase the stain of being a losing loser who fucked his own party nearly out of existence.I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT. IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE! President DONALD J. TRUMPThis is now the second time he’s posted this nonsense. Overcompensating much, dumb-ass? Shut up, loser. You’re a losing loser who loses, and everyone knows it.Which brings us to our of schadenfreude.Outgoing Republican Senator Bill Cassidy is very perplexed right now. Apparently, it has just come to the Senator’s attention that an elected official has to — it says here, “If you look at the shellacking our party took, it’s pretty clear that most voters don’t think that we were there to serve them. They thought, once more, that the politicians wanted to keep power so much that they were willing to change the rules to make the people serve the politicians.”Wait, was that wrong, to ignore the needs of We the People, opting instead to allow Dear Leader to do whatever the fuck he wanted, and to actually aid and abet him?I tell ya, Bill Cassidy has to plead ignorance on this thing. Because if anyone had said anything at all to him when he first became a senator that that sort of thing was frowned upon…Cassidy was the deciding vote on Todd Blanche. He can eat a dick.Hang on, we should fact-check this. Is that true? Can Senator Cassidy eat a dick?Yes, he can. Because not only was Cassidy the deciding vote on letting the Donny’s personal ambulance-chaser become Attorney General — he was also the deciding vote on Bobby Brainworms being put in charge of our nation’s healthcare. Sorry, but the Esteemed Senator doesn’t get to go on cable news and point his finger at everyone else. His hands are as dirty as the rest of his party’s.Bill Cassidy can go pound salt.Remember how bleak and hopeless things seemed, that morning? bleak and hopeless, for a good long while. It Here’s what I wrote in that post from November 6, 2024.America is about to go through some things. This hurts a lot, I know. Remember, we still have each other. We’re all in this together.Let the events of the past week be a reminder that situations can and do change for the better, when we all work together. We will always be here for each other. We will always be in this together.Which brings me to . Someone’s come up with an all-new reason for canceling their paid subscription. It’s because I’m obsolete! Okay, that made me laugh out loud. I can’t even get disgruntled by it. Seriously, if anyone feels they no longer need a daily dose of this shit, Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here’s Ms Spouse, so bemused by something she saw going on in the background in Half Moon on March 8, 2024, that she took out her phone and captured it.Have a great Friday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Reshaping The Electorate
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I wanted to flag this critical data point: across the Deep South (AL, MS, SC, LA, GA) the percentage of the electorate made up by Black voters rose dramatically — by 3 percentage points in all those states except for, Alabama where it rose by 4 percentage points. For instance, in Mississippi, it rose from 30% in 2024 to 33% in 2026. Put differently, Black voters turned at out at 96% of their 2024 turnout whereas white voters managed only 71%. The impact of this gap showed up especially in Senate races in South Carolina and Mississippi. This was, needless to say, critical to Democratic victories throughout the region. Paradoxically the increase was greatest in Alabama which didn’t have a Senate race and lacked a high profile governor’s race, judged by national attention, though Democrat Doug Jones made it a much closer race against Tommy Tuberville than most anticipated. There was a closely watched House race where Rep. Shomari Figures (AL-2) retained his seat despite an attempt to gerrymander him out of it. These numbers can be compared to a stable share of the electorate in the Northeast and Industrial Midwest. So much of 2026 was a rebellion against Donald Trump and MAGA. Here it’s at least slightly different: all the evidence we have tells us this as a reply to the decision in which the corrupt Court majority essentially struck down what remained of the Voting Rights Act and unleashed a string of rushed gerrymanders to eliminate Black majority districts across the region. How different this is is hard to say: SCOTUS is pretty much MAGA at this point. But it’s a distinct wave or tsunami within the larger one.

item.title: Now We Know How Much Money Bill Simmons Had His Daughter’s Boyfriend Bet For Him
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: Bill Simmons got himself into some trouble a few weeks ago, when he admitted on his podcast that he had engaged in proxy betting. Simmons, who lives in California, where online sports gambling is still illegal, told his listeners that he had instructed his daughter's boyfriend, who lives in gambling-friendly Massachusetts, to log into his FanDuel account and place bets on his behalf. Because this practice is strictly prohibited by FanDuel's policies, his bets were voided. But a question remained: How much action was Simmons denied?Now, thanks to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission, we have an answer to that question. Sports betting reporter Geoff Zochodne pointed out that the commission's Investigation and Enforcement Bureau made a presentation to commissioners Thursday about Simmons's infraction. A memo announcing the presentation provided some details about how much Simmons was trying to bet:The incident involved an admission made by media personality Bill Simmons on his August 30, 2026, podcast pertaining to his placement of proxy wagers on his FanDuel account in Massachusetts through an acquaintance who was physically present in Massachusetts. FanDuel reported that the matter involved 22 wagers with a total handle of $21,800 placed over three (3) dates: August 5, 2026, August 7, 2026, and August 19, 2026.

item.title: "Feather letters" (Fjäderbrev) were forerunners of express mail
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: In the era before the invention of adhesive postage stamps, postal services in Scandinavia used feathers affixed to the envelope to indicate that delivery was urgent and should be expedited. The envelope above has a wavy line (known as a meander) with two horizontal lines through it and several stylized "crowns" in the spaces (together known as a Crown Coil or Kronoslinga) indicating that this was to be sent through the Royal Swedish Crown PostExtra feathers indicated increasing degrees of urgency. The envelope above has both white and black feathers affixed, apparently indicating the need for transport both by day and by night.

item.title: That’ll About Do It For The Joe Fagnano Experience
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Plenty of teams have lost their starting quarterbacks, to things like knee surgery (Giants), blood clots (Eagles), or an ancient Hittite curse (Chargers). But it's unlikely that anyone's had a rougher go of it under center this year than the Baltimore Ravens. Already sliding out of the ranks of the contenders, Baltimore was without Lamar Jackson for three punchless games due to an ankle sprain, and then, last weekend, he tore up his thumb on his very first snap in his return. His replacement Snoop Huntley is presentable as far as QB2s go, having been here on and off since 2020; Huntley was then promptly injured in the second quarter, and is out for the season with turf toe.Just about any NFL team is dead meat after the loss of two quarterbacks, but the Ravens are extra-pungent carrion. Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie out of Maine and UConn who walked on and played seven years in college, was the sacrificial lamb for Thursday night's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. And while I have plenty of sympathy for Fagnano and the Ravens offense for only having a short week to prepare, this was indeed Thursday-ass football. https://twitter.com/DanDGriffis/status/2118536909962019135

item.title: New from Chicago: A full-color visual history of how we connected the world
item.author: 557489585.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
item.content:encoded:
A beautifully illustrated, first-of-its-kind chronicle of road maps through the ages.
Road maps are the most common form of map that most of us regularly interact with while we all seek to find our way from here to there. Today, the digital maps on our devices are just the latest in a series of cartographic innovations designed to make transportation of people and goods easier and more predictable. Whether traveling on foot, in a vehicle, or by animal, people have long created and relied on roads, and efforts to map these overland routes predate the invention of the printing press. Yet the vast majority of road maps have been produced only within the last five hundred years—and even more specifically within the last century.
Historian Jeremy Black is the first to chart the tale of road maps, beginning with the “Peutinger Map,” which illustrated the roads famously connecting the Roman Empire. From the time of antiquity, Black guides the reader through the centuries all the way to the modern age, when the invention of the automobile spurred the creation of roads and road maps like nothing before. Over the course of this journey, Black illuminates the integral role maps played in the development of government infrastructures through time and across all the inhabited continents. And, arriving in the present day, Black shows how technology may soon make the paper road map obsolete even as it builds on the conventions of the preceding centuries.
Featuring a series of full-color maps from the British Library’s collection and beyond, is an eye-opening visual story of how modern civilizations traversed, constructed, and connected their worlds.

item.title: When your home is on a wooded lot...
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: ... sometimes the woods come to visit.Several days ago we were startled by what sounded like rolling thunder on a storm-free evening. A quick peek out back revealed the cause. We knew the tree was dead, and has been so for many years, but we like to leave standing deadwood for the benefit of the insectivorous birds. We have seen four different types of woodpeckers from that deck (Downy, Red-bellied, Red-headed, and Hairy) plus some 40+ other species of birds over the years. Those recurrent joys fully justify the occasional hassle of cleanup duties in the yard, woods, and now the deck. We've been less happy with visits from local raccoons. Having trees near the house is not a significant risk factor for raccoon molestations, because those critters are fully capable of scaling a brick wall at the corner. Once on the roof they look for accessible soffits, and with those dextrous paws they can rip the soffits off in order to gain entrance into crawl spaces and attics. We used Havahart traps for a while, but eventually contracted with a company called Skedaddle that sent out a crew of five young women with ladders, tools, and wire mesh to render the soffits raccoon-proof.Now I have to find a neighborhood kid with a chain saw...

item.title: The night sky over rural New Zealand
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: To create his spectacular image – now viewed millions of times online – Brendan Larsen spent two hours in September snapping hundreds of photographs of the night sky over Mount Taranaki in the North Island.Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 45 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites...

item.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: Since the midterms were largely about affordability and fairness, and featured a rejection of the nonstop, unregulated data center sprawl, it may be tempting for some to celebrate the idea that the hubristic AI industry finally got theirs. But they don’t get theirs without you getting yours. The rising tide of AI may not have lifted all boats, but the draining of economic enthusiasm around that industry could sink us all. It’s the AI economy, stupid. AI drives big tech and together they drive the entire economy. Stocks, bonds, credit markets, hedge funds, bank lending, stock portfolios, your retirement account, investments, venture capital … no part of our financial system, from Wall Street to Main Street to 21 Jump Street, would escape a bubble burst unscathed. “Any downturn in the AI industry, either in the buildout of its infrastructure or the valuations of its stocks, will reverberate far beyond Silicon Valley. Technology companies have dominated the stock market for years, but artificial intelligence has pushed the concentration to new heights. Tech now accounts for nearly half the value of the benchmark S&P 500 Index.” (Gift Article): AI Has Taken Over Every Corner of the Market. Eugene Levy, John Candy, Catherine O’Hara, Martin Short, Rick Moranis … SCTV was a cult favorite that introduced a generation of mainstream stars. On Netflix, check out SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of.+ My local sports radio station’s weekly interview with Warriors coach Steve Kerr is now sponsored by the Contra Costa Library (which is about all you need to know about the current economics of radio). Kerr was recently asked for a book rec (which I took and enjoyed). Check out (in general, or even from the Conta Costa Library) Liz Moore’s The God of the Woods, in which a teenager vanishes from her Adirondack summer camp. (And yes, they’re already filming the Netflix version…)Killing the Death Penalty: “State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us. I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.” Gavin Newsom Commutes the Sentences of California’s 548 Death Row Inmates. It’s worth noting that California hasn’t executed anyone on death row since 2006. So this move won’t necessarily have a significant, tangible impact, but it will certainly have a political impact.+ A Dollar Sign of Things to Come: “Whether prediction markets can accurately anticipate election results has become a key question after the midterms. An analysis by The New York Times, using statistical methods, found that for most of the midterm race, prediction markets performed no better than election forecasts, which produce odds using polling and other indicators instead of betting activity. But as Election Day neared, prediction markets performed better as forecasts and polling became stale.” How Accurate Were Prediction Markets at Picking Midterm Winners? (Aren’t most of the people betting on elections on the prediction markets using traditional election forecasters as their guide? I mean, they’re not just betting on a hunch.)+ You Thought Your Fill Up Was Expensive: “After Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea and seized territory commanding the strategic Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint, the kingdom reached out to the group to see what it would take to arrive at a negotiated halt to the hostilities. The answer it got back: $51 billion.”+ “It was a reflection on the warm embrace Brand, a comedian and actor, has received from prominent Trump administration officials and other leaders in Kennedy’s ‘Make America Healthy Again’ (Maha) movement, where Brand has used his star status to criticize vaccines and vaccine mandates.” Weeks before rape conviction, Russell Brand was featured speaker for Maha group allied with RFK Jr. (Well, it’s not exactly like MAGA is anti-rape…)+ “We’re in the era of the ultralong movie. Some of this year’s biggest films, including ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’ run nearly three hours. With no intermissions, viewers have to hold it or risk missing crucial moments. They’re flocking to RunPee, an app that recommends the best times for bathroom breaks with synopses of what they’ve missed.” Hollywood’s New Superhero Is the Guy Who Tells Moviegoers When to Pee.

item.title: The Woodmans (2010) ★★★★
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: A documentary about Francesca Woodman and her family. I love her work.Francesca was a troubled genius who ended her life way too soon.The movie was grim and kind of depressing. Her parents were indifferent, jealous, narcissistic, and aloof. Her dad was a failed artist and ended up stealing is daughter's visual language after her death. I never new that and it pissed me off.

item.title: Vainqueur
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Vainqueur, a German electronic musician. The man behind the project, René Löwe, grew up in East Berlin and would tune into a Western radio station that played Detroit techno and hip-hop.After the wall came down, he got into the minimalist techno scene around the Berlin record store Hard Wax, along with Moritz von Oswald. collects six long tracks from that period, which loop interesting synth lines that modulate gradually over steady drums. from 2007 has two nine-minute collaborations with fellow German producer Substance, which have more of an ambient techno sound.

item.title: Why challenges to a fair count in Mississippi and Alaska will fall flat
item.author: delivery_20261105064035.48275920.3584@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
Tensions were high going into Election Day, not only because control of Congress was up for grabs but also because President Donald Trump and his administration had spent months attempting to interfere with states’ electoral processes. Lawsuits were filed, letters were sent, and threats were made, yet in the end Democratic candidates across the country notched definitive wins with margins that, in the words of Trump, were simply “too big to rig.” Even Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton—and Trump himself—was forced to concede defeat. The judiciary played a major role in tamping down frivolous legal challenges before the vote, and now Democrats, with their handsome majorities in both the House and Senate, have a mandate to fulfill.
Consequentially, the two biggest legal challenges that consumed the days leading up to the midterms have effectively been shut down. The Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California election officials, which argued that they must set aside some 20,000 mail ballots the federal government suspected of being cast by noncitizens, was shut down by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. And the day before, a federal judge dismissed the DOJ’s lawsuit in Alaska, which sought to separate and preserve certain ballots cast in the state’s Senate election in the event that Republican Dan S. Sullivan lost his race. Across the country, in almost every instance of the DOJ suing states for access to their voter rolls, the federal government lost its case.
With all of that said, it’s worth looking at what the state of play is for any ongoing election challenges with a pair of major Senate races and a number of House seats yet to be called. The AFL-CIO, one of the largest national labor unions, sued the DOJ to stop it from demanding that state and local election officials separate disputed ballots and threatening prosecution if those ballots were counted. The case has been ping-ponging between judges at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and on Election Day, the AFL-CIO asked the full court to weigh in—all 29 federal judges—and it remains to be seen where that may take this case. Over in Alaska, there was also new DOJ activity; this time, the agency sent 20 Democrats letters informing them that they may be targets of a federal investigation over donor fraud and conspiracy charges and that they should preserve certain records. Among those who received the letters was Marc Elias, a well-known elections lawyer who has represented Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, whose Alaska race has yet to be called. It’s not clear yet where this investigation will go, if anywhere, though Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, noted in her Substack: “The idea of prosecuting these people is odd since the Alaska Supreme Court has already determined that both Dan Sullivans could be on the ballot.”
These legal challenges, though significant, are not exactly to the tune of what was happening in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election. In fact, the tone and temperature of the president and his allies have been markedly subdued since Tuesday night, with Vice President J.D. Vance putting out a surprisingly candid assessment of the Republican Party’s losses, while House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly acknowledged that the party had lost control of the House. Come Wednesday morning, Johnson also informed his staff that he does not intend to stay on as leader in the new Congress. To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, this more muted reaction is likely because there is a realization setting in that “these intellectual wars, election administration wars, are not getting them what they’re trying to achieve, either on the political side or on the strategic side.”
Even if a worst-case scenario breaks out in which the Trump administration or Republican candidates challenge election results or processes in tight Senate races in Alaska or Mississippi, “the heavy hitters of both the Democratic and Republican parties, with respect to legal talent, will not be spread thin,” Stewart told me. “I think it will be much easier for attacks on the democratic process to be beaten back.” That is especially true when considering Democrats’ margins of victory in certain states, like Texas and Georgia, where their candidates earned double-digit wins. Even in races that were closer, Democratic candidates secured comfortable vote counts that largely fall outside margins of error. This gives way to a math problem that Republicans simply cannot solve for; Democrats have so far earned 54 seats in the Senate, a body that confirms election results, and the Trump administration does not have a meaningful enough majority of Republicans to pressure its legal shenanigans onto this time around.
“The margins last night are too big for DOJ meddling to make any sense, and it definitely won’t work,” Ankush Khardori, a former federal prosecutor, wrote. Harry Litman, a former U.S. attorney and deputy assistant attorney general, also expressed skepticism about meddling: “The most important defense/pushback/insurance policy against attempted election interference always has been a Democratic rout, which takes away the Trumpian bogus premise of a close election decided by illegal votes.” The bigger question now is if and how Democrats will use their congressional majorities. They will take over as chairs of the most powerful congressional committees capable of subpoenaing every single administration official, ally, or donor and deciding whether to penalize—or even possibly impeach—any of them for actions they’ve undertaken since Trump began his lawless second term.

item.title: Saturday 80s Jam: I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking for – U2
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: When U2 released “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” in 1987, they were already one of the biggest rock bands of the decade. But the song represented another step forward for a group that had spent much of its career trying to expand the possibilities of what a rock band could sound like.Released as the second single from , the song was built around a deceptively simple idea: the search for something meaningful that never quite ends. It could be interpreted as a love song, a spiritual reflection, or a statement about ambition and dissatisfaction. That ambiguity helped make it one of U2’s most enduring recordings.The song began with a very different musical foundation than the finished version. Drummer Larry Mullen Jr. had been experimenting with a rhythm that producer Daniel Lanois and the band developed into something with a distinctive gospel influence. Guitarist The Edge then created the shimmering, echo-heavy guitar sound that became one of the recording’s defining characteristics.The result was unlike much of the arena rock dominating the 1980s.It was big without being bombastic.The rhythm was steady and hypnotic, while The Edge’s guitar seemed to float above the arrangement. Then Bono’s voice entered, delivering the song with a mixture of certainty and doubt.That contradiction is central to the recording.The singer is searching, but he hasn’t arrived.He has experienced love, traveled, struggled, believed, doubted, and continued moving forward, yet something remains unresolved. The song never provides a neat answer.That made it particularly powerful.“I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” became one of U2’s biggest American hits, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100. It also became a major international success and helped become one of the defining albums of the 1980s.The song’s gospel influence was especially notable. U2 had incorporated religious imagery throughout their career, but here the connection between rock music and gospel was unusually direct. The backing vocals and arrangement gave the song a spiritual atmosphere without turning it into a conventional religious recording.Then there was Bono’s performance.Rather than singing the song like a traditional rock anthem, he gradually increases the emotional intensity. His voice sounds both powerful and vulnerable, perfectly matching the central idea of someone who continues searching despite never finding exactly what they want.The song also represented the evolution of U2’s sound during the 1980s. They had started the decade as a relatively straightforward post-punk band from Dublin. By 1987, they were making expansive, atmospheric rock that incorporated American blues, gospel, roots music, and experimental production. was the culmination of that development.“I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” was one of the clearest examples of how far they had come.It wasn’t built around a flashy guitar solo or a complicated arrangement. Instead, its power came from atmosphere, repetition, vocal performance, and an idea almost everyone can understand.The feeling that you’ve accomplished something but still aren’t quite where you want to be.That feeling doesn’t belong to 1987.More than three decades later, the song remains one of U2’s signature recordings and one of the defining rock songs of the late 1980s. Its combination of rock, gospel, and atmospheric production helped broaden the sound of mainstream rock while giving U2 one of their most enduring songs.And perhaps the most interesting thing about the title is that it never promises the search will end.And somehow, that uncertainty is exactly what makes the song so powerful.

item.title: Everyone Everywhere Hated Meta’s New AI Training Terms. Now, They’re On Pause
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Following widespread backlash, Meta announced earlier this week it’s putting a planned update of its commercial terms of use on pause. The terms would have required business accounts to allow Meta to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products. The new terms were initially set to go into effect on October 30, but after outcry from journalists and users who didn’t want Meta reaching far beyond Instagram and Facebook and into their websites to suck up their work as training data for its generative AI products, Meta announced it was pushing the change to November 20. Now, it’s on hold entirely. “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms,” Meta says on the commercial terms announcement used to be. “These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.” which first reported the change, notes that following a case supported by the Norwegian Media Businesses’ Association and 180 Norwegian media companies, a court in Norway granted a temporary injunction suspending Meta’s new terms, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority said it would do its own investigation into the terms. After pushing the update to November, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, , and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products.

item.title: Accountability, Government and Freedom
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I’ve seen a few comments over the last couple days to the effect that our system turned out to be more robust, stronger than some of us feared. Trump tried to tamper with and rig the 2026 election. But he mostly failed. I would put it a little differently. We turned out to be — the American people — stronger, more robust than many of us feared. This may seem mawkish or merely semantic. But it’s more than that and the difference speaks directly to the current debates about accountability and how it should shape the next Congress and the next two years.The singular lesson of the Trump Era has been that no system can be stronger than its participants’ willingness to follow and enforce the rules that govern it. It’s worth sitting with that for a moment. No constitution or system of laws and protections can be stronger than its participants’ willingness to follow the rules that govern it. Trump was faced with the big challenge that states control the administration of elections. But the White House came up with numerous quite ingenious angles to overcome those obstacles. It took an immense amount of work by voters, elected officials, judges, lawyers, countless Americans in myriad positions and professions to stop it. A governmental system provides a framework, a playing field. But as the authors of the federal Constitution debated and largely decided: there is no machine that runs of itself. It lives or dies, degenerates or perseveres, based on the people, the citizens who make it up.
