item.title: The Confessions of an AI Fraud Kingpin
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: A few years ago, Yuriy Nazarenko sat at a desk in his grandfather’s apartment in Ukraine and, on a diet of cigarettes, Lay’s chips, and beer, painstakingly made digital copies of fake identity documents. One of his four computer screens had the messaging app Telegram open. Another displayed a scan of a passport in Photoshop filling the entire monitor.Pixel by pixel, with rap music blaring, Nazarenko edited each part of the passport. That included the MRZ codes, the block of text printed at the bottom of identity documents; the portraits to superimpose someone else’s face into the document; and the overall dimensions and quirks of each different type of passport. Nazarenko would sometimes sit for more than 12 hours at his computer, obsessively tinkering away, with a single, high-quality fake identity document taking up to a week of work.When someone thinks of fake IDs, maybe they imagine a spotty underage teen buying a physical counterfeit driver’s license so they can score some beer. But in the global criminal underworld, digital copies or scans of IDs are like a skeleton key. A convincing scan of an ID or utility bill, loaded with a bogus name or someone else’s identity, can unlock the ability to make bank accounts, bypass checks on cryptocurrency exchanges to buy or sell more Bitcoin, or rent a safehouse, all while keeping the criminal’s real identity hidden. The digitally altered IDs need to fool both human reviewers and automated systems that scan them for inconsistencies. Making fake IDs requires exquisite attention to detail.All of that manual labor doesn’t really scale, Nazarenko thought to himself as he meticulously edited passport after passport. He went on to make templates of fake identity documents that sped up the process, but it was still slow. After many of these nights, he had an idea. He built a website to automate the process that autopopulated a fake ID with the personal data a customer wanted, rather than having him do it by hand. Then, when generative AI became mainstream a short while later, he incorporated that too.“That gradually became OnlyFake,” Nazarenko told me.OnlyFake, the underground website Nazarenko made, landed like a bomb in the fraud world. It allowed anyone to generate not only convincing scans of driver’s licenses or passports, but also realistic looking photos of those fake identity documents laying on a sofa, carpet, or desk, as if someone had taken the ID out of their wallet and snapped a picture of it on their phone. Needed a convincing looking photo of a California driver’s license to open a cryptocurrency account in someone else’s name? Or a British passport to incorporate a company overseas? Or a Social Security card? No problem. The results were photos of identity documents that didn’t really exist, of people who may not be real, but yet could trick the sorts of people and companies that verify documents.With OnlyFake, you didn’t have to be a master forger like Nazarenko to make fake documents. Now, anyone could churn out fake IDs at scale, sometimes even hundreds or thousands at a time. OnlyFake threatened the entire idea of know-your-customer, or KYC, where financial institutions take steps to know who exactly are using its services. When anyone can make a photo of a fake ID for just a few dollars in Bitcoin, is anyone really who they say they are?Nazarenko didn’t know it then, hunched over his desk, but OnlyFake would soon become so influential that it would spawn copy cats, and the FBI would eventually hunt Nazarenko and shut down some of OnlyFake’s competitors. The Department of Justice said in an announcement about Nazarenko’s guilty plea that OnlyFake made more than a million dollars selling fake IDs which cost just $15 a pop.Now for the first time, Nazarenko, 28, free after a year in prison and living in Asia, is telling his story: how North Korean fake IT workers used his creation, how he ended up in ICE detention after serving his sentence in the U.S., and how OnlyFake unleashed a new age of AI-powered fraud. Nazarenko said he wanted to talk to me because I was the first journalist to reveal that OnlyFake existed. This article is based on interviews with Nazarenko and his lawyer, court records, and my own reporting in the online world of fraud that OnlyFake inhabited. “OnlyFake was the first time I saw how quickly a small internet project could turn into something global. Unfortunately, it also taught me, in a very painful way, what can happen when the scale of something grows faster than your understanding of its consequences,” Nazarenko told me.Growing up, Nazarenko’s parents questioned whether Nazarenko would ever find a job. His father worked for the Security Service of Ukraine. Raised in a suburb outside of Odesa, Nazarenko jumped between a few different gigs. He worked as a cook, a waiter, at a supermarket, and as a cameraman at a local Ukrainian TV station.Nazarenko also ran a YouTube channel about video games. Having a constant need for new graphics and thumbnails, he picked up Photoshop. Over the years, he got better and better. After searching for ways to make money, he discovered that people online would pay for high quality copies of identity documents. Nazarenko got into the business of fake IDs.“When you zoom in several hundred percent, you begin to understand how complicated even an ordinary passport or driver’s license really is. What looks like a simple plastic card to most people is actually made up of a huge number of small security and design elements,” he told me.Nazarenko said he hired programmers to start automating the generation of fake identity documents, including one hacker who “used to break into government websites.” He also hired designers; he said he met the workers through personal contacts and “online communities.” At first, OnlyFake didn’t use any AI. Automating parts of it was more about cutting out the busy work. Customers would fill out what name and other personal information they wanted to appear on the ID, upload whatever photograph they wanted, and OnlyFake would then automatically produce an image that looked like a scanned driver’s license or passport.Eventually, Nazarenko introduced more AI components. His team made a massive bank of fake, AI-generated faces that customers could place into the identity documents. For the backgrounds that the fake IDs would appear on, Nazarenko and his small team first photographed them themselves, then, “as neural networks advanced, we started generating them using AI,” Nazarenko said. The key to being able to generate all sorts of different IDs was obtaining lots of different scans. These showed what a Nevada driver’s license, or a Russian passport, or a U.S. passport card looked like, for example. Nazarenko put out a call to action on Telegram. If you have good scans of IDs, I will pay handsomely for them. And he was especially interested in U.S documents. Soon, Nazarenko had a huge library of fake IDs, stretching from Argentina to Spain. He fed these images into OnlyFake. “The era of rendering documents using Photoshop is coming to an end,” a post on OnlyFake’s Telegram account read. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Nazarenko left Ukraine and moved around Europe.Customers could buy individual generations of IDs, or sign up to various subscription plans. The ‘Light’ package for $99 a month gave a user 10 generations. The ‘Ultimate’ $1,500 tier, meanwhile, let a customer upload a spreadsheet of the personal data they wanted to appear on the IDs, making the process even faster, and even came with a direct customer support representative on Telegram. Nazarenko said other criminals were selling fish, while he “was selling the fishing rod.” Rather than paying a forger to make a fake ID, so a criminal could then open a cryptocurrency account under a different name, OnlyFake let the criminals generate the IDs themselves.It didn’t take long for customers to roll in. Nazarenko would then reinvest the money back into OnlyFake, including advertising his service, pushing development, and making the project bigger.“At some point, I realized that what I was doing had almost stopped being design work. It had become a constant engineering problem,” Nazarenko said. Beyond making the documents was building infrastructure, automating it all, and keeping the site secure. “In practice, we started operating much like a normal technology startup, except we were operating in an illegal market,” he recalled. Later the Department of Justice said OnlyFake generated at least 10,000 fake IDs, and made $1.2 million over the years.With customers also comes competitors. OnlyFake had identified a gap in the market for the automatic generation of fake identity documents in bulk, and other people wanted a slice of those profits. Nazarenko said competitors constantly fired distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks at OnlyFake, where hackers bombard a site with so much bogus web traffic that it becomes unusable. Hackers also tried to access OnlyFake’s template database. A rival managed to unmask one of Nazarenko’s employees, and demanded certain concessions from OnlyFake, which Nazarenko says he denied. Nazarenko’s days were consumed with customers and orders; then nights were spent working on tweaking the documents. To stay up, he turned to coffee and energy drinks. Then cocaine.With real money coming in, competitors hounding him, and the stress and paranoia that comes with that, Nazarenko started using other drugs to try to cope with the pressure, he said. He used LSD, magic mushrooms, and ecstasy. “That wasn’t about work anymore, it was about feeling something other than anxiety, about switching off a head that hadn’t switched off in years,” he said.In early 2024, I discovered OnlyFake myself while scrolling through Telegram. I logged in, sent a small amount of cryptocurrency to the site, and generated some photos of fake IDs. I was blown away by the pictures of fake IDs laying on a carpet and upholstery. The implications for fraud were staggering, I thought. It seemed like it would shatter KYC practices — where cryptocurrency companies, for example, verify someone’s identity by having them upload a copy of their passport. What use is KYC when anyone can generate an identity document of essentially anyone else?I entered the name David Creeks, put in a random birthday, and the site autofilled a bunch of other important information like the license’s issue and expiry dates. Just minutes later, I had photos of my California driver’s license laying on a rug. I made a British passport too.After I made a couple of fake IDs with OnlyFake, I put them to the test. I successfully signed up for an account on OKX, a cryptocurrency exchange, using my fictitious ID. Former OKX employees later told me my test triggered a wave of changes inside the cryptocurrency exchange, who scrambled to make its systems more resilient to AI-generated IDs. (OKX did not respond to a request for comment for this story.)While reporting that initial article, Abhishek Mathew, a cybersecurity researcher who followed the site’s growth, told me criminals were using OnlyFake to make bank accounts, or to unban their cryptocurrency accounts on Binance when asked for identification. At the time, I messaged the administrator of OnlyFake, who went by the handle John Wick. Only now do I know that to be Nazarenko. Nazarenko, by then living at an apartment in Poland, said the generated photos could be used to bypass verification on all sorts of other sites, including Airbnb, Coinbase, and Revolut. Nazarenko also said, unconvincingly, “using our site for the purpose of forging documents is prohibited.”At the time, the article received a lot of attention from researchers in the fraud world, and the public saw for the first just how AI could supercharge the creation of fake IDs. With the article spreading, Nazarenko panicked. He deleted all of his personal emails, destroyed his laptop, and bought a new phone. He thought authorities would arrest him that very same day. Nazarenko also made an announcement on the OnlyFake Telegram channel to his customers, and anyone else who might have taken a sudden interest in the site: “The news says that our generator was used to forge documents. This is complete nonsense. This has never happened before. At a minimum, because it cannot be used to forge documents.”Charitably, perhaps Nazarenko was positing a deeply philosophical point about truth and reality: how can these documents be forgeries if the documents don’t actually exist? Really, he was covering his ass, fully aware he was offering a service that enabled criminals, and had been for years. “At the time I hid behind ‘the client decides how to use it.’ That's a convenient thing to tell yourself so you don’t have to look at the real picture,” Nazarenko told me later. He knew that the documents he was creating could be used by someone to drain another person’s account, or launder money, or hide who they really were while doing all sorts of damage, he said. After the article came out, the DDoS attacks against OnlyFake increased, Nazarenko said. He also received word that some very powerful people were taking advantage of his site.On February 26, 2024, the United Nations wrote a letter to OnlyFake. It was on official UN letterhead, but OnlyFake, being a criminal enterprise, did not have a public office. So the UN sent a PDF of the letter to OnlyFake’s email account listed on the site.“Dear Sir/Madam,” the letter, obviously not knowing who actually ran OnlyFake, started. “The Panel has received information that DPRK IT workers have utilized your service.”The letter said that North Koreans had been using OnlyFakes to apply for remote work in the U.S.As has been widely documented, thousands of North Koreans working for the regime got remote work jobs with U.S. companies, especially during the pandemic, and funnelled their wages back to North Korea to fund its nuclear weapon program. The UN letter said some of these workers were using OnlyFake to make fake IDs to sign up for freelance job sites, social media networks, and payment platforms. Alongside the country’s huge hacking campaigns against cryptocurrency exchanges, it was an ingenious way for North Korea to make more money.The UN said it had information showing DPRK IT workers used OnlyFake to generate fake passports and driver’s licenses. Now, the UN wanted Nazarenko to hand over a ton of user data: a list of DPRK IT workers who had used OnlyFake; copies of all the documents OnlyFake had made for the DPRK; and what steps, if any, OnlyFake had taken to stop DPRK workers from using the site. (North Korean hackers recently stole $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is widely seen as one of the biggest hacks ever.)The letter also addressed PassportCloud, a website that sold Photoshop templates of fake IDs and utility bills, and said North Koreans had used it to make fake bank statements and credit cards. I originally found OnlyFake after I first discovered PassportCloud and the sites appeared to be connected (one clue: it also used John Wick in its marketing). I asked Nazarenko multiple times if he was behind Passport Cloud too, but he never directly confirmed nor denied his involvement.The UN demand was surreal to Nazarenko. He said he felt like he had only recently been working on a relatively small project. Now the UN was contacting him about how North Korean moles were probably using his service. He refused to give the UN anything, but looking back later, he said this is one of the first moments he realized he was in over his head. And for Nazarekno, it was about to get worse. A deeper threat was watching the growth of OnlyFake too: the FBI.In May 2024, a few months after I published my article, a law enforcement agent working with prosecutors in the Southern District of New York went undercover. First, they bought a fake New York state identification card from OnlyFake, according to court records. Then they bought a fake U.S. passport card. Just over a week later, they purchased a New York state driver’s license and a U.S. passport. A couple of days later, they bought a fake Social Security card. OnlyFake, of course, happily provided all of these. OnlyFake’s customer support also told an undercover agent how best to use the fake IDs to circumvent KYC at cryptocurrency exchanges.For someone who made a living protecting the identities of other criminals, Nazarenko had been very sloppy with his own security. When making the site and cashing out its proceeds, he sent Bitcoin to a cryptocurrency exchange account in his own name. Despite being a forger, he hadn’t bothered to make another identity.It was trivial for authorities to identify who ran OnlyFake. Ukrainian authorities searched his parents’ house, Nazarenko said. Then on June 13, 2025, when Nazarenko flew to Bucharest, Romania, with his girlfriend for a friend’s birthday, the border officer took Nazarenko’s passport and spent an unusually long time looking at his computer. While being questioned in another room, authorities told Nazarenko there was a U.S. warrant out for his arrest. He was handcuffed, and for Nazarenko, everything “suddenly became very real.” Authorities seized some of OnlyFake’s servers too, Nazarenko said.He spent three months in a Romanian prison before being extradited to New York. In Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center, prison officials transferred Nazarenko to another part of the facility when gang members assaulted him, according to a letter his lawyer later submitted in court. “I was building something that could be used to harm people, and I was making money from it. I did not fully understand that until I was sitting inside a concrete cell,” Nazarenko said.Igor Litvak, Nazarenko’s lawyer, said Nazarenko offered to cooperate with the authorities, including providing potential customers’ information. Litvak said he even showed the UN’s letter to the FBI, which indicated the sort of person who used this platform. But prosecutors didn’t take Nazarenko up on his offer. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Southern District of New York acknowledged a request for comment but did not respond to an email asking why authorities didn’t enter a cooperation arrangement with Nazarenko.This June, around a year after his initial arrest, a judge sentenced Nazarenko to time served of 12 months, a remarkably light sentence compared to the maximum penalty of 15 years in prison. Perhaps this was due in part to the fact that authorities did not identify any specific victims of OnlyFake — only that the site existed and it was used to make IDs. For much of his time in prison, OnlyFake continued to be up and running, just with its owner locked away, Litvak said.That wasn’t the end of Nazarenko’s time in detention, though. As he prepared to leave the court room, thinking his lawyer would immediately drive him to the airport so he could self-deport, ICE officials detained Nazarenko. He spent another two months in detention. “It was much, MUCH worse than prison,” Nazarenko said, referring to having to sleep on the floor and people dying in the facility.On August 17, Nazarenko was deported along with several other Ukrainians on a chartered flight. When he finally walked out of the airport in Poland, then was taken by land to Ukraine, he had only what he was holding. “Everything’s gone, and I’m still here,” he remembered thinking. Nazarenko said he was then taken to a military enlistment office and drafted for the war. He says he escaped, left Ukraine on foot, and then flew eventually to Thailand. OnlyFake spawned a bunch of copycat sites. The FBI targeted at least one and some of them have already shut down, but more keep springing up. In some ways, criminals don’t even need an underground site to make fake IDs. Researchers have used commercial AI chatbots to make photos of people holding up identity documents, although the main labs continue to put safeguards around their tech. And companies have bolstered their defenses against at least some AI-generated fake IDs, including those from OnlyFake during its lifespan, meaning they can detect signs the ID is fake even if it looks real to a person.Now Nazarenko is working on an app, called TapMap, a social network and event finding app that his lawyer brought up as evidence that Nazarenko won’t go into crime again. “For the first time in a long while, I had something I wanted a clear head for,” Nazarenko told me, referring to making the app and stopping drinking.Nazarenko first sent me an email on August 21, just a few days after he was deported. When I asked him to send something to help verify he was the real Yuriy Nazarenko, he sent me a photo of his passport.I used an online tool to figure out whether this was a genuine photo of his passport, or whether any part of it was AI-generated. Those tools said there was no evidence of AI manipulation.

item.title: The World is Flat
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: I was recently visiting Harvard Square, where I was looking forward to showing my daughter around. But it quickly became clear that she would be the one giving me the tour (even though she had never been there before). Between social media and the ubiquity of chains, she knew all the places where we should look, eat, and drink, and thanks to her superior GPS skills, I ended up following her from place to place. My daughter had never been to this specific neighborhood. But she had definitely been there and done that. While standing on some street in some city, the Dutch Australian data scientist Lauren Leek explained the feeling: “What we see in front of us used to be culturally diverse. Now it is culturally generic. Most of what we see is the big chains we see everywhere. It creates a sense of placelessness. We could be anywhere.” (Gift Article): Why Does Culture Feel So Monotonous? A Walking Tour Reveals the Math. “Leek recently posted a Substack article, with the headline ‘Temperature Zero for Culture: Why Everything Is Starting to Look the Same,’ that analyzed the ‘flattening’ effect that predictive algorithms have had on music, movies, hospitality and almost every aspect of today’s consumer culture … Taking 640 shopping streets in London as a test case, Leek used advanced data-analysis tools to examine how predictive algorithms have helped create what she calls a homogeneous ‘monoculture’ in which, she writes in her Substack post, ‘we lose the ability to tell the difference between what people wanted and what the system made easy to want.'” (I’m thinking of taking my daughter back to the street where I grew up. I could use a tour guide.)The heart wants what the heart wants. And it wanted something very different deep in the heart of Texas. The adage that everything is bigger in Texas definitely held up during Tuesday’s election, when an epic blue wave swept across the state and proved (in a shocking manner) that those who assumed that Texas would be forever red were all hat and no cattle. Consider that James Talarico “got 4,397,474 votes in early voting—more than the 4,249,373 votes that his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General James Paxton, received overall.” From Rachel Monroe in : The Night That Texas’s Seemingly Unchangeable Republican Identity Vanished. “Last night, I drank tequila and exchanged stunned, giddy texts with friends back home, as it became increasingly clear that something extraordinary was happening. Paxton and Abbott were losing, but so was Dan Patrick, the lieutenant governor, who fought to install the Ten Commandments in every public-school classroom in the state; and Don Huffines, the comptroller, who has equated abortion with murder; and Bo French, the candidate for railroad commissioner, who once asked on X whether Muslims or Jews were a bigger threat to the country. The whole statewide G.O.P. apparatus—men who felt so secure in their power that they had nearly persuaded me to accept their inevitability—was teetering. Before yesterday, Texas had not elected a Democrat to statewide office in thirty-two years; now, nearly every key position will be held by a Democrat.” (I can’t wait to see how the characters on Landman react to all of this.)+ “Elon Musk warned that Talarico would usher in the end of the American experiment. Ted Cruz said that “if Texas falls, everything changes.” Texas has fallen now, in almost every conceivable way. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats are poised to flip all 17 statewide offices that were on the ballot and take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2002. They could net one seat in Congress from a map Republicans just redrew to flip five. Democrats went into Election Day cautiously optimistic. They ended it with the single most shocking set of results, at scale, that I have seen in my lifetime.” Tim Murphy in : The Texas Miracle.“The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing ‘billions of location data points.’ … The Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that law enforcement agencies must obtain a warrant from a judge to obtain location data from telecommunications companies. But the Justice Department has since argued that the principle does not apply to location data that agencies purchase from commercial sources, and Webloc users now include US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, at least two branches of the US military, and more than a dozen American police forces.” (Gift Article): Ads in Popular Apps Give Police a Powerful Tool to Spy on Users.“The Korean government has a K-pop contract template that guarantees the right to education and to physical and mental health. The NewJeans contracts stripped away that language. The contracts banned such behavior as having an ‘insincere attitude,’ entering ‘inappropriate romantic relationships’ or criticizing the record label. The agreements included steep exit clauses and allowed the label to sell NewJeans music after the end of the deal, while slashing payments to the band. And it gave the label the right to use A.I.-generated NewJeans voices indefinitely.” (Gift Article): Secret Deals Reveal K-Pop’s Firm Grip on a Top Girl Group. (Gift Article): “Americans’ vote for candidates and ballot measures to ban or slow data-center development could rein in AI’s rapid growth and become a big business problem for the companies on the edge of technological progress. It also threatens to hobble an AI boom powering the U.S. economy.” (Data center contempt is part of a broader distrust of AI, specifically, and big tech more broadly. Election results aside, tech companies have to address these issues.) Meanwhile, the day after the election, the market soared. The day after that, things turned upside down.+ JD Vance is trying to save someone from the blue wave: JD Vance. “The vice president and 2028 hopeful is desperately trying to evade responsibility for the GOP’s bloodbath this week—by laying all the blame on his boss.” (To establish himself as the GOP frontrunner in 2028, JD Vance has to do two things: One, distance himself from Trump. Two, stop being a charisma-free, hateable, evil, boring, awful in every way, piece of garbage loser who is immediately despised by all who encounter him. It should be interesting to watch.)+ “Speaking at the White House, the first lady expressed hope that the six-day ceasefire around Oleshky would inspire a peace ‘more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,’ before praising the ‘highly cooperative’ Russian and Ukrainian leaders for helping bring about the pause.” Is Melania now in charge of peace talks? Does her husband know? Last we checked, he was back in the ballroom. “Now envision chandeliers all over.”+ “If passed by enough states, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would effectively nullify the Electoral College and, with it, the possibility of a candidate being elected president without winning the popular vote. Since the compact was introduced in 2006, 19 states have passed it, agreeing to assign their electoral votes to whichever candidate wins the national popular vote. That amounts to 222 of the 270 electoral votes that a candidate needs to win the presidential election.” Democrats Win Enough Seats Nationwide to End Electoral College.+ Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for the second time in a week. “Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair’s Helsinki-Rome flight.”+ Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault. The judge told Brand the consequence of the verdicts was a ‘significant custodial term.’ Here’s the latest from The Times.+ “Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week.” Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayor’s race.+ “Even as LIV Golf circled the drain in bankruptcy court, people around the league insisted that it had the means and vision to turn around the troubled outfit. Just last week, two-time major champion Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s most popular player, appeared on a podcast saying he was hopeful it could live forever.” (Or, maybe not.) LIV Golf Is Finished After Last-Ditch Revival Efforts Fail.

item.title: Nisennenmondai
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Nisennenmondai, a Japanese band from Tokyo. Sayaka Himeno (drums), Masako Takada (guitar), and Yuri Zaikawa (bass) were college friends and started the band in 1999. They drew inspiration from noise and krautrock, favoring a longform repetitive, improvisatory style reminiscent of Neu! or Oren Ambarchi. Their 2013 album, , has three tracks, each about 15 minutes long, beginning with guitar loops that cue in the rest of the band; the drum and bass precisely keep time while Takada’s guitar plays freely with mixed effects. from 2009 is rawer, recorded in single takes, with more melodies and a sense of humor. Their albums are glimpses of the energy of their live performances (see YouTube); they recently reunited for a tour after a nine-year hiatus.

item.content:encoded: Whether you stayed up until 3 a.m. watching Steve Kornacki work his magic at the big board or woke up to a lock screen full of frantic all-caps texts, the political map was completely remade overnight. Democrats took both chambers of Congress in a blue tsunami, delivering a broad, sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump. A result this massive brings new faces and a fresh agenda, but it also sets up immediate, high-stakes fights. A newly empowered majority is on a direct collision course with the White House, the legal firewalls will be tested all over again, and the scramble for 2028 is already underway. And Slate will be with you every step of the way.

item.title: How Much Did Polls Underestimate Democrats? A First Measure …
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: A number of you have written in to ask how the polls ended up doing in the 2026 midterms. I think we know that they underestimated Democratic strength. But how much? How consistently? What I’ve assembled below is just a provisional, back-of-the-envelope read. Others will do this more comprehensively, looking across all polls, comparing them with the final certified results and then adding additional fancy numbers stuff. But I wanted to come up with a provisional read.I took 12 Senate races that by the widest measure appeared to be contested. I took the final poll average in each from Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin and I compared them to the current posted results on The New York Times results page. Votes are still being counted, but margins won’t change much. With the poll average and the final result I rounded to the closest whole number before comparing them to find the amount of error or miss.Here’s what I came up with.

item.title: I've got some demands for our new woke overlords
item.content:encoded: Joy. Joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy joy.Can you feel the joy, dear reader? I can. Tuesday night, voters nationwide handed the Democratic Party decisive power in both chambers of Congress. Democrats won in California, as they always do. But they also won in Michigan, and Georgia, and Wisconsin, and Texas. They might even win in Mississippi once all of the ballots are tallied. Mississippi! I didn’t even know they HAD voting in Mississippi! Holy crap! I wanna kiss all of you on the mouth, I’m so happy!Now, what happened Tuesday night doesn’t automatically correct everything that’s happened over the past decade and beyond. You and I will still have to call out the usual suspects whenever the Democratic establishment gives into its eternally timid instincts. Some of those party regulars have already pre-caved. But that’s for another day. Regardless, today is for joy. Today is for you and I to pop bubbly with breakfast and hold our middle fingers aloft at the lame, overweight duck in the White House. Today is a day for celebration.Article continues below this adIn that spirit, I’ve cobbled together a quick to-do list for our new blue majority government. I bring you these demands as a voter, not a political analyst. Do not expect me to outline how I want all of the following things accomplished. That’s not my problem, Democrats. Figuring out the how of things is what I and my fellow taxpayers are paying you to sort out. I never want you to tell me why you do something anymore. Not after we just colonized Texas … emphatically.Like Jon Rosenthal — the Democrat who just kicked a bigoted cowboy’s ass to win a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission — I’m feeling myself this morning. I was a VERY good voter this year, blue Santa Claus. Most of us were. Therefore, you’re gonna have to bring us everything that’s on our wish list, which I’ve written down below in loose priority order. Nothing about Tuesday night will amount to anything as long as President Trump can go running to his lackeys on the bench to overturn any new law he dislikes, to suddenly legalize sexual assault, or to magically bestow upon Trump the power of wingless flight. I am sick to death of SCOTUS being the most actively malevolent political force in this supposedly free country. So first things first: Fix it. Again, the how is your problem, Dems. Not mine. If it means expanding the court to 24 judges, College Football Playoff-style, do it. If it means instituting term limits, so that an allegedly handsy fossil like Clarence Thomas can’t rule over our lives for and counting, do it. Or if it means impeaching evidentially corrupt justices like Thomas and the dreaded Sammy Alito, do that too. Speaking of which … Article continues below this ad You and I have already endured two failed impeachment attempts on President Stands Weird, so I understand why you might groan at anyone who tells you that the third time will be the charm. But America can’t have a functional government if our new woke overlords allow proven criminals to get away with their evildoing. You saw Tuesday night’s returns. That wasn’t voters saying, “Maybe we should go easy on dear old Donald.” That was America screaming, “WE WANT BLOOD.”Because Trump has presided over a still ongoing crime spree at the highest level of government, and the only way to prevent him and future leaders from committing more atrocities is to, you know, prosecute them. All of them. Not just Trump. I want the hammer to also fall on Alito, on Thomas, on Elon, on that zooted-up scumbag Pete Hegseth, and — well, look, it’s a long list and the internet only has so much memory storage. Even with all those shiny new data centers going up, there’s still not enough room for me to name every name. But you get the idea.Article continues below this ad Would you like to know why, on an otherwise lovely night, Californians rejected a tax on the state’s billionaires? Or how the discourse around the Michigan Senate race got sidetracked by Israel, which is not in Michigan? Through the magic of donations, that’s how. Ever since the Supreme Court — there those bastards are again — decided in 2010 that campaign finance restrictions were somehow a violation of free speech, the American political system has been wholly captured by big-money interests, from Israel to Mark Zuckerberg. Last year, a trio of Democrats proposed an amendment to overturn this disastrous SCOTUS decision. If they can get this amendment through with a majority now, it will end the essentially legalized bribery that has poisoned all political parties this century. That might give America the chance to be an actual democracy again. Tell ’em, Peggy Flanagan:I don’t want a kinder, gentler ICE. I don’t want a better-trained ICE. I want ICE, and I want any ICE goons who killed innocent people to be put in the slammer. Again, we can’t move forward as a country if we don’t hold the bad guys accountable. And we know who the bad guys are, because they all have X accounts where they confess on a daily basis. Time to put them out of commission.Article continues below this ad It was an illegal war from the very outset, and it has accomplished less than nothing. So let’s take the war keys away from Trump and give him a Whoozit to play with instead. Listen to how it squeaks, Mister President! They’re saying it’s the greatest toy ever invented! I’m a 50-year-old man, and even wanna get an abortion now. I should have that right! After all, you never know!I’m nursing a theory that Americans actually like monopolies because the board game taught them that monopolies are good. That is incorrect. I’d prefer there be MANY companies to get my news and entertainment from, instead of just one owned by some billionaire’s asshole kid. These monopolies are the reason why I need to take out a home equity loan just to afford my groceries. If Democrats really care about affordability, as they claim, breaking up the big boys is the first step. Their product is crap, it eats up generations’ worth of energy, and it doesn’t make any money! So I don’t wanna hear about how we have to bail out Sam Altman and OpenAI to the tune of literal trillions because we might lose 300 jobs or whatever if they go bust. I’d rather that money be used toward far more promising endeavors, like:Article continues below this ad That includes abortions, and not just boner pills!I wanna ride more choo choo trains!Or pay my ass to stay home and raise these little bastards myself!Article continues below this adMake NFL Sunday Ticket free! That one’s just for me, really.Clean up Washington, D.C.! I mean this in the literal sense. Even if you live far away from the nation’s capital, you’re likely aware of the myriad ways in which Trump has desecrated it. He destroyed the Reflecting Pool. He destroyed the Kennedy Center. He destroyed a local public golf course. He’s destroying whatever portions of the Smithsonian he finds distasteful. And, of course, he’s bulldozed the East Wing of the White House in order to build a ballroom/war bunker/casino/Best Buy outlet. Just as you and I are represented by the people working in D.C., we’re also represented by the physical landscape of D.C. itself: the buildings, the museums, the monuments … all of it. The ruined D.C. that Trump is currently attempting to remodel in his bloated image is emblematic of the widespread damage he’s wrought on the nation itself. So please Democrats, give D.C. back to the American people. And don’t let Trump build that f—king arch. This is a celebration, and he’s not invited.

item.title: The Extraordinary Power of an Ordinary Act
item.author: bounce_ffd21a6f-9bd8-f111-bf5b-000d3a54442e_prod@bounce.myngp.com
item.content:encoded: As an organization with the word “democracy” in its name, yesterday felt particularly special, unrelated to the actual results. It was special because the country did the ordinary extraordinary act of voting in massive numbers, responding with affirmation of the vision of the nation’s founders as “We the People.” After months of warnings about ICE at the polls and National Guard troops patrolling nearby, after threats of seized ballots and real efforts to challenge ballots in advance of a singe vote, after planning to protect the election officials who make this system work, and after worrying about and planning for all that could go wrong, Americans voted quietly and with dignity. They waited in line with patience, and their individual voices produced a loud response. The political meaning of the results will be parsed for weeks and that is where we defer to the analysis of others. We, instead, see a nonpolitical message that is simple and crucial, no matter your political leanings. We see an electorate that said no to cruelty, no to hooded and disguised federal employees aggressively patrolling their streets and harming individuals, no to deplorable and inhumane detention conditions, and no to the deportation of their long-time friends, neighbors, classmates, and workers within their communities. We see an electorate that said it was tired of the grifting, the shouting, and the retribution. Most importantly, we see an electorate that is begging for kindness and decency. We see an electorate that waited for its moment to say clearly that it wanted – no, needed – respect for themselves and for each other. To us, that is how to explain results that represent America far more than a political ideology. These new government leaders will include people from all walks of life – men and women from vastly different economic backgrounds, religions, ethnicities, family configurations, ages, and personal beliefs. There remains much work ahead. But today is a day to feel gratitude for an election that served as a fitting end-of-year tribute to the signing of the Declaration of Independence 250 years ago. The people met the vision and for that we should all be grateful. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.Lawyers Defending American Democracy

item.title: Colom Looking More and More Likely In Mississippi
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: As I mentioned last night, the data analysts I trust think Scott Colom is more likely than not to win the Mississippi Senate race. A short time ago I noticed that DecisionDeskHQ has more votes reported than most reporting sites which mostly use the data feed provided by the AP. DDHQ is a several year old upstart elections service which has aimed to compete with AP’s data service. They’re legit. They provide data to RCP and many other sites, but not as many as the AP. I’d still like to see these numbers confirmed by another source. But I’m pretty sure they’re real. They now show Colom opening up a lead of 1,864 votes. Add to this that the remaining votes appear to be in Colom-friendly areas. We can’t be sure of the outcome yet. But his odds look good.

item.title: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors.Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes."These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for , told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.American voters in the communities where they’re being built They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 million of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

item.title: Jon Ossoff’s not-so-secret weapon against JD Vance and Marco Rubio
item.content:encoded: For more than a year, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan had been trying — and largely failing — to raise awareness about the very strange story of Donald Trump and his aide Natalie Harp. Shortly after the 2024 election, the New York Times journalists published a profile of the lithe blonde in her early 30s, complete with photos of her gazing at Trump adoringly, explaining how she left him love letters with language like, “You are all that matters to me.” On Aug. 16, Haberman was still trying to raise the issue during an appearance on MS NOW, describing Harp as Trump’s “human binky.”But in the end, it was Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who woke up much of the public to this disturbing relationship by mentioning Harp on the campaign trail. “The defensive reaction from the White House was so over-the-top that it backfired, drawing more attention to the relationship. But a mystery remained. Haberman, Swan and many others had been talking about Harp, but it wasn’t until Ossoff said something that the White House truly lost their minds. The reaction likely had little to do with Ossoff’s comments, as elegantly as they were constructed. No, this recoil was more about the messenger than the message. At 39, Ossoff isn’t just young. He is strikingly handsome. The boyish good looks of his early career have matured into something closer to the old-fashioned allure of a 1960s-era movie star, such as Gregory Peck or Warren Beatty. Broad-chested, with great hair and a winning smile, Ossoff has a cool demeanor, good sense of humor and moral seriousness in a proportion that’s rare in politics — and that hasn’t really been seen since Barack Obama. Ossoff, in other words, can get it.Put another way, Ossoff is everything the 80-year-old president wishes he were, but isn’t. Harp’s presence is a touchy, daily reminder to both Trump and his staff of the president’s thick catalog failings as a human being. Having a young, handsome, talented man mock Trump for his emotional support aide had to have stung with a special precision. No one needs to tell the president or his staff that Ossoff feels just fine about himself — and doesn’t need a full-time emotional support aide to follow him around, praising his every move.Considering how much the White House communications staff is extremely online, they are also likely to know that Ossoff has become quite the thirst trap, even among young women and gay men who otherwise aren’t especially political on social media. As Grace Panetta of The 19th recently explained, the senator is a reliable, if unwitting, model for light-hearted crush content, much like what creators generate in tribute to movie stars like Timothée Chalamet or Tom Holland. “Take a scroll through Instagram and TikTok, and you’ll see fan edit-style videos of Ossoff Ossoff’s sex appeal doesn’t just offer a striking contrast with Trump’s oversized suits and comical combover. He’s also very different than men in the Republican ranks who are closer to his own age and, like himself, are widely seen as potential 2028 presidential candidates. At 42, Vice President JD Vance is also the subject a lot of online content. But most of it portrays him in a comically unflattering manner, with tiny dead eyes, oversized cheeks and a maniacal grin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, 55, isn’t mocked for his looks, but he is often portrayed as a sad sack, a man too slow-witted and spineless to be much use beyond his role as Trump’s patsy. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, 46, is blessed with good looks that even three breakfast gin-and-tonics can’t take away. But with the help of Colin Jost on “Saturday Night Live,” he is mostly viewed like an overgrown frat boy crushing beer cans on his forehead. None come even close to the dreamboat treatment Ossoff receives. This disparate treatment is especially amusing because the MAGA movement has insisted for years that they are bringing back a more virile masculinity — supposedly to cure all the allegedly poisonous feminism inflicted upon America by those WNBA-loving Democrats. No doubt there are some people impressed by all the workout videos posted by MAGA leaders, though that audience probably doesn’t have much crossover with people who get second dates. But what all the chest-thumping and push-up contests of the right really communicates is overcompensation rather than reclaiming some “lost” masculinity.Beneath the right’s meltdown over Ossoff’s relatively tame comment about Harp was a molten layer of male insecurity. Steven Cheung, the volatile White House communications director, tweeted, “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.” White House spokesman David Ingle called the senator a “cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid.” Both unwisely lobbed these insults from X accounts featuring photos of themselves. The handy comparison left the observer to contemplate how, with MAGA, it’s typically true that every accusation is itself a confession. Similarly, Trump compared Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman, a reference to a film that is older than the senator and only served to underscore how old and out of touch the president is. MAGA’s belief that masculinity is on the decline is more a reflection of their personal fears and resentments than an accurate picture of the world. Men who can just act normal continue to do fine, or as much as one can in this economy. As with many of the thirst-trap Democrats that are rising stars, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate hopeful Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a large part of Ossoff’s charm is that he possesses an easy masculinity, one comfortable with women’s equality. MAGA influencers may deny it, but men who actually like and respect women tend to be more attractive to women and gay men.Being chill with women’s power projects confidence. Insecure men are the ones who demand that women are forced into subservient roles, just so men can feel bigger. It speaks to an internal belief that they can’t win without cheating. That’s loser energy, not the Big Dictionary Energy being given off by Ossoff and this new crop of young, vigorous Democratic men.

item.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed
item.content:encoded: I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotels. Elevator banks. Free continental breakfast. A sad gym on the third floor where one treadmill is always busted. You know the kind of hotel I mean. The Phoenix, which opened in the 1980s at the influence of legendary rock promoter Bill Graham, is not that kind of hotel. This was a place dreamed up to serve real-deal rock stars, and to make anyone else staying there feel like part of the greater entourage.Article continues below this adAnd until early this year, it was all set to die young, as so many of its more famous guests had, Kurt Cobain chief among them. Late in 2025, b. Patisserie co-owner Michel Suas was readying to take over the Phoenix’s lot and close down the hotel permanently, presumably using the land to build some kind of overpriced but good boulangerie. But at the last second, Suas had a change of heart! HONH HONH HONH! Enter local hotelier Binoy Patel, who took the reins of the property and is keeping the hotel open. That’s right, like a phoenix rising from the ashes. You read my mind to the letter.Given this fortuitous stay of execution, my SFGATE bosses thought that I should stay at the Phoenix during my annual “Drew comes to the Bay Area for a weekand eatsway too much” trip two months ago. As a Marylander, I was ignorant to the Phoenix’s charms before booking my room. It is now my favorite hotel in the city, and if new owner Patel messes with so much as a single AC outlet in the place, he and I will have words.I didn’t expect to love the Phoenix as much as I did, certainly not at first glance. No one stays in the Tenderloin for the Tenderloin. You stay in this part of town because you have some work engagement nearby. That’s why hotelier Chip Conley founded the hotel in the first place; it was close to venues where Graham booked gigs for headline acts. Otherwise, the place is located on a nondescript, run-down stretch of Eddy Street that’s a relative desert. The hotel itself is a refurbished roadside motel, the kind of place I’d normally expect to be murdered in. The only thing shielding your room door from the rest of the world is a red iron gate to the street next to the hotel office. So my first thought before ringing the front office door was, “This place better not suck.”Article continues below this adI was buzzed by a clerk who bore more than passing resemblance to Sweetums the Muppet: a bulky, tatted-up fellow with long scraggy hair and the beard to match. Sweetums could have been the bouncer at a Hells Angels bar if he wasn’t such a sweetheart. Instead, he manned the front desk at the Phoenix and warmly offered me a number of vital pointers. I needed to use my key card at the red gate anytime I came or went, there was always free coffee in the front office if I needed it, and logging onto the hotel’s Wi-Fi required him to perform a live demo for me.“I can’t do it the usual way?” I asked Sweetums.“Doing it the usual way here is s—t,” he told me. But doing it his way worked like a charm.Article continues below this adI walked into a concrete courtyard loosely festooned with palm trees, potted succulents, and basket chairs surrounding a fat round pool. An outdoor performance stage loomed toward the back. No one was swimming in the pool when I first entered the courtyard; the water was populated exclusively by aging pool noodles, some of which had bite marks in them. But the water looked clean, which is more than you can say for the average Motel 6 pool. I crossed the courtyard to the outdoor staircase leading up to my second floor room. Standing sentry by the staircase was a huge, colorfully tiled sculpture of a frog playing the guitar. Your mother would describe this hotel as “kind of funky,” and she’d be correct.But the ultimate test for this kind of novelty hotel is your room itself. You want a hotel that’s only seedy. I’ve stayed at actual seedy hotels … the kind of hotels where s—t doesn’t work. They are not charming. So my room at the Phoenix would determine which side of the line the hotel fell on.If you’ve read this far, you won’t be surprised to learn that my room was perfect. One side of it was dominated by a floor-to-ceiling window looking out onto the courtyard, just in case any other guests wanted to watch me and a groupie going at it. Seeing as how I’ve been faithfully married for 24 years, the chances of me indulging in that particular rock star fantasy were minimal. But it was nice to know I had the option if I so chose.Article continues below this adAs for the room itself, it had everything I would have wanted from a mainstream hotel room. The bed was comfy. There were multiple charging outlets available to me, many hidden inside of retro furnishings that scanned like film props. And I didn’t need a tutorial from Sweetums on how to operate the shower or the light switches. My only beef was that the soft neon lamp hanging over my bed didn’t work, but I probably wouldn’t have used it for longer than two minutes anyway.This was a goodass hotel room, and it served as a perfect base of operations for me as I spent all week covering assignments in North Beach, Cow Hollow, Marin, Palo Alto, and elsewhere. Anytime I was slogging through my day of field reporting, I knew that my plush room at the Phoenix would be waiting for me. Best of all, when I asked Sweetums if there were any good places for breakfast nearby, he immediately told me to hit Brenda’s French Soul Food, another local institution I had been heretofore unaware of. I went to Brenda’s the following morning and ordered the bananas foster French toast, plus a breakfast sandwich. You know, for balance. I ate so well that brunch, I needed to burn some serious calories afterward.And where better to do that than in the Phoenix pool?Article continues below this adThis was August, mind you. Temperatures in San Francisco that time of year aren’t always conducive to pool days, so I suited up with the mercury hovering around a crisp 65 in the hotel’s courtyard. I fully expected the water to be even colder than that, so imagine my surprise when I jumped off the edge and KERSPLOOSH! Suddenly I was warmer and happier than I’d been all trip. The Phoenix pool isn’t so hot as to feel gross, it’s just well calibrated for a warm swim in a city that wants you to slowly freeze to death. Once in the pool, I knew immediately that leaving the pool would render me a pile of chattering teeth. So I grabbed one of the chewed-up pool noodles and lounged to my big fat heart’s content.I felt no danger from the dirty street outside, nor did I feel embarrassed to be a 49-year-old man, rash guard and all, swimming all by himself in the middle of a random weekday. I know that Sweetums was standing sentry at the front desk, and I knew that I was exactly where I wanted to be: kicking back in the heart of one of the best cities in the world, with not a single worry on my mind. If that’s not the life of a rock star, I don’t know what is.
